### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references) or small-print qualifications appear in the supplied D001 evidence (pp. 13–14). The following embedded qualifications/claims nonetheless carry forecast-relevant implications and must be verified downstream:

- **"Non-core assets defined as non-contributing assets with no intention for development in the next five years"** `[D001, physical PDF p. 13]` — the five-year horizon is a definitional qualifier, not a disposal commitment date. No disposal values, carrying amounts, or expected proceeds are disclosed here; the claim that "proceeds from selling non-core assets will be used to reduce net debt and fund working capital" `[D001, p. 14]` is unquantified. Must be tested against actual disposal note disclosures and cash flow statement.
- **"Strategic target of cash collections covering Group overheads and annual interest expense"** (Memorial Parks pillar) `[D001, p. 13]` — a coverage target with no stated ratio, measurement basis, or current achievement level. Requires verification against Memorial Parks segmental cash generation and Group finance costs.
- **"ROIC in line with Group target"** `[D001, p. 13]` — target value not disclosed in this section; the "ROIC metrics used to bolster economic value" `[D001, p. 14]` is referenced but undefined. WACC/target ROIC must be sourced later.
- **"Manage the relationship between the Group's net debt level in relation to its market capitalisation"** `[D001, p. 13 and p. 14]` — an unusual net-debt-to-market-cap metric (not a conventional covenant ratio). No target level, current level, or market cap reference date is given. This is a strategy statement, not a covenant; must not be conflated with Net Debt/EBITDA covenant tests.
- **"Maximum of five integrated projects of scale in a minimum of two South African provinces"** `[D001, p. 14]` — concentration-risk qualifier; implies project count reduction from current base (base not stated here).
- **Pipeline table qualifications** `[D001, p. 13]`: Fleurhof ">10 (excluding new land parcels)"; BDC ">15" years and "20 000" units; total "> 30 000" units. These are aspirational multi-decade figures, not contracted backlog — must not be treated as order book.
- **"Currently assessments are underway on parcels of land in the non-core asset basket… to be repurposed for a Memorial Park development"** `[D001, p. 14]` — contingent, unquantified; potential reclassification of non-core land carrying values.
- **"Our strongest moat is the experience and ability we have of successfully balancing the initial high infrastructure and building cost with innovative and cost-effective top structure designs"** `[D001, p. 14]` — qualitative margin claim; no gross margin evidence supplied here.

Strategic review and achievements
The 2026 financial year saw the implementation of refined strategic 
priorities centred on four key pillars aimed at driving long-term 
sustainable growth, these include:
1. Sale of non-core assets;
2. Strategic portfolio optimisation and risk diversification;
3. Reduction of net debt in the long term; and
4. Enhancing staff expertise.
Strategic pillar 1: Sale of non-core assets
This strategic pillar focuses on enhancing liquidity and improving 
shareholder returns through the disposal of assets that the Group 
does not intend to develop. This approach supports the focus on 
integrated residential developments, while unlocking value from 
underutilised assets.

--- Section D002 | [AR] physical page 16 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---

assets, with defined short, medium and long-term objectives for the 
portfolio. Organic expansion is underway through the repurposing 
of non-core land parcels from the Residential Property Development 
business for future Memorial Parks. These repurposed land parcels 
were previously earmarked for mid-to-high residential developments. 
Strategic pillar 2: Strategic portfolio optimisation and risk 
diversification
Trade-out of non-core projects

allocation decisions during the current financial year, with capital 
investment being directed towards the non-core project pipeline. 
This pipeline refers to those projects outside of the Group’s large￾scale integrated core portfolio. This resulted in a notable shift in

Core project roll-out
Construction activity within the core integrated developments 
pipeline added to the year’s performance. Within the Belhar

Strategic pillar 3: Reduction of net debt in the long term
Liquidity and cash flow management remain critical to the successful 
execution of the Group’s strategy, with available liquidity of R283 million

debt, borrowings increased during the year to fund infrastructure 
development within the BDC project and support the development and 
hand over of non-core projects. These projects require capital investment 
in order for the units to be brought to a sale ready state. Negotiations 
are ongoing to recover infrastructure spend on the BDC project.

The development of key talent remains a priority to the Group with

The strategic objective of the Residential Property Development

geographic diversification across provinces, currently being the

delivery of value-for-money homes within integrated developments, 
catering to a broad spectrum of market segments, with particular 
emphasis on addressing housing demand in underserved communities. 
Non-Core Developments
In line with this strategy, the current financial year saw meaningful 
progress in the disposal and completion of non-core projects, which 
accounted for 70% of total units handed over, demonstrating the 
business’ commitment to completing these developments within the 
next three to five years. The most meaningful reduction arose from the 
Scottsdene development within the Western Cape, where all units were 
successfully completed and sold during the year. The next phase of 140 
units commenced construction in the second half of the financial year. 
Core Developments
The Residential Property Development business has commenced with 
the BDC project, a landmark development that will grow into the 
anchor project within the development business. This project broke 
ground during the year with the rollout of bulk and link infrastructure, 
including the construction of key arterial and connector roads within 
the precinct. The project is expected to deliver a minimum of 20 000 
housing opportunities across a range of affordable housing typologies, 
strategically located within walking distance of the Marlboro Gautrain 
Station, in close proximity to job opportunities in adjacent Linbro Park 
Industrial Area as well as the Sandton and Waterfall City Central 
Business Districts (“CBDs”). Phase 1 bulk and link infrastructure 
installations are anticipated to be completed by the end of the current 
financial year, after which internal infrastructure development will 
commence over an estimated six-to-eight-month period. The initia

in Belhar for a private investor and the commencement of construction

Western Cape. Within Gauteng, the completion of phase one of the 
mixed typology development in Fleurhof was achieved. This 
development with units selling from R399 000 and where the typology 
mix ranges from bachelor to three-bedroom apartments, has 
demonstrated encouraging demand across product types, with entry￾level units performing particularly well in the current market. 
Revenue for the segment increased marginally to R806 million (2025: 
R800 million), while the gross profit margin declined to 24% (2025: 
27%), reflecting margin pressures experienced during the year while 
trading out non-core projects. Combined revenue decreased to 
R942  million (2025:  R1.1 billion), primarily due to reduced activity 
within joint ventures and the impact of the change in accounting 
treatment of the BDC development from a joint venture to a joint 
operation (refer to the financial commentary below for further detail). 
Bulk and link infrastructure continued to be installed within Fleurhof, 
Belhar and Jabulani, collectively delivering 968 serviced opportunities 
into the pipeline for development in the next financial year.
The business remains committed to exploring opportunities to 
enhance affordability without compromising quality, in line with its 
guiding philosophy of “Building legacies. Changing lives”.

integrity and avoids excess inventory. During the year, construction 
activity was moderated relative to initial expectations, reflecting a

Residential market dynamics and expanding middle￾income demographics 
South Africa’s affordable housing sector remains a key driver of 
residential market activity in 2026, supported by ongoing 
urbanisation, population growth, and sustained demand from low￾to middle-income earners. Similarly, numerous studies show the rise 
of the middle class in South Africa. The middle class is defined by 
varying income thresholds (often between R8 000 and R30 000 per 
month), with education and location being key drivers of this status.
Macroeconomic conditions have shown gradual improvement, with 
a more stable interest rate environment and easing inflation 
providing some support to affordability; however, elevated 
construction costs, increasing municipal charges, and broader cost￾of-living pressures continue to constrain both the business and 
consumers. 
Access to credit remains a critical enabler, with increased lending 
activity – particularly to first-time buyers – supporting demand in the 
entry-level segment. As a result, the affordable housing market 
remains resilient, particularly in key metropolitan regions such as 
Gauteng and the Western Cape, where access to economic 
opportunities continues to underpin housing demand.
Interest rates and the cost of living
The home buyer has experienced a gradual easing of interest rates, 
with the repo rate at 6.75% and the prime rate at 10.25% following 
a late 2025 cut. While inflation has slowed to around 3.5%, the cost 
of living remains high due to rapid increases in essential services, 
particularly electricity and water, which have outpaced general 
inflation. At the time of writing, given the Iran war and the impact on 
the oil price, transport and general cost of living are expected to 
increase. The Group’s countermeasures include the long-term 
development cycle of its projects, enabling it to navigate multiple 
economic cycles, as well as the strategic location of integrated 
developments in close proximity to employment hubs to reduce 
transport costs and commuting time. 

--- Section D002 | [AR] physical page 20 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
Government infrastructure spending and housing initiatives
The South African government continues to address housing demand across the lower to 
middle-income segments through a combination of subsidy programmes, institutional 
reforms under Operation Vulindlela Phase II, and increased collaboration with the private 
sector. Fully subsidised housing under the BNG programme remains focused on low-income 
households, while the FHF programme supports first-time buyers in the gap housing market 
by assisting with deposits and mortgage affordability. In parallel, the expansion of social and 
rental housing aims to provide higher-density accommodation in urban areas closer to work 
and economic opportunities. Recent policy direction has increasingly emphasised public￾private partnerships, the release of state-owned land, and infrastructure-led development to 
accelerate delivery. This commitment to infrastructure investment, with a focus on expanding 
capacity to meet growing demand and rehabilitating existing infrastructure, is evidenced by 
the allocation of over R1 trillion in the 2026 National Budget, to be deployed over the next 
three years. Notwithstanding these interventions, implementation remains constrained by 
fiscal pressures, infrastructure backlogs, and administrative inefficiencies, reinforcing the 
need for sustained private sector participation to meaningfully address the housing backlog. 
Outlook 
The outlook for the Residential Property Development segment remains positive but 
measured, supported by strong demand for affordable housing and a focused strategy on 
large-scale integrated developments. The continued rollout of infrastructure, particularly at 
BDC, is expected to unlock value through phased, demand-aligned delivery.
A disciplined, demand-led construction approach will remain key, ensuring development is 
aligned with sales trends and mitigating the risk of excess stock. The ongoing wind-down of 
non-core projects and targeted land acquisitions will further strengthen the portfolio and 
support long-term growth.
Cost adjustments from current macroeconomic conditions are being closely managed, 
however price escalations may impact overall contract values and ultimate price to market.
Overall, the business is well-positioned to deliver sustainable growth over the medium to long 
term, driven by a strong development pipeline, disciplined execution, and continued 
alignment with the affordable housing segment, which remains the most resilient and scalable 
component of the South African residential property market.

During the year, the Memorial Parks business successfully launched the Rustenburg Memorial Park, expanding its footprint into the North￾West province. The new park has delivered a strong performance, with burial rates and sales volumes exceeding those achieved at 
comparable parks at a similar stage of development. Benefits have been gained from increased brand awareness and few viable burial 
options in Rustenburg, with our entry into the area with a strong product offering being well received. This expansion, together with another 
year of growth in revenue, profit and cash collections, reflects a strong set of financial results for the business. 
The memorial parks industry, inherently linked to the certainties of life, requires not only sound business acumen but also a deep sense of 
empathy and responsibility. Guided by these principles, the Group continues to navigate evolving market dynamics and customer needs, 
ensuring that growth is aligned with its commitment to service excellence.
Revenue increased to R86 million (2025: R68 million) through both increasing market share and the completion of layby sales in the year. 
The business maintains a semi-fixed cost structure and improvements in sales volumes positively impacted the gross profit margin of 
54.90% (2025: 50.90%). 
One strategic objective for this business remains maintaining cash collections to a level that fully covers Group overheads, allowing the 
Group to commence integrated developments of scale with initial lumpy cash flows, the medium-term goal remains the generation of 
sufficient, stable income to also absorb the Group’s financing costs. The long-term objective aims to generate a ROIC in line with the Group 
targets.

Change in accounting treatment of BDC development
During the current financial year, the shareholders of Bankenveld District City Proprietary Limited
finalised an amended shareholders’ agreement, necessitating a reassessment of the accounting
treatment of the investment. Under the previous agreement, the investment was classified as a joint
venture. However, the revised agreement confers in substance rights to the underlying assets and
obligations for liabilities to the shareholders, resulting in the investment being accounted for
prospectively as a joint operation. Accordingly, the Group has proportionately consolidated its share of
the assets, liabilities, income and expenses from the effective date of the change. No adjustments are
required to prior period financial information.

  Dividend policy                                      
  The approved Dividend Policy is to pay dividends annually, calculated at a minimum of 5% of the HEPS.
  Dividends will be declared by the Board post-approval of the annual audited financial statements, with
  all registered shareholders eligible.                
  Dividend declaration                                 
  Notice is hereby given that the Board has approved and declared a final gross cash dividend, consistent
  with the previous financial year, of 8.63703 cents per ordinary share (2025: 8.63703 cents per share)
  from income reserves in respect of the year ended 28 February 2026. The dividend was approved and
  declared on Monday, 18 May 2026. The net cash dividend payable to shareholders subject to dividend
  tax is 6.90962 cents per share (2025: 6.90962 cents per share). The total dividend for the year amounts
  to 8.63703 cents per share (2025: 8.63703 cents per share).
  As of this announcement’s date, the Company has 113 054 050 shares in issue, of which 17 673 449
  are held in treasury. The total dividend payable is R9.76 million (2025: R9.87 million).
                                                       
  The Board has confirmed that the solvency and liquidity test as contemplated by the Companies Act,
  No. 71 of 2008, has been duly considered, applied and satisfied. This is a dividend as defined in the
  Income Tax Act 58, 1962 and is payable from income reserves. The dividend is subject to a South
  African dividend withholding tax rate of 20%, resulting in a net dividend of 6.90962 cents per ordinary
  share, unless the shareholder is exempt from paying dividend tax or is entitled to a reduced rate of
  dividend tax in terms of an applicable double-taxation agreement.
  The income tax number of the Company is 9613501155.

 Where to from here?                                  
 Looking ahead, the Group will continue to execute its strategic pillars, with a clear focus on unlocking
 value and strengthening long-term sustainability. Priority will be given to disposing of non-core assets,
 accelerating the completion of remaining non-core projects, and expanding the Memorial Parks
 footprint to boost recurring cash flows, whilst continuing to deliver serviced opportunities in the core
 pipeline.                                            
                                                      
 Although net debt is expected to increase in the short term to support ongoing development and
 infrastructure investment, the long-term objective remains the reduction of debt through balance sheet
 optimisation and asset realisation. The continued rollout of the BDC project marks a significant step in
 redefining the Group’s integrated housing delivery model, providing a scalable platform for phased,
 demand-led development. At the same time, active management of concentration risk through
 diversification across multiple projects, ensuring that production is balanced across the core project
 portfolio. This approach allows for a mix of milestone-based and point-in-time contracts to be executed
 within a year, enabling effective management of cash flows and enhancing overall financial resilience.
 Collectively, these initiatives position the Group to enhance operational efficiency, improve capital
 allocation, and drive sustainable value creation.    
 Appreciation                                         
 We would like to thank our employees, their families, our clients, and shareholders for your ongoing
 support. Thank you to all members of the management team for remaining dedicated and loyal to the
 Group.                                               
 Additionally, we extend our appreciation to the Chairman and the Non-Executive Board members for
 their continued guidance, wisdom, and support, for which we are genuinely grateful.
 Our commitment to “Building legacies. Changing lives” remains steadfast, entrenched in the DNA of
 Calgro M3, as we continue to address a critical need in the South African marketplace for homes and
 memorial parks.

- **Answer & evidence**: Net debt-to-equity **0.74:1** (2025: 0.65:1), target 0.75:1, covenant threshold 1.5:1 [D002, p. 24]. Borrowings R1,358m; cash R183.7m. Covenant headroom on this ratio ≈ 0.76x of equity. **No interest cover ratio (ICR) covenant disclosed** — flag for D005.

---

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Memorial Parks pipeline footnotes `#` and `*`** [D002, p. 22]: Bloemfontein (`#`) turnover of R582.8m is "anticipated total grave density and turnover once second phase burial rights and outstanding regulatory matters have been approved"; Rustenburg (`*`) R512.6m is "anticipated grave densities and turnover once outstanding regulatory matters have been resolved." **Implication**: ~R1,095m of the R2,157m Memorial Parks pipeline (~51%) is **contingent on regulatory approvals not yet obtained** — the headline R31.8bn combined pipeline is materially overstated relative to secured/approved capacity. Must verify approval status in D005.

- **BDC joint operation reclassification** [D002, p. 23]: Change from joint venture to joint operation, prospectively consolidated, "no adjustments required to prior period financial information." **Implication**: Current-year figures include **R206m asset** brought onto balance sheet not in comparatives [D002, p. 24]; combined revenue fell to R942m (2025: R1.1bn) partly due to this change [D002, p. 18]. Comparability of YoY revenue, JV share of profit (down 44% to R24m), and total assets is impaired — must verify in D005.

- **BDC cost recovery qualification** [D002, p. 24]: "BDC, currently with **no finalised infrastructure cost recovery agreement** in place, requires approximately **R150 million** to finalise the first phase of infrastructure. Once these agreements are finalised the Group will recover the costs incurred to date." **Implication**: R150m additional cash outflow with **no contractual recovery right yet**; recovery is contingent, not secured. This is a material working-capital and impairment risk on the R2.1bn construction contract balance. Must verify in D005.

- **Construction contracts balance composition** [D002, p. 24]: R2.1bn balance (+26%); "investment in both infrastructure and completed units accounts for approximately **50%**" (~R1.05bn). **Implication**: Half the contract asset is capitalised infrastructure/completed stock, not billed WIP — recovery depends on future unit sales and BDC cost recovery. Verify split (contract asset vs inventory) in D005.

- **Net debt-to-equity "regulatory covenant threshold of 1.5:1"** [D002, p. 24]: Wording "regulatory covenant" is unusual — likely a **bank covenant**, not regulatory. Must verify actual covenant definition and ICR covenant in D005.

- **Debt maturity table** [D002, p. 24]: FY2027 R240.5m; FY2028 R395m; FY2029 R450m; FY2030 R210m; FY2031 R62.5m = **R1,358m** (reconciles to closing balance). **Implication**: R240.5m refinancing need in FY2027 — verify refinancing status in D005.

- **Layby default qualification** [D002, p. 22]: "cancellation/default rate on laybys remaining within 5% of the total sign-up value"; revenue recognised only on full collection. Active layby book R59.7m (+29.7%). **Implication**: Conservative recognition supports quality of Memorial Parks revenue, but R59.7m is a contingent future revenue/cash item — verify in D005.

- **"Iran war and oil price"** [D002, p. 19]: Forward-looking cost pressure on transport/cost of living — no quantification. Flag as macro risk for D005 cost assumptions.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote markers `[^e]`, `[^n]`, `[^o]`, `[^i]`, `[^r]`, `[^u]`, `[^t]`, `[^s]`, `[^c]`, `[^l]`, `[^p]`, `[^a]`, `[^m]`, `[^d]`, `[^h]`** appear throughout the D003 p. 27 capitals table (embedded in garbled OCR text within the "Our value creation" column). **The corresponding footnote definitions are NOT present in this section capture.** Per the workflow rule, I will not fabricate their text. A verification question is raised below to locate their definitions in later sections (likely D005 notes or D004).

- **"Margin of 27.20%, above target range of 20% to 25% due to unit mix developed and sold in the year"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 27]` — This is a forward-looking qualification: the margin is above target *because of unit mix*, implying it is not necessarily sustainable. Must verify in D005 whether the 27.20% is Group gross margin or Residential Property Development segment margin, and whether management guides to a normalisation toward 20–25%.

- **"Undeveloped land within inventory to the value of R519.57 million – valued at cost as no revaluations of land is done"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 27]` — Confirms cost model for land; no revaluation uplift. Implication: any non-core land sale "in line with or in excess of book value" `[D003, p. 28]` would generate accounting gains only if proceeds exceed cost. Must verify in D005 whether disposal gains are recognised and at what magnitude.

- **"76% of pipeline serviced (excluding BDC)"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 27]` — The BDC exclusion is a qualification: the R31.8bn pipeline figure excludes BDC. Must verify in D005 the BDC-inclusive pipeline and the definition of "serviced."

- **"Construction contracts investment in the current year R226.4 million"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 27]` — This is a cash outflow figure for construction contract investment; must reconcile to the R2,107m construction contract balance disclosed in D002 and to contract assets/liabilities in D005.

- **"Total available liquidity amounts to R283 million"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 29]` vs **"Available facilities of R268.75 million"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 27]` — Two different liquidity figures. Must verify in D005 which is undrawn facilities vs total liquidity (cash + undrawn), and reconcile the R14.25m difference.

- **"Memorial Parks contributed R103 million to cash receipts to support the funding of Group overheads"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 29]` — Compare to D002's R106.9m VAT-inclusive Memorial Parks revenue. The R103m here appears to be cash receipts (possibly ex-VAT); must verify in D005 the VAT treatment and reconciliation to revenue.

- **"Bankenveld District City development... bulk and link infrastructure expected to be completed in mid-FY28"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 29]` — Forward-looking capex commitment; must verify in D005 the capex phasing and funding source.

- **"The current long-term target is to grow the ROIC to 15% in the next five years"** `[D003, physical PDF p. 29]` — Forward guidance; must verify in D005 the ROIC bridge (current 4% → 15%) and WACC.

- **Risk table (p. 31–32)**: Public sector instability, land invasions, illegal occupations, community unrest, retention of executive management — all flagged as operational risks with no quantified financial exposure. Must verify in D005 whether any of these have crystallised into provisions or impairments.

I am pleased to present the chairperson’s report to Calgro M3 
shareholders and stakeholders for the year ending February 2026. 
Towards the end of the 2025 calendar year, Calgro M3 reported on 
a strategic direction that it would embark on, in an effort to ensure 
sustainability into the future. These #sustainableactions broadly 
include:
Hatla Ntene | Chairperson
I am pleased to report that the sale of non-core assets gained 
traction towards the end of the year, as did the positioning to trade 
out of non-core projects. These are projects which Calgro M3 does 
not have the intention of progressing over the next five years, and 
so readying them for sale makes sense. 
This initiative will leave the Residential Property Development 
business with core projects to focus on, the largest one being the 
BDC project. This has become a core focus of the Group and will be 
part of our story for the next 15 years. Much the same as the 
experience, expertise and commitment that Calgro M3 has shown 
towards the Fleurhof project, which remains an important project to 

--- Section D004 | [AR] physical page 41 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
us and which has grown in stature, size and importance for the 
community it houses – a well-integrated development, close to 
places of work and providing the community with a host of 
amenities.
Turning to the year under review, despite challenging economic 
conditions, the Group commenced infrastructure installation at BDC, 
made progress on units transferred from non-core developments, 
achieved strong organic growth from Memorial Parks through the 
repurposing of Group-owned land parcels (previously earmarked for 
mid-high projects) and progress on our newest memorial park in 
Rustenburg, and retained level 1 B-BBEE accreditation. 
The Group’s revenue increased to R893 million, driven by higher unit 
sales in the non-subsidised categories. This supported a gross 
profit margin of 27%, above the 20% to 25% target, aided by past 
infrastructure costs. Although reducing net debt is a long-term goal, 
borrowings grew to fund the completion of non-core project 
development, infrastructure within BDC, and units to a sale-ready 
state.
Liquidity and cash flow management remain critical to the successful 
execution of the Group’s strategy, with available liquidity of R283 
million at year-end. The Group continues to debt repayments and 
the refinancing of existing facilities to ensure sufficient capital is 
available to support ongoing development activities and execution 
of the strategic priorities as the bedrock to sustainability.
EPS decreased to 167.36 cents (February 2025: 171.72 cents), 
while HEPS decreased to 156.76 cents (February 2025: 171.36 
cents). The Group bought back 1,327,525 shares in the period, the 
full impact of this will be seen in the 2027 financial year.
The combined core development pipeline remains robust, 
comprising approximately 31 874 residential opportunities and 
114 827 burial opportunities. This pipeline reflects projects aligned 
to the Group’s strategic focus and long-term growth objectives and 
provides a combined total pipeline worth R31.8 billion which 
excludes opportunities in non-core project.

What will set Calgro M3 apart and continue to support 
#sustainablegrowth?
I believe it is valuable to spend some time analysing Calgro M3’s capacity to 
sustain growth in the future. This applies to both the Residential Property 
Development business and Memorial Parks, although the latter is a more

because it has carved out a niche within a large area of need in South Africa. 
The same can be said for the Residential Property Development business. 
Our strategic pillars codify what we have done successfully for many years, 
rather than introducing untested ideas, and our vast success at Fleurhof 
and a host of other developments is testament to this. These lessons have 
provided the foundation from which new ideas and learnings have grown, 
and these learnings, along with consistency, have led to growth rather than 
constraints. 
Commitment to governance
Calgro M3 is committed to the highest levels of governance and continues 
to apply the 16 principles of King IV™. Given that King V™ will be applied 
in the new financial year, we have included our performance against the 16 
principles in the ESG report as well as the inclusion of a gap analysis on 
focus areas for the coming year’s update. 
Environment, Social Impact, Governance (“ESG”) reporting

of our ESG Report, contained in this Annual Report on pages 30 to 31, 
contains examples of progress made in areas of importance to us, but for a 
full appreciation of our seriousness across all ESG metrics, it is recommended 
to take a look at the full 2026 ESG Report, which is on the Calgro M3 website. 
We are proud of taking into account the UN Sustainable Development Goals 
(“UN SDGs”) and explaining how we focus on seven that are central to

--- Section D004 | [AR] physical page 42 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
achieving our strategy and five that support it. Greater detail 
on these can be found on page 4 of the 2026 ESG Report.
Annual General Meeting
Our Annual General Meeting (“AGM”) will take place on 
Thursday, 25 June 2026. 
At the AGM held on 25 June 2025, all resolutions were passed 
by the requisite majorities of the Company’s shareholders, 
except for the non-binding advisory votes on the remuneration 
policy and the remuneration implementation report. As the 
non-binding advisory votes did not pass by the requisite 
majorities, engagement with dissenting shareholders was 
undertaken, as is required. Calgro M3 extended an invitation 
to dissenting shareholders to engage with Calgro M3 around 
their reasons for voting against the relevant resolution/s.
Additional information on the process of engagement with 
shareholders can be found in the Remuneration Report on

Board of Directors
The Board operates as a unitary entity consisting of three 
Executive Directors, five Independent Non-Executive Directors

and one Non-Executive Director. The Chairperson of the Board is an

include acting as a sounding Board for the Chairperson, enhancing

Appreciation and outlook
I express my sincere appreciation to the Executive Management 
team, diligent staff, reliable suppliers, dedicated contractors, and 
esteemed fellow Board members for their unwavering commitment 
and tireless efforts in support of Calgro M3. Through exceptional 
teamwork, we made significant progress over the past year. I am 
proud to lead such a talented and committed group of individuals 
who have contributed immensely to the business’s success.
By embracing #sustainablegrowth we continue to support our 
fellow South Africans by tackling the shortfall of housing and burial 
sites in South Africa. We remain confident that Calgro M3 will 
continue to capitalise on this need and ensure continued 
sustainability. This is especially true as we move forward on the 
ground-breaking BDC project. 
The strategic pillars, which form the foundation of the strategy and 
are primarily focused on our largest business, Residential Property 
Development, are all about doing the most value-accretive activities 
even better. The Memorial Parks business delivered another 
excellent result and coupled with brand awareness, marketing, a 
strong pipeline and outstanding products that are in demand, we are 
confident that this segment will continue to provide annuity income 
to the Group.
We look forward to the year ahead, prepared to roll out the pipeline 
and secure #sustainablegrowth for Calgro M3’s stakeholders and 
shareholders.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers or table notes present in this capture.** D004 pp. 41–42 is narrative chairperson's text with no `[^1]`/`*` markers, no tables, and no small-print qualifications. There is therefore no footnote text to unpack or flag as missing in this section.
- **Embedded qualification — "aided by past infrastructure costs"** `[D004, physical PDF p. 41]`: This is the only material qualification in the section. It implies the 27% gross margin beat vs the 20%–25% target is **non-recurring in nature** (legacy low-cost infrastructure already sunk into cost of sales), which is critical for forecasting: the model should not extrapolate 27% forward; it should trend toward the 20%–25% band as legacy infrastructure is consumed. Must be verified against segmental cost-of-sales detail in D005.
- **Embedded qualification — "which excludes opportunities in non-core project"** `[D004, physical PDF p. 41]`: The R31.8bn pipeline is explicitly a **core-only** figure. Any forecast using R31.8bn as total addressable pipeline must add back non-core separately (or treat non-core as disposal-only, not development revenue). Verify against D005 pipeline reconciliation.
- **Embedded qualification — "the full impact of this will be seen in the 2027 financial year"** (re: 1,327,525 share buyback) `[D004, physical PDF p. 41]`: Confirms FY2026 EPS/HEPS are **not** yet reflective of the reduced share count; FY2027 EPS base must be built on the post-buyback weighted average share count. Verify share count in D005.
- **Embedded qualification — "The Group continues to debt repayments and the refinancing of existing facilities"** `[D004, physical PDF p. 41]`: Grammatically garbled but signals active refinancing during the year; no quantum, tenor, or rate disclosed. Must be verified against the debt schedule in D005.
- **Governance qualification — AGM remuneration votes failed** `[D004, physical PDF p. 42]`: Non-binding advisory votes on remuneration policy and implementation report did not pass; dissenting shareholder engagement undertaken. Not a financial driver but a governance flag; verify resolution in Remuneration Report (pp. 40–52) if captured.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

D005 as captured contains **no footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, etc.) and no footnote definitions**. However, several **embedded qualifications and restatements** function as de facto footnotes and materially affect the forecast:

1. **"Restated 2024" and "Restated 2023" column headers** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - Two of the five comparative years are restated. This means the FY2024 and FY2023 figures as originally reported differ from those shown. **The nature and quantum of the restatement are not disclosed in this capture.** This is critical: restatements in a construction/property business typically signal revenue-recognition corrections (IFRS 15), contract-asset/liability reclassification, or prior-period error corrections. **Verification required in D006/D007** — the restatement note must be located and the FY2024/FY2023 deltas quantified before any trend or CAGR is used in the forecast.

2. **"Trade and other payables (2025 reclassification of maintenance liability)"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - An explicit reclassification of a "maintenance liability" in FY2025. The parenthetical is the only disclosure. This affects payables comparability (FY2025 R310.93m vs FY2024 R300.28m) and may indicate a provision (possibly IAS 37) reclassified into payables. **The counterpart line and rand amount of the reclassification are not shown** — must be verified in D006/D007 to avoid double-counting or mis-stating working capital.

3. **Construction contracts line formatting anomaly** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - The row reads "2 107 206 825 1 668 283 132" with the 2025 figure appearing to run into the 2026 column, and the 2024/2023/2022 figures (1,355,384,620 / 1,162,393,952 / 909,322,057) sitting in the 2025/2024/2023 columns. **This is a column-alignment defect in the captured table.** The 2026 figure (R2,107.21m) is corroborated by D002, but the 2025 comparative (R1,668.28m) and the restated 2024 figure must be re-verified against the AFS. Same defect affects the **Borrowings** row ("1 380 291 293 1 105 722 194"). **Do not rely on the 2025/2024 borrowings and construction-contract comparatives until re-verified in D006/D007.**

4. **"Cash generated from operations (14 786 334)"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - A **negative** operating cash generation of R14.79m in FY2026 vs +R107.90m in FY2025 — a **R122.69m swing**. This is the single most consequential number in the section and is presented without any footnote or explanation. Combined with "Net cash utilised in operating activities (99 073 160)", the gap between cash generated from operations (−R14.79m) and net operating cash (−R99.07m) is **R84.29m**, implying ~R84m of interest and/or working-capital/other operating outflows not visible in the summary. **Must be decomposed in D006/D007** (interest paid, tax, working capital).

5. **"Return on invested capital 4%"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - Presented without definition. Given borrowings of R1,380m and equity of ~R1,541m (retained income), invested capital is likely ~R2.9bn; 4% ROIC on that base implies NOPAT ~R116m, which is inconsistent with PBT of R207.60m unless the definition is after-tax and includes a large capital base (construction contracts + inventory + PPE). **The ROIC definition must be obtained in D006/D007** before the 4%→15% bridge can be modelled.

6. **No footnote for the EPS–HEPS gap** `[D005, physical PDF p. 58]`
   - Basic EPS 167.36c vs HEPS 156.76c — a 10.60c gap — is shown with no reconciliation. In a construction/property company this typically comprises impairments, disposal losses, or fair-value movements. **The non-headline items note must be located in D006/D007.**

Independent auditor’s report
Report of the Independent Auditor on the Financial Statements
Opinion
We have audited the consolidated and separate financial statements of 
Calgro M3 Holdings Limited and its subsidiaries (the group and company) set 
out on pages 14 to 88, which comprise the consolidated and separate 
statements of financial position as at 28 February 2026, and the consolidated 
and separate statements of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, 
consolidated and separate statements of changes in equity and consolidated 
and separate statements of cash flows for the year then ended, and notes to 
the consolidated and separate financial statements, including material 
accounting policy information. 
In our opinion, the consolidated and separate financial statements present 
fairly, in all material respects, the consolidated and separate financial position 
of Calgro M3 Holdings Limited and its subsidiaries as at 28 February 2026, 
and its consolidated and separate financial performance and consolidated 
and separate cash flows for the year then ended in accordance with IFRS®
Accounting Standards as issued by the International Accounting Standards 
Board and the requirements of the Companies Act of South Africa.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit in accordance with International Standards on 
Auditing (ISAs). Our responsibilities under those standards are further 
described in the Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Consolidated 
and Separate Financial Statements section of our report. We are independent 
of the group and company in accordance with the Independent Regulatory 
Board for Auditors’ Code of Professional Conduct for Registered Auditors 
(IRBA Code) and other independence requirements applicable to performing 
audits of financial statements in South Africa. We have fulfilled our other 
ethical responsibilities in accordance with the IRBA Code and in accordance 
with other ethical requirements applicable to performing audits in South 
Africa. The IRBA Code is consistent with the corresponding sections of the 
International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants’ International Code of 
Ethics for Professional Accountants (including International Independence 
Standards). We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient 
and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.
In terms of the IRBA Rule on Enhanced Auditor Reporting for the Audit of 
Financial Statements of Public Interest Entities, published in Government 
Gazette No. 49309 dated 15 September 2023 (EAR Rule), we report:
Final Materiality
The scope of our audit was influenced by our applicable materiality. Based on our professional judgement, we determined 
materiality for the financial statements as a whole as follows:
Consolidated and Separate financial statements
Materiality
We have determined the final materialities to be as follows:
` Calgro M3 Holdings Limited: R46 387 850
` Calgro M3 Holdings Company: R6 571 000
Basis for 
determining 
materiality
We used 3% of Total Equity as the basis for final group materiality and 3.5% for the company 
materiality.
Rational for the 
benchmark applied
We have determined that Total Equity is an appropriate quantitative indicator of materiality as 
Total Equity best reflects the financial performance of Calgro M3 Holdings Limited and its 
subsidiaries. The group is capital intensive with a substantial amount of debt and therefore 
equity was the most suitable benchmark. 
Equity has been stable and has shown growth over the past 5 years. It is considered to be the 
most reliable threshold to base materiality on as it does take into consideration the group’s 
high levels of external debt as well as the entity’s recent financial performance.
Group Audit Scope
The group audit scope was determined on indicators such as the contribution from each component to revenue. We have 
subjected all the group entities within the group to full scope audits. The group engagement partner is responsible for all audits 
within the group.
We tailored the scope of our audit in order to perform sufficient work to enable us to provide an opinion on the consolidated 
financial statements as a whole, taking into account the structure of the group, the accounting processes and controls and the 
industry in which the group operates. 
To the Shareholders of Calgro M3 Holdings Limited

Key Audit Matters 
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgement, were of most significance in our audit of the consolidated financial statements of the current period. These matters were addressed in the 
context of our audit of the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not provide a separate opinion on these matters. 
In terms of the EAR Rule, we are required to report the outcome of audit procedures or key observations with respect to the key audit matters and these are included below.
Matter #01
Residential Development Segment – Contract revenue recognised over 
time
Description of 
the key audit 
matter
Refer to the following accounting policies and notes to the consolidated and 
separate financial statements:
` Note 1: Segment information;
` Note 3.4: Significant estimates and judgements;
` Note 9: Construction contracts; and
` Note 23: Revenue.
The Group has significant long-term construction contracts within the “Residential 
Property Development” operating segment.
The Group uses the input method to account for revenue over time. Under this 
method the Group compares the actual costs incurred to date with the forecasted 
cost at completion. 
Project feasibilities, which estimates future contract revenue and costs on a 
project, are prepared by management with the assistance of internal experts, 
consulting engineers and appointed contractors. Internal experts include town 
planners, quantity surveyors and architects.
We have determined the accounting of these long term contracts within the 
Residential property development segment to be a key audit matter, due to the 
extensive effort and high degree of judgement and estimation involved in the 
preparing project feasibilities, the degree of involvement of internal experts in the 
process and the magnitude of the resulting revenue and costs associated with 
these contracts.
Matter #01 Property Development Segment – Contract revenue recognised over time
How we 
addressed the 
key audit matter
In response we performed the following audit procedures:
Contract costs:
1. We tested the occurrence and accuracy of contract costs incurred and 
allocated to projects by testing a sample of these, per the Forvis Mazars Audit 
Methodology, and agreeing the cost to supporting documentation ad 
confirming allocation to the relevant project.
Contract revenue and construction contracts:
1. We evaluated whether the revenue recognition policy applied by the group, 
specifically with regards to timing and identification of performance 
obligations, is in accordance with the requirements of IFRS 15: Revenue from 
Contracts with Customers.
2. Using the Forvis Mazars sampling methodology, we selected a sample of 
contracts within the Residential Property Development operating segment, 
where revenue is recognised over time and performed the following:
a. We agreed cumulative costs incurred to date and billings on the contract 
against current year ledgers and prior year contracts in progress 
calculations.
b. We agreed forecasted costs and revenues used in the contracts in 
progress calculations to project feasibilities.
c. We recalculated the following:
i. Stage of completion (Costs incurred as a percentage of total expected 
costs);
ii. Cumulative and year to date revenue to be recognised (Stage of 
completion x forecasted revenue).
d. Contracts in progress balance – Cumulative revenue to be recognised 
less progress billings to date. We obtained the project feasibilities for 
these projects and performed the following procedures thereon:
i. We confirmed that all casts and calculations were mathematically 
accurate.

--- Section D002 | [AFS] physical page 14 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
Matter #01 Property Development Segment – Contract revenue recognised over time
ii. We obtained a detailed understanding of the contract deliverables, 
the remaining scope of works to be completed, contractors appointed 
as well as project specific risks.
iii. We reviewed the forecast methodology and assumptions applied to 
create the forecast.
iv. We verified the underlying data used in the cost forecast, to the extent 
possible, to supporting documentation which included engineers’ 
reports, supplier agreements (contractors are appointed on a fixed 
cost basis) and progress reports.
v. Based on our understanding of the risks associated with the project, 
we evaluated with reference to industry related data, whether 
reasonable provision for contingent costs was included in project 
feasibilities. The purpose of cost contingencies is to allow for 
unforeseen events, such as changes in design, delays or unexpected 
site conditions that can increase the cost of a project. The percentage 
chosen for the contingency will depend on various factors such as the 
complexity of the project, the level of uncertainty in design, the 
experience of the contractors and the level of risk associated with the 
project.
vi. We evaluated whether forecasted revenue was calculated in 
accordance with the pricing stipulated in the contract, taking into 
account subsidies that can be claimed.
vii. For ongoing projects, we assessed the reasonability of changes in 
forecast costs and revenue from the prior year.
3. In line with the requirements of ISA500, we assessed the competence, 
objectivity and capabilities of internal experts involved in preparing project 
feasibilities (town planners, quantity surveyors and architects) by obtaining 
supporting documents on their qualifications, experience and professional 
memberships.
4. We assessed the adequacy of the disclosures in the financial statements to 
ensure compliance with the requirements of IFRS 15: Revenue from Contracts 
with Customers.

Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the consolidated and separate 
financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and 
to issue an auditor’s report that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, 
but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with ISAs will always detect a material 
misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, 
individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions 
of users taken on the basis of these consolidated and separate financial statements. 
As part of an audit in accordance with ISAs, we exercise professional judgement and maintain 
professional scepticism throughout the audit. We also:
` Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated and separate financial 
statements, whether due to fraud or error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those 
risks, and obtain audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. 
The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting 
from error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the 
override of internal control.
` Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures 
that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the 
effectiveness of the group and company’s internal control.
` Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting

` Plan and perform the group audit to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) or table notes with commentary appear in the supplied D002 evidence. However, several embedded qualifications and auditor-report disclosures carry forecast-relevant implications:

- **Materiality basis (p. 12):** Group final materiality R46,387,850 = 3% of Total Equity → implies Total Equity ≈ **R1,546.3m** (46,387,850 ÷ 0.03). Company materiality R6,571,000 = 3.5% of Company equity → implies Company equity ≈ **R187.7m** (6,571,000 ÷ 0.035). The auditor explicitly cites "substantial amount of debt" and "capital intensive" as the rationale — confirming a leveraged balance sheet where equity, not earnings, is the binding benchmark. *Verification needed: reconcile implied equity to the actual statement of financial position (D003) and equity note (D007).*
- **Key Audit Matter #01 (pp. 13–14):** Revenue over time in the Residential Property Development segment is the sole KAM. Critical embedded facts: (i) input method = costs incurred ÷ forecast cost at completion; (ii) contractors are appointed on a **fixed cost basis** (lump-sum exposure sits with the group's contractors, but feasibility risk sits with management); (iii) forecast revenue includes **subsidies that can be claimed** — a public-sector/subsidy receivable risk; (iv) auditor tested "reasonability of changes in forecast costs and revenue from the prior year" — implying prior-year feasibilities were revised, a margin-restatement red flag; (v) auditor evaluated "whether reasonable provision for contingent costs was included" — i.e., contingency adequacy is a judgement area, not a certainty. *These must be tested against Note 9 (Construction contracts), Note 3.4 (estimates/judgements), Note 23 (Revenue) in D007.*
- **Going concern (p. 15):** Standard ISA wording only; **no material uncertainty paragraph and no emphasis-of-matter** — a clean, unmodified opinion. This is a positive solvency signal but does not substitute for covenant-headroom arithmetic.
- **Audit tenure (p. 15):** Forvis Mazars 4 years — no auditor-change signal.
- **Scope (p. 12):** All group entities subjected to **full-scope audits**; no component-scope limitations disclosed.
- **Cross-reference gap:** Opinion covers "pages 14 to 88" while the Report Map places the AFS from p. 16 — page-label offset to reconcile when reading D003/D004.

- **Maintenance provision reclassification footnote (`%` marker)** `[D003, physical PDF p. 16]`: The note states the Maintenance provision (previously "Maintenance liability – Memorial Parks" within trade and other payables) has been **reclassified to a separate line item** "to better reflect its nature as a provision for future maintenance obligations, rather than a payable." This is a **non-debt cash obligation** that will absorb future cash flows and should be modelled as a recurring maintenance outflow, not a trade payable. Growth from R57.7m to R66.3m (+14.9%) exceeds revenue-implied growth — verify the driver (new parks sold vs discount-rate/unwinding adjustments) in D007.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in the supplied D004 table.** The only small-print qualification is the standard statement: *"The notes on pages 17 to 74 are an integral part of these consolidated financial statements."* [D004, p.16]. This is a **page-label reconciliation flag**: D002 auditor's report referenced "pages 14 to 88" and D003 referenced "pages 17 to 74"; D004 now says "pages 17 to 74." The printed page labels are inconsistent across sections and must be reconciled to physical PDF pages before citing any note (carry Q10 forward). [D002, p.12; D003, p.16; D004, p.16]
- **No segmental split, no order-book/backlog disclosure, no contract asset/liability breakdown, and no onerous-contract provision line appear on the face of D004.** All of these are buried in Notes 9, 23, 24 and the provisions note — none of which are in this capture. The face of the P&L therefore gives **no visibility** into lump-sum vs reimbursable mix, percentage-of-completion catch-ups, or loss-making project provisions. These remain the highest-priority D007 checks.
- **"Other income" jumped to R19.1m from R9.3m (+106%)** with no footnote explanation on the face. This is a material swing (+R9.8m, ~4.7% of PBT) and its nature (subsidy income? insurance recovery? JV fee? government grant?) is unverified — flagged as a new question for Note 25.
- **"Expected credit losses" flipped to a R7.7m credit** (from a R3.7m charge). A credit to the ECL line means prior provisions were released/recovered — this is a **non-cash, non-recurring-quality item** that must be stripped out of underlying operating profit for forecasting. Flagged for Note 28.
- **Finance income R56.1m vs finance costs R43.5m → net finance income of R12.6m** (2025: net income R3.9m). A construction company running net finance *income* is unusual and points to interest earned on JV loans (R387.5m per D003) and/or cash balances — the gross-up (R56m income on a balance sheet with R387.5m JV loans implies ~14% yield, or includes JV interest) must be verified in Notes 29/30 and cross-checked to the JV loan note (Q14). [D004, p.16; D003, p.16]
- **Share of JV profit fell sharply to R24.0m from R42.9m (−44%)** — the single largest driver of the PBT decline (PBT −R4.9m despite revenue +R24.3m). This is the key earnings-quality question: JV profit is equity-accounted (non-cash until dividend) and its halving must be explained (JV completion? margin squeeze? impairment?) in Note 11. [D004, p.16]

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `@` — NCI dividend** [D005, p. 17]: *"Dividends declared are payable to The Calgro M3 Educational Trust, which the Group does not exert control over. The current year dividend declared was Rnil."*
  - Implication: The FY2025 NCI dividend line (R1,560,744 retained-income credit / R1,728,668 NCI debit / net −R167,924) relates to a trust the Group does **not** control — i.e., the "NCI" is effectively a trust holding, not a trading subsidiary minority. FY2026 declared Rnil. This means the NCI balance (R3,248,556) is essentially static/trust-related and should **not** be modelled as a growing minority share of subsidiary profits. Verify in D007 (note 34) whether the trust is consolidated and why.

- **Footnote `#` — JV to joint operation reclassification** [D005, p. 17]: *"Please refer to note 39 for the change in investment in joint venture to investment in joint operation."*
  - Implication: A **R19,252,380 debit directly to retained income** in FY2026 reflects reclassification of a JV investment to a joint operation. This is a material equity movement bypassing P&L. It changes the accounting for that vehicle (proportionate consolidation of assets/liabilities/revenue rather than equity-method single line) — which will affect future revenue, contract assets/liabilities, and debt presentation. **Must be verified in D007 note 39** (which JV, carrying value, any impairment embedded in the R19.25m, and pro-forma effect on segmental revenue/margins).

- **Dividend note (below table)** [D005, p. 17]: *"The Board has approved a dividend on 15 May 2026 of 8.63703 cents per share. In the 2025 financial year the Board approved a dividend of 8.63703 cents per share which was paid in June 2025."*
  - Implication: FY2026 dividend declared in the SOCIE is only **R6,592,427** (vs R10,857,999 in FY2025) — a ~39% cut in cash dividend despite profit only slightly down. The 8.63703 cps rate is unchanged, so the lower rand amount implies a **lower share count** (consistent with buy-back) — but the arithmetic (R6.59m ÷ R0.0863703 ≈ 76.3m shares) does **not** reconcile to the ~95.7m implied weighted average from EPS. This is a **material discrepancy** requiring verification: either the dividend was declared on a different share base, or the EPS share count is wrong, or the dividend was pro-rated. Flag for D007 (note 18 / dividend note) and D004 re-check.

- **"Notes on pages 17 to 74"** [D005, p. 17]: Confirms the notes run to printed page 74 — consistent with the D002/D003 page-label reconciliation question (Q10). No new issue, but reinforces that physical PDF pages ≠ printed page labels.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **"The notes on pages 17 to 74 are an integral part of these consolidated financial statements."** `[D006, p. 18]` — This is a printed-page cross-reference, not a substantive footnote. It confirms the notes run to printed page 74, consistent with the D003/D004/D005 label ("pages 17 to 74"). It does **not** resolve the D002 label ("pages 14 to 88") — Q10 remains open. No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in the supplied cash flow table; therefore no missing-footnote-text flag is triggered for this section.
- **Note references embedded in the table** (not footnotes, but cross-references that must be verified in D007):
  - **Note 32** — "Cash (utilised in)/generated from operations" reconciliation. This is the single most important unread note for cash quality; it will contain the non-cash add-backs (JV profit R24.0m, ECL credit R7.7m, depreciation, working-capital movements) needed for Q30.
  - **Note 33** — "Tax paid" (R3,890,706 vs R2,659,727). Tax paid is low relative to any plausible tax charge; must check against D004 tax expense and D007 Note 31/33 for assessed-loss utilisation or deferred tax.
  - **Note 14** — PPE purchases (R828,063 vs R972,384). Capex is trivially small relative to a construction/materials business — flags possible fleet/plant leasing (IFRS 16) or under-investment; check D007 Note 14 and lease note.
  - **Note 20** — Borrowings: proceeds R566,425,000, capital repayments R297,500,000. Net new debt R268.9m. This is the financing that masks negative operating cash flow. Must reconcile to D003 Note 20 balance and maturity/covenant schedule (Q2/Q13).
  - **Note 18** — Shares bought back R6,662,637 (Q33/Q29).
  - **Note 6** — Cash and cash equivalents at end: R183,722,961 (vs R154,722,535 opening). Must check Note 6 for composition (restricted cash? overdrafts netted?).
- **Qualification implication**: The headline "Net increase in cash and cash equivalents R29,000,426" is entirely driven by R250.5m net financing inflows, offsetting R99.1m operating outflow and R122.4m investing outflow. Any forecast must treat this as **debt-funded liquidity**, not operational cash generation. The absence of a going-concern emphasis paragraph (per D002 clean opinion) must be stress-tested against this cash profile in D007 (covenants, facility headroom).

 1. Segment information                               
    The appointed Chief Operating Decision Maker (“CODM”) within the Calgro M3 Group is the
    Group’s Executive Committee (“Exco”). It is Exco’s responsibility to meet on a regular basis
    (through weekly meetings and more frequently if required) and develop and implement the
    strategy for the Group, set and review budgets, which are approved by the Board of Directors.
    The CODM allocates Group resources to the operating segments and assesses the performance
    of the operating segments.                        
    At Exco meetings, summarised feedback are provided by management of the different operational
    activities within the Group.                      
                                                      
    The CODM manages the Group activities in two distinct segments namely:
                                                      
                                                      
                 Residential                          
                                  Memorial            
                 Property                             
                                    Parks             
                 Development                          
    The operation of the Residential Property Development segment encompasses the following
    product range: The development of integrated housing developments and mid to high income
    housing projects. Integrated housing developments remains the core of the business’s operations
    and comprises affordable housing, Grassroots Affordable People’s homes (“GAP”), First Home
    Finance (“FHF”), rental housing, social housing, Community Residential Units (“CRU”) and
    Breaking New Ground (“BNG”) units. The Group’s customer base includes the government,
    financial institutions and the general public.    
    The Group’s products relating to the Memorial Parks segment consist of burial rights and the
    associated burial and maintenance services.       
    The segmental information provided to Exco for the year ended 28 February 2026 has been
    provided below. The table indicates from where the Group’s revenue has been earned, including
    its joint ventures. The revenue earned by the joint ventures, in their own capacities, have been
    disclosed in note 11.                             
                                                      
    The CODM assesses the performance of the operating segments based on two measurement
    methods, firstly a fully consolidated statement of comprehensive income per segment (including
    the elimination of inter-segmental transactions) and secondly a statement of financial position per
    consolidated segment (transactions between segments have not been eliminated for the
    statement of financial position).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `%` — Maintenance provision reclassification [D005.1, physical PDF p. 19]**
> *"The Maintenance provision has been reclassified from trade and other payables (previously 'Maintenance liability – Memorial Parks') to a separate line item in the current period. This presentation better reflects its nature as a provision for future maintenance obligations, rather than a payable."*

- **Effect on headline numbers**: FY2025 trade and other payables are **restated** to R368,645,305 (from an unstated pre-restatement figure that included the R57,720,206 maintenance liability). FY2026 trade and other payables R263,334,249 therefore compare against a restated base. The apparent **−28.6% YoY fall in payables** (R368.6m → R263.3m) is partly a reclassification artefact, not purely a cash settlement — the true payable movement must be computed excluding the R57.7m carve-out. On a like-for-like basis, payables fell from ~R310.9m (R368.6m − R57.7m) to R263.3m, i.e. **−R47.6m**, not −R105.3m.
- **What must be verified**: (i) the pre-restatement FY2025 payables figure to confirm the carve-out arithmetic; (ii) whether the provision is discounted and at what rate; (iii) whether the provision is treated as debt-like for covenant purposes (it is a long-dated obligation, not a trade payable); (iv) the FY2026 **increase of R8,608,003** in the provision — is this accretion (unwinding of discount, a finance cost) or new maintenance obligations (an operating expense)? This determines whether R8.6m belongs in finance costs or cost of sales.

**Footnote `$` — Borrowings allocation to Memorial Parks [D005.1, physical PDF p. 19]**
> *"The Group allocated borrowings and finance costs to the Memorial Parks segment aligning to the capital injections made into the segment less repayments thereof."*

- **Effect on headline numbers**: FY2025 borrowings were split Residential R1,088,500,524 / Holdings R17,221,670. FY2026 shows **100% Residential (R1,380,291,293)** with Memorial Parks and Holdings nil. The R17.2m Holdings borrowing has been **reallocated into Residential** in the current presentation. This means the Residential borrowing increase of R291,790,769 (+26.8%) is **overstated by R17.2m** relative to a like-for-like comparison; the true Residential increase is ~R274.6m (+25.2%). More importantly, the footnote reveals that **Memorial Parks is funded by internal capital injections, not external debt** — so the segment's R49.0m operating profit and R2.4m finance cost are not comparable to a debt-funded segment. For forecasting, Memorial Parks finance cost is a **notional internal charge**, not a cash interest outflow.
- **What must be verified**: (i) whether the R17.2m reallocation is a genuine refinancing or a presentational reallocation (if the latter, group-level debt is unchanged but segment margins are distorted); (ii) the interest rate applied to the notional Memorial Parks allocation; (iii) whether the "capital injections less repayments" methodology is consistent year-on-year.

**Footnote `*` — Combined revenue definition [D005.1, physical PDF p. 20]**
> *"Combined revenue is the total segment revenue plus the total revenue of joint ventures. The revenue included represents the gross revenue of each joint venture and does not include any inter-Group eliminations. Refer to note 10 for details on revenue attributable to joint ventures."*

- **Effect on headline numbers**: "Combined revenue" of **R1,028,368,369** (FY2026) and **R1,229,096,437** (FY2025) is a **non-IFRS, non-consolidated metric** that grosses up JV revenue without elimination. It is **not** the group's IFRS revenue (R893,174,205). The FY2026 combined revenue fell **−16.3%** vs IFRS revenue **+2.8%** — the divergence is entirely the JV revenue collapse (R360.2m → R135.2m, −62.5%). Any forecast built on "combined revenue" would materially overstate the group's economic activity and would double-count JV revenue that is already captured in "share of profit of joint ventures" (R24.0m) on an equity-accounted basis.
- **What must be verified**: (i) Note 10 — the exact JV revenue attributable to the group (equity-accounted share) vs the gross JV revenue shown here; (ii) whether any JV revenue is already included in the R806.9m Residential segment revenue (potential double-count); (iii) the inter-Group eliminations that are explicitly excluded.

**Unmarked but material qualification — "transactions between segments have not been eliminated for the statement of financial position" [D005.1, physical PDF p. 18]**
- **Effect on headline numbers**: The segment **balance sheet** totals (R3,690,857,834 assets; R2,119,679,186 liabilities) are **gross of inter-segment balances** and therefore **do not reconcile to the consolidated statement of financial position**. The segment income statement, by contrast, *does* eliminate inter-segmental transactions. This asymmetry means segment asset/liability figures cannot be summed to group totals without adjustment, and segment-level leverage ratios (e.g. Residential borrowings ÷ Residential assets) are distorted by inter-segment funding.
- **What must be verified**: the inter-segment elimination amount (likely the R387.5m JV loans and inter-company funding between Residential and Holdings) to reconcile segment totals to D002 consolidated totals.

**Unmarked but material qualification — "including the elimination of inter-segmental transactions" for income statement [D005.1, physical PDF p. 18]**
- Confirms the segment income statement is on a **consolidated-eliminated basis**, so segment revenues (R806.9m + R86.2m = R893.2m) **do** reconcile to group revenue. This validates the segment margin analysis in Section 1 above.

**Missing footnote text — none identified.** All footnote markers (`%`, `$`, `*`) in this capture have corresponding definitions present. No footnote text is missing from this section.

 2. General information                                 
    Calgro M3 Holdings Limited (“the Company”), its subsidiaries and joint arrangements (together
    “the Group”), specialises in the development of Integrated Residential Developments and the
    development and management of Memorial Parks. The aim is to lead and assist the South African
    property industry to change and adapt traditional social structures, through the delivery of
    sustainable housing solutions and increasing the availability of quality burial sites.
    The Company is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.
                                                        
 3. Material Accounting Policies                        
    3.1 Summary of material accounting policies         
        The most significant accounting policies have been presented as part of the relevant notes
        in these financial statements. The remainder of the accounting policies not relating to a
        specific note is dealt with in the section below. All policies have been consistently applied
        to all the years presented, unless stipulated otherwise in note 3.5.1.
    3.2 Basis of preparation                            
        The Group and Company financial statements have been prepared in accordance with
        IFRS Accounting standards, SA Financial Reporting Requirements, the Companies Act 71
        of 2008 and the JSE Limited Listings Requirements. The financial statements have been
        prepared on the historical cost basis, except as stipulated otherwise in the material
        accounting policies below.                      
    3.3 Operating cycle                                 
        The Calgro M3 Group has a operating cycle in excess of one year for inventories,
        construction contracts and work in progress. A typical integrated development generally
        varies between one and 10 years, depending on the project size and type, which includes
        different typologies and infrastructure requirements. As a result, the order of liquidity
        provides a more reliable and relevant reflection of the nature of the Group’s assets and
        liabilities. Amounts expected to be recovered or settled within 12 months are included in
        the relevant notes to the consolidated and separate annual financial statements.
