         Impact of standards issued and effective         
         Amendments to IAS 21: The effects of changes in foreign exchange rates. The
         amendments clarify when a currency is exchangeable into another currency, and how a
         company estimates a spot rate when a currency lacks exchangeability. The amendments
         had no impact on the Group.                      
     3.6 Basis of consolidation                           
         The consolidated and separate audited annual financial statements incorporate the
         financial statements of the Group and all its subsidiaries. Subsidiaries are entities
         (including structured entities) which are controlled by the Group. The Group has control of
         an entity when it is exposed to or has rights to variable returns from involvement with the
         entity and it has the ability to affect those returns through use of its power over the entity.
         In the case of joint ventures, these entities are equity accounted, and are presented as
         single line items in the statement of comprehensive income and statement of financial
         position (refer to note 10). Transactions and balances with subsidiaries are eliminated
         on consolidation. Consistent accounting policies have been applied across the Group in
         the preparation of the consolidated and separate audited annual financial statements.
         The Group treats transactions with non-controlling interests that do not result in a loss of
         control as equity transactions. Gains or losses on disposals to non-controlling interests
         are also recorded in equity.                     
     3.7 Impairment of non-financial assets               
         The Group assesses at each end of the reporting year whether there is any indication that a
         non-financial asset may be impaired. If any such indication exists, the Group estimates the
         recoverable amount of the asset. Goodwill is tested annually for impairment regardless of
         any indicators of such.                          
                                                          
         If there is any indication that an asset may be impaired, the recoverable amount is
         estimated for the individual asset. If it is not possible to estimate the recoverable amount
         of the individual asset, the recoverable amount of the cash-generating unit to which the
         asset belongs is determined. The recoverable amount of an asset or a cash-generating
         unit is the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use. In assessing
         value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using
         a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of
         money and the risks specific to the asset.       
         If the recoverable amount of an individual non-financial asset is less than its carrying
         amount, the carrying amount of the asset is reduced to its recoverable amount.

--- Section D005.2 | [AFS] physical page 24 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 2,3 ---
                                                      
                                                      
      That reduction is an impairment loss and is recognised directly in profit or loss.
                                                      
      Impairment losses recognised in respect of cash-generating units are allocated first to
      reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill allocated to the units and then to reduce the
      carrying amounts of the other assets in the unit on a pro rata basis.
      When an impairment loss subsequently reverses, the carrying amount of the asset (or
      cash-generating unit) is increased to the revised estimate of its recoverable amount, but
      limited to the carrying amount that would have been determined had no impairment loss
      been recognised for the asset (or cash-generating unit) in prior years. A reversal of an
      impairment loss is recognised immediately in profit or loss. An impairment loss in respect
      of goodwill is not reversed.                    
  3.8 Provisions and contingencies                    
      Provisions are recognised when there is a present legal or constructive obligation as a
      result of a past event for which it is more likely than not that an outflow of resources will
      be required to settle the obligation and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of
      the obligation. The amount of a provision is the present value of the expenditure expected
      to be required to settle the obligation.        
      The Group assesses at the end of each reporting period, whether or not contingent assets
      require disclosure. Probable and contingent liabilities are not recognised but rather
      disclosed in the notes to the financial statements if an outflow of resources is not remote.
      No contingent assets or liabilities existed at year-end.
                                                      
  3.9 Functional and presentation currency            
      Items included in the financial statements of each of the Group’s entities are measured
      using the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates (“the
      functional currency”). The consolidated and separate audited annual financial statements
      are presented in South African Rand, which is the Group’s presentation currency.
  3.10 Financial instruments                          
  3.10.1 Classification and measurement of financial instruments
      Under IFRS 9, on initial recognition, a financial asset is classified as measured at:
      ` Amortised cost;                               
      ` Fair value through other comprehensive income (“FVOCI”); or
      ` Fair value through profit or loss (“FVPL”).   
      The classification of financial assets under IFRS 9 is generally based on the business
      model in which a financial asset is managed and its contractual cash flows characteristics.

--- Section D005.2 | [AFS] physical page 25 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 2,3 ---
                                                        
  3. Material Accounting Policies (continued)           
     3.10 Financial instruments (continued)             
     3.10.1 Classification and measurement of financial instruments (continued)
         Financial assets                               
         At initial recognition, the Group measures a financial asset, except for trade receivables
         which are initially recognised at transaction price under IFRS 15, at its fair value plus, in
         the case of financial asset not at FVPL, transaction cost that are directly attributable to the
         acquisition of the financial asset and it is subsequently measured at amortised cost.
         Financial assets can be measured at amortised cost if the financial asset is held where the
         objective is to hold the financial asset in order to collect contractual cash flows, and the
         contractual terms of the financial asset give rise to cash flows that are solely payments of
         principal and interest on the principal amount outstanding.
                                                        
         All trade receivables, contract assets and loans to joint ventures are held based on the
         objective to collect the contractual cash flows and all contractual terms of these financial
         assets give rise to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest on the
         principal amount outstanding.                  
         The effective interest method is used to determine the amortised cost of the relevant
         financial assets held at amortised cost. Interest income is recognised using the effective
         interest method for all financial assets measured at amortised cost.
         Transaction cost of financial assets carried at FVPL are expensed in profit or loss.
                                                        
         Any gain or loss arising on derecognition is recognised directly in profit or loss and
         presented in other expenses.                   
                                                        
         Financial liabilities                          
         At initial recognition the Group measures a financial liability at fair value less any
         transaction cost capitalised to the financial liability at initial recognition.
         All of the Group’s financial liabilities are classified as “financial liabilities at amortised cost”
         and are therefore subsequently measured at amortised cost.
     3.10.2 Impairment                                  
         The Group assesses on a forward-looking basis the expected credit losses (“ECLs”)
         associated with its financial asset instruments carried at amortised cost. The impairment
         methodology applied depends on whether there has been a significant increase in credit
         risk. The Group considers credit risk to have increased significantly when the outstanding
         balances exceed the expected contractual repayment dates. ECLs are a probability
         weighted estimate of credit losses.            

--- Section D005.2 | [AFS] physical page 25 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 2,3 ---
                                                   
                                                   
    Credit losses are measured as the present value of all cash shortfalls (i.e. the difference
    between the cash flows due to the entity in accordance with the contract and the cash
    flows that the Group expects to receive). ECLs are discounted at the original effective
    interest rate of the financial asset.          
    The Group has three types of financial and contract assets that are subject to the
    expected credit loss model:                    
    ` Loans to joint ventures                      
    ` Contract assets relating to construction contracts
    ` Trade receivables                            
    Due to the trade receivables and contract assets being linked to long-term projects, the
    simplified approach has been applied to determine the lifetime expected credit losses for
    the relevant financial assets. A life time ECL represents the expected credit losses that will
    result from all possible default events over the expected life of a financial asset.
                                                   
    The general expected credit loss model for loans to companies outside of the Group held
    at amortised cost has been applied. There has been no significant increase in the credit
    risk since initial recognition. The Group considers credit risk to have increased significantly
    when the outstanding balances exceed the expected contractual repayment dates. The
    Group considers a financial asset in default when contractual payments are 90 days past
    the contractual repayment dates.               
    The Group takes the following into account when determining the applicable ECL rates for
    financial and contract assets:                 
    ` The probability of each project achieving its budget and probability of misestimating
      the outcome of a project thus having a negative impact on the project results.
    ` The relevant stage of completion of the project. If the project is at a more advanced
      stage of completion the certainty of revenue and cost can more accurately be
      determined which would lower the overall risk of default.
    ` The improvement/decline in the recoverability of the receivable based on historical
      data. If the average number of days between invoice date and receipt date improved,
      the probability of default would be lower.   
    ` If the project has government exposure and relies on subsidies provided by
      government to install the related infrastructure and services required.
    ` The nature of the outstanding debtors at year-end included in each distinct category
      will increase/decrease the value of the expected credit loss allowance.
    ` The impact of a cancellation of a project. The probability of this is higher for a project
      where ground construction has not yet commenced.

**Q24 / Q52 [High] — ECL credit R7.7m: which receivables/contract assets released; sustainability against growing book; public-sector/municipal debtor concentration and aging.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D007 Note 7 / Note 9)`
- **Answer & evidence**: The R7,692,016 net ECL credit decomposes as: trade & other receivables −R6,413,164 (release), contract assets +R4,203,719 (charge), JV loans −R5,482,571 (release) `[D005.2, p.29]`. The trade-receivable release is attributed to (i) settlement of the prior-year "receivables from sale of investment" (2025: R40.9m) and (ii) reassessment of ECL rates plus mix change — **not** to improved collections on the enlarged book `[D005.2, p.29]`. Contract-asset ECL rose in line with the gross balance (R1,092.0m → R1,270.3m) `[D005.2, pp.27–29]`. JV-loan release is driven by the Bankenveld JV→joint-operation deconsolidation, not credit improvement `[D005.2, p.29]`. **Remainder open**: aging buckets, municipal vs national split within the R258,827 government trade-receivable exposure, and whether the Belhar land-sale receivable (flagged as "anticipated to be recovered in the short term") is provided against `[D005.2, p.29]`.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 3.3 Operating cycle (p.22)**: Explicitly states the Group's operating cycle **exceeds one year** for inventories, construction contracts and WIP; integrated developments run **1–10 years**. Consequence: the statement of financial position is presented in **order of liquidity, not current/non-current**. This is a material forecast constraint — "current" asset/liability labels in D002 cannot be read as 12-month buckets, and working-capital cycle assumptions must be modelled over multi-year project horizons. It also means contract assets/liabilities will not self-liquidate within a single forecast year.

- **Note 3.4 Significant estimates and judgements (p.22)**: Confirms the following are judgemental and must be stress-tested in the forecast: ECL on financial assets (Note 3.10.2); **percentage-of-completion method for construction revenue (Note 9 and Note 23)**; **scope of construction agreements (Note 9 and Note 23)**; **assessment of control over subsidiaries, joint arrangements and related entities including trusts (Note 11, Note 34, Note 39)**; inventories (Note 12); PPE (Note 14); goodwill impairment (Note 16); taxation (Note 17/31); performance obligations/transaction price for residential and memorial parks revenue (Note 23); share-based payments (Note 35). The explicit flag on **"scope of construction agreements"** and **"assessment of control … including trusts"** are the two highest-risk judgement areas for forecast reliability — the first drives revenue recognition boundary, the second drives consolidation (and explains the Bankenveld JV→joint-operation reclassification and the NCI trust).

- **Note 3.5.1 / 3.5.2 New standards (pp.23–24)**: IFRS 9/IFRS 7 amendments effective 1 Jan 2026 — **not expected material**. IFRS 18 effective 1 Jan 2027 — **presentation/disclosure only**, retrospective, Company still assessing; will change face-of-P&L categories and require audited management performance measures (relevant to how segmental margins are presented in future years, not to cash flows). IFRS 19 effective 1 Jan 2027 — not material. IAS 21 amendments — no impact. **Forecast implication**: no accounting-policy-driven earnings distortion expected in FY2027; IFRS 18 may reclassify line items but not totals.

- **Note 3.6 Basis of consolidation (p.24)**: Joint ventures are **equity accounted** and presented as single line items (Note 10). Transactions with NCI not resulting in loss of control are **equity transactions**. This confirms the JV profit line in D004 is equity-accounted (non-cash to CFO except dividends), and the NCI movements in D004/D005 are equity, not P&L-operating.

- **Note 3.7 Impairment of non-financial assets (p.24)**: Goodwill tested annually regardless of indicators; impairment reversals permitted for non-goodwill assets but capped at pre-impairment carrying amount. Relevant to the static R159.7m intangibles (Q57) and goodwill (Q18) — no impairment trigger disclosed here.

- **Note 3.8 Provisions and contingencies (p.24) — CRITICAL QUALIFICATION**: States **"No contingent assets or liabilities existed at year-end."** This is a strong, explicit representation. It means: (i) no disclosed performance-bond/guarantee contingent liabilities, (ii) no disclosed litigation/claims contingencies, (iii) no disclosed JV joint-and-several guarantee contingencies. **This must be tested against Note 20 (borrowings security/guarantees), Note 37/38 (commitments/contingencies, if any) and the auditor's report (D001)** — if guarantees or claims exist elsewhere, this statement is contradicted. It also means onerous-contract provisions (IAS 37) would sit in "provisions" (Note 21) rather than contingencies, so Q6 remains open.

- **Note 3.10.1 Financial instruments (p.25)**: All trade receivables, contract assets and JV loans are classified at **amortised cost** on the SPPI basis. All financial liabilities at amortised cost. No FVPL debt. Forecast implication: no fair-value volatility in debt; interest is effective-interest based.

- **Note 3.10.2 Impairment — ECL methodology (pp.25–29) — HIGH-VALUE FOOTNOTE**:
  - **Simplified (lifetime) approach** applied to trade receivables and contract assets; **general (12-month) approach** applied to JV loans, with **no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition** stated `[p.25]`. Default defined as **90 days past contractual repayment** `[p.25]`.
  - ECL drivers explicitly include **"probability of each project achieving its budget and probability of misestimating the outcome of a project"** and **"government exposure and reliance on subsidies"** `[p.25]` — i.e. ECL is partly a proxy for project-margin risk, not pure credit risk.
  - **Three macroeconomic scenarios** applied: Baseline (S0), Stronger near-term recovery (S1), Moderate Recession (S3), using **Moody's** sovereign/municipal recovery rates `[p.26]`. Forecast implication: ECL is scenario-weighted and will move with macro assumptions.
  - **ECL rate table (2026)** `[p.26]`: Government institution exposure **1.19%–1.61%**; Normal business risk **1.19%–6.19%**; Financial institution risk **1.91%**; **Specific exposure 0%–100%**. Local-municipality exposure carries a **higher** rate than national government `[p.26]`. Prior-year rates (2025) were 1.38%–1.61% / 1.38%–6.13% / 1.11% `[p.27]` — government floor rate **fell** from 1.38% to 1.19%, which mechanically contributed to the trade-receivable ECL release (Q24/Q52).
  - **Concentration table (2026)** `[p.27]`: JV loans R401,758,095 (normal business R360,704,747; financial institution R41,053,348; government nil). Contract assets R1,270,275,234 (government R149,370,126; normal business R1,120,905,108; **specific exposure R938,118,972**). Trade receivables R157,327,059 (government R258,827; normal business R157,064,501; financial institution R3,731; **specific exposure R4,099,483**).
  - **Concentration table (2025)** `[p.28]`: JV loans R493,118,681 (government R165,006,545; normal business R314,734,048; financial institution R13,378,088). Contract assets R1,092,024,671 (government R633,123,343; normal business R454,002,996; financial institution R4,898,332; **specific exposure R393,911,487**). Trade receivables R82,292,542 (government R29,194,836; normal business R53,097,706; **specific exposure R24,926,356**).
  - **KEY ANOMALY**: The **specific-exposure bucket within contract assets jumped from R393.9m to R938.1m (+R544.2m)** while the government-institution bucket within contract assets **fell from R633.1m to R149.4m (−R483.7m)** `[pp.27–28]`. This suggests a large reclassification of government-linked contract assets into the individually-assessed "specific" bucket — a material deterioration in assessed recoverability that is **not** reflected in the headline ECL charge (contract-asset ECL rose only R4.2m). This is the single most important forensic flag in this section and must be reconciled to Note 9 and Note 23.
  - **ECL reconciliation (2026)** `[p.29]`: opening R40,301,005; current-year movement **−R7,692,016** (net credit); closing R32,608,989. By class: trade receivables 9,537,498 → 3,124,334 (−6,413,164); contract assets 10,988,850 → 15,192,569 (+4,203,719); JV loans 19,774,657 → 14,292,086 (−5,482,571). Cash nil.
  - **ECL reconciliation (2025)** `[p.30]`: opening R36,648,521; movement +R3,652,484; closing R40,301,005. By class: trade receivables 6,954,733 → 9,537,498 (+2,582,765); contract assets 10,374,304 → 10,988,850 (+614,546); JV loans 19,319,484 → 19,774,657 (+455,173).
  - **Commentary on movements (p.29)**: Trade-receivable release driven by (i) Belhar land-sale receivable "anticipated to be recovered in the short term" and (ii) settlement of prior-year investment-sale receivable (2025: R40.9m) and (iii) ECL rate reassessment. Contract-asset increase driven by **sectional-title units in Fleurhof and Jabulani not yet transferred at year-end** plus **significant infrastructure and internal services work performed** — i.e. the contract-asset build is partly a **transfer-timing** issue (revenue recognised, units not yet registered/handed over), which is a cash-conversion risk, not necessarily a margin risk. JV-loan release driven by **Bankenveld JV→joint-operation reclassification** and a new **Table View Properties** loan.
  - **Prior-year commentary (p.30)**: FY2025 JV-loan increase driven by **R110m increase in Bankenveld loan** (land purchase liability + trading) partly offset by **settlement of Witpoortjie Calgro M3 Development Company loan (2024: R34m)** — this names the Witpoortjie entity referenced in Q25/Q56.

- **Financial liabilities table (p.30)**: Trade & other payables (financial, excl. non-financial) **R214,090,444** (2025: R286,306,157); borrowings **R1,380,291,293** (2025: R1,105,722,194); total **R1,594,381,737** (2025: R1,392,028,351). Note the **R72.2m decline in trade payables** alongside a **R274.6m increase in borrowings** — a possible substitution of supplier credit with debt (working-capital financing shift) that must be tested against Note 19 and Note 32.

No missing-footnote verification question is required for this section.

 4. Risk management                                          
    4.1 Financial risk management                            
        The Group’s activities expose it to a variety of financial risks: market risk (including cash
        flow interest rate risk), credit risk and liquidity risk.
                                                             
        Risk management is carried out by the Executive Committee that identifies and evaluates
        financial risks, in close cooperation with the Group’s Board of Directors that are
        responsible for overall risk management, as well as guidance that cover specific areas,
        such as interest rate risk and credit risk, and investment of excess funds.
        (a) Market risk (cash flow interest rate risk)       
           The Group’s interest rate risk arises mainly from its borrowings (refer to note 20)
           and loans to joint ventures (refer to note 10).   
                                                             
           The interest rate exposure is monitored and managed by the Executive Committee
           and has not been hedged in the current year. The Executive Committee monitors the
           cash flows relating to borrowings, interest-bearing loans, interest-bearing trade
           payables and interest-bearing trade receivables, i.e. interest paid or received, more
           so than the changes in the interest rate. Refer to the statement of cash flows for
           more information on interest paid and interest received.
           The impact on post-tax profit of a 2% shift in the interest rate would be a maximum
           increase/decrease of:                             
                                         2026     2025       
                                                             
           2% increase/(decrease) on finance income on       
           interest-bearing assets    9 082 872 4 846 229    
           2% increase/(decrease) on finance charges on      
           interest-bearing borrowings 19 826 800 15 799 406 
                                                             
           A 2% shift is considered appropriate by management taking into account the current
           economic environment in which the Group operates. 
        (b) Credit risk                                      
           Credit risk consist mainly of contract assets, loans to joint ventures, cash deposits
           and cash equivalents and trade and other receivables (including retention debtors).
           The Group only deposits cash with major banks with a minimum rating of “BB” and
           limits the exposure to any one counter party. Trade and other receivables comprise
           a widespread customer base. Customers include government institutions, private
           sector entities and individuals. Management evaluates credit risk relating to trade
           debtors (excluding trade receivables owing by joint ventures) on an ongoing basis
           taking into account their financial position, past experience and other factors. Credit

--- Section D005.3 | [AFS] physical page 31 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 4 ---
                                                 
                                                 
     risk is limited due to the nature of trade debtors which consist of outstanding draw
     downs from banks and government institutions. In cases where management deems
     the risk level to be unacceptable, payment guarantees or collateral are insisted upon.
     The Group considers its credit risk relating to the loans and trade receivables owing
     by joint ventures on a case by case basis. Any credit risk related to loans to joint
     ventures is mitigated by the fact that management has insight into the financial
     position of the joint ventures as a result of the joint venture relationship.
     For loans to joint ventures, loan receivables, trade and other receivables (including
     retention debtors), and cash and cash equivalents, the maximum exposure to credit
     risk is limited to what is disclosed in the statement of financial position.
                                                 
  (c) Liquidity risk                             
     Prudent liquidity risk management implies maintaining sufficient cash, as well as the
     availability of funding through an adequate amount of committed credit facilities.
     Due to the dynamic nature of the underlying businesses, the Executive Committee
     maintains flexibility in funding by maintaining availability under committed credit
     lines.                                      
                                                 
     The Group manages liquidity risk by monitoring forecasted cash flows.
     The Group strives to match the maturity profile of borrowings with expected cash
     flows from the development projects.        
                                                 
     A specific liquidity risk associated with the Group is the raising of loans at specified
     dates of repayment, against delivery of construction projects that have the same
     maturity profile.                           
     The related cash inflows from these construction projects are, however, uncertain
     and dependent on factors not under the control of the Group.
                                                 
     The financial liabilities to be settled within one year will be funded by cash and cash
     equivalents as well as the realisation of trade and other receivables and construction
     contracts.                                  
     The table below analyses the Group’s financial liabilities into relevant maturity
     groupings based on the remaining years at the reporting year date to the contractual
     maturity date.                              
                                                 
     The amounts disclosed in the table are the contractual undiscounted cash flows
     which include future interest payable. Balances due within 12 months equal their
     carrying balances as the impact of discounting is not significant.

 4. Risk management (continued)                        
    4.2 Capital risk management                        
        The Group’s objectives when managing capital are to safeguard the Group’s ability to
        continue as a going concern in order to provide returns for shareholders and benefits for
        other stakeholders.                            
        The Group monitors capital on the basis of its Net Debt/Equity ratio. The maximum
        allowed Net Debt/Equity ratio for the Group is 1.5:1.
                                                       
         Net Debt/Equity ratio                         
         This ratio is calculated as Net Debt divided by Equity. Net Debt is calculated as total

The Group monitors capital repayments and interest serviceability on the basis of its Debt Service
Cover ratio (DSCR). The minimum allowed DSCR ratio for the Group is 1.2.
Debt Service Cover ratio (DSCR)
This ratio is calculated as available cash flow divided by debt service requirement. Available
cash flow is calculated as cash generated from/(utilised in) operating activities plus new
financial indebtedness incurred plus cash and cash equivalent at the beginning of the year less
the aggregate amount spent on the purchase of property, plant and equipment, purchase of
intangible assets, acquisition of businesses, acquisition of subsidiaries, and loans advanced to
joint ventures for investment purposes (Capex).
Debt service requirement is calculated as interest and fees plus principal repayments.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote on p. 34 — Maintenance provision reclassification** `[D005.3, p. 34]`:
  > "* The Maintenance provision has been reclassified from trade and other payables (previously "Maintenance liability – Memorial Parks") to a separate line item in the current period. This presentation better reflects its nature as a provision for future maintenance obligations, rather than a payable."
  - **What it changes**: The R66,328,209 (2025: R57,720,206) maintenance provision is now shown as a separate current liability rather than buried in trade and other payables. This means the "trade and other payables" figures in the liquidity table (R263,334,249) and the maturity table (R193,529,600) are **not directly comparable** — the maturity table appears to exclude the maintenance provision (R193.5m + R66.3m ≈ R259.8m, close to but not exactly the R263.3m liquidity figure; residual ~R3.5m unexplained). This reclassification also affects the DSCR and liquidity ratio calculations. **Must verify**: Note 21 measurement basis, discount rate, and whether the R8.6m increase is accretion or new obligation.

- **Qualification on p. 32 — "The above amounts will be repaid by utilising cash generated from operations, available cash, working capital facilities and the refinancing of borrowings"** `[D005.3, p. 32]`:
  - **What it changes**: This is a forward-looking funding statement that explicitly relies on **refinancing** of borrowings. Given CFO was **negative R14.8m** in FY2026, the repayment of R224.3m due within 1 year (incl. interest) cannot be met from operations — it depends on refinancing and working-capital facilities. This is a material liquidity risk qualification. **Must verify**: Note 20 refinancing arrangements, committed facility headroom, and covenant compliance.

- **Qualification on p. 31 — "The interest rate exposure ... has not been hedged in the current year"** `[D005.3, p. 31]`:
  - **What it changes**: The Group is fully exposed to interest-rate movements on R1,380.3m of borrowings. The 2% sensitivity shows a **R19.8m post-tax impact on finance charges** (2025: R15.8m) — material relative to operating profit. No hedging means forecast finance costs are highly sensitive to rate assumptions. **Must verify**: Note 20 fixed vs floating split.

- **Qualification on p. 31 — "A 2% shift is considered appropriate by management taking into account the current economic environment"** `[D005.3, p. 31]`:
  - **What it changes**: Management's own sensitivity assumption. The implied interest-bearing borrowings base (~R991.3m) is **lower than gross borrowings of R1,380.3m** — suggesting either a portion is non-interest-bearing, or the sensitivity is computed on a net basis. **Must verify**: Note 20 instrument-level interest rates.

- **Qualification on p. 31 — "Credit risk is limited due to the nature of trade debtors which consist of outstanding draw downs from banks and government institutions"** `[D005.3, p. 31]`:
  - **What it changes**: This is a **management assertion** that credit risk is "limited." Given trade receivables grew +93.0% to R159.6m while revenue grew only +2.8%, and given the prior flag that government exposure fell from R29.2m to R0.26m, this assertion needs testing. **Must verify**: Note 7 aging and ECL provision.

- **Qualification on p. 32 — "Balances due within 12 months equal their carrying balances as the impact of discounting is not significant"** `[D005.3, p. 32]`:
  - **What it changes**: Confirms the <1yr maturity column (R224.3m borrowings, R193.5m payables) approximates carrying value. But the **entire R1,380.3m borrowings balance is classified as current** in the liquidity table `[D005.3, p. 34]` — a direct tension with the maturity table showing only R224.3m due within 1 year. **Must verify**: Note 20 current/non-current split.

- **Note 5 fair value qualification** `[D005.3, p. 34]`:
  > "With the exception of the Group's borrowings and investments, the financial instruments' carrying values approximate their fair values, due to the short-term nature of the instruments."
  - **What it changes**: Borrowings and investments are carried at fair value (or fair value disclosed). The fair-value hierarchy table is **not included in this capture** — the actual Level 1/2/3 classification of investments (R20.7m) and borrowings is missing. **Must verify**: Note 12 / Note 20 fair-value disclosure.

 5. Fair values                                        
    Financial instruments                              
    To determine the fair value of the financial instruments, future contractual cash flows are
    discounted using current market interest rates available to the Group for similar financial
    instruments.                                       
                                                       
    With the exception of the Group’s borrowings and investments, the financial instruments’ carrying
    values approximate their fair values, due to the short-term nature of the instruments.
    These investments (refer to note 12) are accounted for at fair value through profit or loss.
                                                       
    Fair value table                                   
    The table below analyses the valuation levels used to determine the fair values of the applicable
    line items in the statement of financial position. 
    Level no Level definition                          
                                                       
    1.    Quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities
    2.    Inputs other than quoted prices included within level 1 that are observable for the
          asset or liability, either directly (that is, as prices) or indirectly (that is, derived from
          prices)                                      
    3.    Inputs for the asset or liability that are not based on observable market data (that is,
          unobservable inputs)

     The carrying values for loans to and from joint ventures, trade and other receivables and trade and other payables are a reasonable approximation of their fair value. The balances exclude any non-financial
     instruments. Refer to note 3.10 for details on financial instruments.                                    
     Non-financial instruments                                                                                
     The value of investment properties as at 28 February 2026 was determined by management using the Discounted Cash Flow (“DCF”) method. This method takes into account the time value of money
     between the valuation date and the date when the income stream theoretically reverts to prevailing market levels. Properties are valued by discounting the expected future net income for a specific period
     at an appropriate discount rate to give the present value of the expected net income cash flow. The net income is determined taking into account the gross income, vacancies and lease obligations from
     which is deducted all normalised operating expenditure. The fair value increased from R22 492 889 in the prior year to R32 497 786 in the current year. The increase in fair value was driven by changes in
     the assumptions that determines the fair value of the investment property. The changes in these assumptions relate to rental growth, vacancy adjustments and capitalisation rate changes.
     Sensitivity analysis                                                                                     
     Management has assessed the impact of reasonably possible changes in capitalisation rates on the fair value of investment property:
     ` A 5% increase in capitalisation rates would reduce the fair value of the portfolio by approximately R1.4 million.
     ` A 5% decrease in capitalisation rates would increase the fair value of the portfolio by approximately R1.5 million.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 5 — Fair value policy qualification** [D005.4, p.34]: "With the exception of the Group's borrowings and investments, the financial instruments' carrying values approximate their fair values, due to the short-term nature of the instruments." **Implication**: trade receivables (R157.3m), trade payables (R214.1m) and JV loans (R401.8m) are carried at amortised cost assumed ≈ fair value. For JV loans this is a strong assumption given they are Level 3 and long-dated; any credit deterioration would not be captured in fair value. **Verify in Note 10** whether JV loans are short-term/on-demand.

- **Note 5 — Borrowings fair value footnote `*`** [D005.4, p.35]: "Based on quoted prices on the Bond Exchange." **Implication**: Bond Exchange borrowings R393,961,370 are Level 2 and marked to quoted price — a reliable market signal. **Other borrowings R993,735,518 are Level 3** and stated to approximate fair value "when excluding transaction cost amortised" — i.e. the R993.7m is a book figure, not a market figure. **Verify in Note 20** the instrument mix (term loans, overdrafts, leases) and whether any are distressed.

- **Note 5 — Investment property valuation qualification** [D005.4, p.35]: "determined by **management** using the DCF method" — **not an independent valuer**. Increase R22.5m → R32.5m (+R10.0m, +44.5%) driven by "rental growth, vacancy adjustments and capitalisation rate changes." Sensitivity ±5% cap rate → ±R1.4–1.5m. **Implication**: R10.0m of the fair-value gain is management-estimated and flows through P&L (likely in "other income" or fair-value adjustment); it is non-cash and potentially reversible. **Verify in Note 15/Note 25** how the R10.0m gain is presented and whether it is in "other income" (Q23/Q55).

- **Note 5 — Investments footnote `%`** [D005.4, p.35]: "Based on prices for Unit Trusts held by reputable financial institutions containing local equity instruments, bonds and cash." **Implication**: R20.7m FVPL investments are fund-of-fund exposures, Level 3, marked via unit-trust prices — reasonable but not exchange-quoted. **Verify in Note 13** the fair-value movement (R1.47m gain) and whether it is in P&L.

- **Note 7 — Receivable from sale of investment footnote `*`** [D005.4, p.36]: "This relates to the outstanding receivable for the sale of **MS5 Pennyville Proprietary Limited** which accrues interest at **20% on a monthly basis**." **Implication**: R40.9m collected during FY2026 (balance R48,750 remaining). The 20% monthly interest rate is unusually high — likely a default/penalty rate; confirm no interest income still accruing. **Verify in Note 29** finance income for any residual MS5 Pennyville interest.

- **Note 7 — Securing deposits footnote `@`** [D005.4, p.36]: "Deposits paid to secure land for future projects in the prior years." R656,730 unchanged. **Implication**: land-banking deposits; low materiality but confirms land pipeline activity.

- **Note 7 — Related-party receivables qualification** [D005.4, p.36]: "management has insight into the financial position of all joint ventures as at 28 February 2026 and does not believe that there are indicators that these amounts are impaired at year-end. The Group does, however, raise expected credit loss provisions on the receivable balances. These receivables bear interest at market-related rates." **Implication**: R36.8m related-party receivables (mostly South Hills R36.6m) are asserted unimpaired but ECL is still raised — a contradiction worth testing. **Verify in Note 10** South Hills JV financial position and whether the R36.6m receivable is backed by saleable stock.

- **Note 7 — No collateral qualification** [D005.4, p.37]: "The Group does not hold any collateral as security for trade and other receivables." **Implication**: full unsecured credit exposure of R157.3m gross. **Verify in Note 3.10.2** ECL methodology and in Note 20 whether any receivables are pledged.

- **Note 7 — Ageing anomaly** [D005.4, p.37]: "<30 days R112,002,282 (2025: R715,288)" vs "30 days and older R4,802,397 (2025: R30,272,055)." **Implication**: a massive shift from past-due to current — either genuine collection or a reclassification of government/contract balances into "current." The R112.0m "<30 days" figure is implausibly large relative to monthly revenue (~R1.2bn/12 ≈ R100m), suggesting some balances are classified as current by definition rather than by invoice date. **Verify in Note 3.10.2 / Note 9** the definition of "fully performing" and whether contract assets were reclassified into trade receivables.

- **Note 8 — "Balance from joint operations R99,268"** [D005.4, p.37]: new line item, nil prior year. **Implication**: confirms a joint operation was consolidated in FY2026 (consistent with Bankenveld reclassification, Q32/Q69). **Verify in Note 39** the full P&L/balance-sheet effect.

- **Note 8 — Tax payment vs charge** [D005.4, p.37]: payments R3,890,706 vs current-year charge R2,716,478 → net overpayment R1,174,228, closing receivable R1,743,347. **Implication**: cash tax paid exceeds P&L charge — consistent with prior-year underpayment or provisional tax timing. **Verify in Note 31/Note 33** the reconciliation.

 9. Construction contracts                            
     Accounting policy                                
     The accounting policy for construction contracts needs to be read in conjunction with the
     accounting policy for revenue in note 23.        
                                                      
     Construction contracts consist of both contract assets and cost incurred to be allocated to
     future contract assets when the Group enters into an agreement with a customer.
     Future cost to be allocated to contract assets are cost incurred on the development of land
     which includes cost such as direct labour, materials, professional/consulting services,
     commissions and allocation of overhead cost which relate directly to the development of the
     land. These costs are only allocated to the individual units when a contract is entered into with
     a customer to purchase the relevant unit.        
     Contract assets arise on the basis that cost are incurred to satisfying performance obligations,
     the related payment and timing is determined based on each individual contract. These costs
     include costs to fulfil a contract and includes costs such as direct labour, materials,
     professional/consulting services, commissions and allocation of overhead costs which relate
     directly to satisfy performance obligations of the contract. Contract assets are recovered from
     the customer when the relevant performance obligations are completed and payment can be
     obtained from the customer.                      
     If costs are incurred on a contract without a corresponding payment received it is shown as a
     contract asset at the reporting period. If the customer has paid in advance for performance
     obligations to be satisfied it’s shown as a contract liability within trade and other payables
     (refer to note 19).                              
     The Group presents as a liability the gross amount due to customers for contract work for all
     contracts in progress for which progress billings exceed costs incurred plus recognised profits
     (less recognised losses).                        
                                                      
     Costs incurred during the year related to future activity on a contract are excluded from
     contract assets. They are presented as cost incurred to be allocated to future contract assets,
     depending on their nature that will be assessed on a case by case basis.
     The Group presents as an asset the gross amount due from customers for contract work for
     all contracts in progress for which costs incurred plus recognised profits (less recognised
     losses) exceed progress billings. Progress billings that are invoiced but not yet paid by
     customers as well as retentions, if any, are included within “trade and other receivables” (refer
     to note 7).                                      
     The transaction price for each performance obligation is the contractually stipulated price and
     represents the stand-alone selling price at the time when the contract is entered into with
     the customer.

  9. Construction contracts (continued)                 
      Significant estimates and judgements              
      The Group uses the “percentage-of-completion” method (also known as the input method) in
      accounting for its “Over-time” construction contracts where control is transferred to a
      customer over a period of time. Use of the “percentage-of-completion” method requires the
      Group to estimate the construction services and activities performed to date as a proportion
      of the total services and activities to be performed. The Group performs this by comparing
      actual cost incurred on a unit/dwelling/project compared to the forecasted cost of the unit/
      dwelling/project which equates to the percentage of work completed (“percentage of
      completion”). The corresponding percentage of revenue is then recognised in that period.
      The Group allocates non-unit specific cost (future contract costs) which includes land,
      infrastructure, town planning and other project-related cost based on approved feasibilities.
      Estimates are made by management to calculate the forecasted cost of a project which
      includes non-unit specific cost to be allocated to units as and when they are constructed. The
      estimates used are in terms of an approved feasibility study. Refer to note 21 for further
      details on how management forecasts are prepared and approved.
      The Group applies an expected credit loss provision (“ECL”) on the contract asset balances.
      Refer to note 3.10.2 for the relevant method and judgement applied.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `#` — "Development cost for future contract assets" (R852,124,160; 2025: R587,247,311)** `[D005.5, p.38]`
- **What it says**: These are costs incurred in the current year that will only be allocated to contracts with specific performance obligations in the future. They are "a form of inventory but have no related contract with a customer yet due to the long-term nature of property development." They have **no revenue or profit impact** and are **excluded from the input method** when calculating POC. They are **not treated as contract assets on which profit and expected credit losses are recognised**.
- **What it changes**: The headline "Construction contracts" SOFP balance of R2,107,206,825 is **not** a contract asset. Only R1,270,275,234 is a true contract asset (gross of ECL). The R852,124,160 future-cost bucket is effectively land-banking / development WIP inventory sitting inside the construction-contracts line. This has three forecast implications:
  1. **Unbilled revenue days** must be computed on R1,270,275,234, not R2,107m — using the headline would overstate days by ~66%.
  2. **No ECL is recognised** on the R852m — so the R15,192,569 ECL provision covers only the R1,270m contract-asset base (1.20% coverage). If any of the R852m future-cost bucket becomes impaired (e.g., a development is abandoned before a customer contract is signed), there is **no ECL cushion** — it would hit inventory write-down, not contract-asset ECL. This is a hidden impairment exposure.
  3. **Working-capital absorption**: the R852m bucket grew +R264,876,849 year-on-year — the single largest driver of the R439.7m net construction-contract balance increase. This is cash absorbed into land/development WIP with no matching revenue, which explains part of the CFO deterioration (Q48/Q38).
- **Must verify in later sections**: Note 12 (inventories) — is any of the R852m double-counted or cross-referenced? Note 21 (feasibility approvals) — what is the approval status of the developments underpinning the R852m? Note 3.4/Note 21 — impairment testing of future contract-asset costs.

**Footnote cross-reference inconsistency — "Note 18" vs "Note 19"** `[D005.5, pp.37–38]`
- **What it says**: The accounting policy text (p.37) states contract liabilities sit "within trade and other payables (refer to note 19)". The table (p.38) labels excess billings as "Note 18".
- **What it changes**: Minor, but flags a possible renumbering or a genuine split — contract liabilities may be disclosed in Note 18 (trade and other payables) rather than Note 19. Must be resolved when Note 18/19 are read, because the R15,245,364 contract liability needs to be located in the correct payables note for the working-capital reconciliation (Q105/Q88).

**Qualification — "The normal operating cycle for construction contracts is considered to be longer than 12 months"** `[D005.5, p.38]`
- **What it says**: Justifies the current/non-current split of construction contracts (R831,296,364 within 12 months; R1,275,910,461 after 12 months).
- **What it changes**: Confirms that ~60.5% of the construction-contract balance is **not** expected to convert to cash within 12 months. For forecasting, only R831.3m is a near-term cash-conversion source; the R1,275.9m is a multi-year unwind. This materially affects the working-capital release assumption in the forecast — do not assume full conversion in year 1.

**Qualification — "The expected aggregate revenue still to be recognised on the contract asset balance is currently in excess of R2 107 206 825 ... The majority is expected to realise within the next five years"** `[D005.5, p.38]`
- **What it says**: Forward revenue visibility of >R2,107m on the contract-asset balance, majority within 5 years.
- **What it changes**: This is a **backlog-like** disclosure but is **not** a secured order book in the conventional sense — it is the revenue still to be recognised on existing contract assets (i.e., already-contracted units/projects). It is a useful revenue floor but should not be treated as book-to-bill backlog. Note the wording "in excess of" is unquantified — no upper bound given. Also note it is stated on the **gross** R2,107m balance, which includes the R852m future-cost bucket that has "no revenue or profit impact" — so the revenue-still-to-be-recognised figure is arguably inconsistent with the footnote's own statement that the R852m has no revenue impact. Flag as a verification question: is the >R2,107m revenue figure computed on the full R2,107m balance or only the R1,270m contract-asset portion?

**Qualification — "Borrowing costs to the value of R102 143 192 (2025: R63 728 343) have been capitalised (note 30)"** `[D005.5, p.38]`
- **What it says**: R102.1m of borrowing costs capitalised into construction contracts in FY2026, up +60.3% from R63.7m.
- **What it changes**: This is a **material** item. Capitalised interest of R102.1m sits inside the construction-contract balance and is excluded from finance costs in D004. It explains part of the gap between cash finance costs paid (R135.6m) and the P&L finance cost accrual (R43.5m) — Q46/Q50. It also means the true economic cost of the R1,380m borrowings is higher than the P&L finance cost suggests. For forecasting: if capitalisation stops (e.g., developments complete), R102m+ of interest would flow to P&L, materially depressing earnings. Must verify in Note 30 (Q26/Q50) the capitalisation rate, qualifying assets, and whether any capitalisation is aggressive.

**Qualification — ECL on contract assets** `[D005.5, p.38]`
- **What it says**: "The Group applies an expected credit loss provision ('ECL') on the contract asset balances. Refer to note 3.10.2."
- **What it changes**: Confirms ECL is applied to contract assets (R15,192,569 provision on R1,270,275,234 = 1.20% coverage) but **not** to the R852m future-cost bucket. The ECL charge of +R4,203,719 in FY2026 is a P&L charge, contrasting with the R7.7m ECL **credit** in D004 (which must therefore be trade-receivable-related). This divergence is a key forecast input — contract-asset ECL is rising while trade-receivable ECL is releasing, suggesting deteriorating contract-asset quality but improving receivable collection. Must verify in Note 3.10.2 and Note 28.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `*` on Bankenveld District City (Pty) Ltd** [D005.6, physical PDF p. 39]:
  - **Text**: "* Please refer to note 39 for the change in investment in joint venture to investment in joint operations."
  - **Implication**: Confirms the R165,006,544 Bankenveld JV loan was eliminated on reclassification to a joint operation, not repaid in cash. This is a **non-cash** movement that must be excluded from any cash-flow-based JV loan reconciliation. It also means the R19,252,380 direct debit to retained income (Q32) is the equity-side counterpart of bringing Bankenveld's assets/liabilities onto the consolidated balance sheet. **Verification needed**: Note 39 must disclose the full deconsolidation — assets/liabilities brought on, pro-forma revenue, contract balances, borrowings, and whether any gain/loss arose. Carry to D007.

- **Footnote on ECL** [D005.6, p. 39]:
  - **Text**: "Please refer to note 3.10.2 for ECLs (expected credit losses) provided for on loans to joint ventures. Expected credit losses take into account the expected credit losses that will result from all possible default events over the expected life of a financial asset."
  - **Implication**: The JV-loan ECL is measured under the **general approach** (lifetime ECL), not the simplified approach. The R14,292,086 allowance represents 3.56% of gross principal (R401,758,095). The release of R5,482,571 year-on-year is largely driven by the Bankenveld elimination (R165.0m loan removed) and reductions in Table View (R134.0m) and South Hills (R6.3m), partly offset by Witpoortjie growth (R46.0m). **Verification needed**: Note 3.10.2 must disclose the staging (Stage 1/2/3) of JV loans and whether any are credit-impaired. Carry to D007.

- **Accounting policy qualification** [D005.6, p. 39]:
  - **Text**: "These loans are recognised initially at fair value plus direct transaction costs and subsequently measured at amortised cost."
  - **Implication**: Standard amortised-cost treatment. No fair-value option elected. **Verification needed**: Confirm whether the "prime plus 2%" rates are market rates (no below-market loan adjustment) and whether the interest-free Bankenveld loan (now eliminated) required any fair-value adjustment on initial recognition. Carry to D007.

- **Significant estimates and judgements qualification** [D005.6, p. 39]:
  - **Text**: "The Group applies an expected credit loss provision ('ECL') on the joint venture loan balances using the general approach."
  - **Implication**: JV loans are a **significant judgement area**. The 3.56% coverage ratio is low relative to the unsecured nature of all four loans. **Verification needed**: Note 3.10.2 must disclose the probability-of-default and loss-given-default assumptions for JV loans. Carry to D007.

- **Missing footnote text**: No footnote markers in this section have missing definitions — all three footnote references (`*`, ECL note, policy note) are fully defined on the page.

 11. Investment in joint ventures                                                                             
                                                                                                              
     Accounting policy                                                                                        
     Joint ventures are companies in which the Group has an investment where it, along with one or more other shareholders has contractually agreed to share control of the business and where the decisions
     about relevant activities require the unanimous consent of the joint investment partners. In both cases, the Group equity accounts these investments resulting in the Group’s statement of comprehensive
     income reflecting its share of the entity’s profit or loss after tax and the statement of financial position records the Group’s share of the net assets.
     When the Group’s share of losses in a joint venture equals or exceeds its interests in the joint venture (which includes any long-term interests that, in substance form part of the Group’s net investment
     in the joint ventures), the Group does not recognise further losses, unless it has incurred obligations or made payments on behalf of the joint ventures.
     Unrealised gains on transactions between the Group and its joint ventures are eliminated to the extent of the Group’s interest in the joint ventures, unless the transaction provides evidence of an
     impairment of the asset transferred.                                                                     
     Significant judgement and source of estimation uncertainty                                               
     The Group holds more than 50% of the shareholding in the below entities. Refer below to the judgements management exercised in determining whether or not it has joint control over the various entities.

     South Hills Development Company Proprietary Limited^ 50.00%   50.00%   57.50%   57.50% 107 022 234 94 664 782

     ^ Although the Group has majority shareholding in these entities, it does not have control of the Company as the Board comprises an equal number of representatives from both the Group as well as the minority shareholder. Both parties have equal voting
      rights, irrespective of the percentage shareholding or representation on the Board of Directors. Any decision regarding the relevant activities of these entities that significantly affect the returns of the entity are made with the unanimous consent of both parties.
     # On 1 April 2025, the Group increased its shareholding in the Witpoortjie joint venture by R1 000 000. The increase in shareholding had no change in control.
     * On 31 March 2025, the Group increased its shareholding in the Table View joint venture by R7 000 000. The increase in shareholding had no change in control. The Group has a 60.43% (2025: 58.34%) shareholding in this entity and it does not have control
      of the Company as both parties have equal voting rights, and representation on the Board of Directors. Any decision regarding the relevant activities of this entity that significantly affects the returns of the entity are made with the unanimous consent of both
      parties.                                                                                                
     The Group only shares in the above joint ventures’ net assets, as opposed to having a direct rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities.
     The joint ventures are managed by Steering Committees that contain an equal number of representatives from both the Calgro M3 Group as well as the other shareholders.
     The Steering Committees meet on a regular basis to discuss the relevant activities of the project. These activities include the authorisation of budgets, project feasibilities, cash flow forecasts, distributions,
     potential variation orders, cost over runs, determination of sales prices and the appointment of all contractors and professional teams. Any decisions related to the relevant activities that significantly affect
     the returns of the entity need to carry the unanimous consent of both joint venture partners, irrespective of the number of representatives a party has on the Steering Committee or directorate of the
     respective company.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `$` — Bankenveld reclassification** [D005.7, pp. 40, 41, 43, 44]:
- Text: "Please refer to note 39 for the change in investment in joint venture to investment in joint operations."
- Implication: Bankenveld's carrying value is nil at 28 Feb 2026 (2025: R8,011,907); the "change in control" line of R11,599,528 removed the investment during the year [D005.7, p. 44]. The FY2026 share of profit R11,599,528 is included in the R23,982,406 JV profit line [D005.7, p. 41] but is then eliminated on change in control — meaning the **reported JV profit of R23,982,406 overstates the continuing JV contribution** by R11,599,528. Continuing JV profit = R23,982,406 − R11,599,528 = **R12,382,878** (Witpoortjie R103,523 + South Hills R12,357,452 + Table View (R78,097)). This is a material forecasting adjustment. Must verify in D007 (Note 39) whether the R11,599,528 is a P&L gain on deconsolidation or a reclassification through equity.

**Footnote `^` — majority shareholding but no control** [D005.7, p. 40]:
- Text: "Although the Group has majority shareholding in these entities, it does not have control of the Company as the Board comprises an equal number of representatives from both the Group as well as the minority shareholder. Both parties have equal voting rights, irrespective of the percentage shareholding or representation on the Board of Directors. Any decision regarding the relevant activities of these entities that significantly affect the returns of the entity are made with the unanimous consent of both parties."
- Implication: Witpoortjie (88.33%) and South Hills (57.50%) are equity-accounted despite majority shareholding. This is a **significant judgement** — if control were subsequently determined to exist, these entities would be consolidated, materially changing revenue, contract balances, debt, and NCI. The 88.33% Witpoortjie holding with zero revenue and near-zero equity is a particular concern. Must verify in D001 (auditor's assessment of the control judgement) and D007 (Note 39).

**Footnote `#` — Witpoortjie shareholding increase** [D005.7, p. 40]:
- Text: "On 1 April 2025, the Group increased its shareholding in the Witpoortjie joint venture by R1 000 000. The increase in shareholding had no change in control."
- Implication: Shareholding rose from 84.16% to 88.33% for R1,000,000 cash. The investment carrying value rose from R2,133,365 to R3,236,888 (increase R1,103,523 = R1,000,000 cash + R103,523 share of profit) [D005.7, p. 42]. No control change — consistent with the `^` footnote. Must verify in D007 whether the R1,000,000 was a cash subscription or purchase from the minority.

**Footnote `*` — Table View shareholding increase** [D005.7, p. 40]:
- Text: "On 31 March 2025, the Group increased its shareholding in the Table View joint venture by R7 000 000. The increase in shareholding had no change in control. The Group has a 60.43% (2025: 58.34%) shareholding in this entity and it does not have control of the Company as both parties have equal voting rights, and representation on the Board of Directors."
- Implication: Shareholding rose from 58.34% to 60.43% for R7,000,000 cash. Investment carrying value rose from R31,800,000 to R38,721,904 (increase R6,921,904 = R7,000,000 cash − R78,040 opening adjustment − R56 share of loss) [D005.7, p. 44]. Table View has zero revenue and a loss of R93 — the R38.7m carrying value is supported entirely by "inventories/construction contracts" R29,901,495 and "trade and other receivables" R9,052,577 [D005.7, p. 43]. **Impairment indicator**: R38.7m investment against R4.9m net equity and zero revenue. Must verify in D007.

**Qualification — "no further financial risks" and "no obligation to carry losses"** [D005.7, p. 41]:
- Text: "Other than loans to joint ventures (note 10), trade and other receivables (note 7) and related party transactions (note 37) which arose in the ordinary course of business, the Calgro M3 Group has no further financial risks associated with these joint ventures. The Group has no obligation to carry losses over and above its investment into the joint ventures."
- Implication: This is a **management assertion**, not a legal opinion. It directly contradicts any assumption of joint-and-several liability on JV debt. However, the Group's JV loans (R401.8m gross per Q129) and receivables (South Hills R36.6m per Q128) are already material exposures. The assertion must be tested against D001 (auditor's report) and D007 (Note 37 related-party transactions, Note 10 loan terms).

**Qualification — "The Group only shares in the above joint ventures' net assets, as opposed to having a direct rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities"** [D005.7, p. 40]:
- Implication: Confirms equity-accounting treatment (not joint-operation proportionate consolidation) for the four JVs. Bankenveld is the exception — reclassified to joint operation (Note 39). Must verify in D007 that the Bankenveld joint-operation accounting is correctly applied (proportionate share of assets/liabilities brought on).

**Qualification — "The joint ventures are managed by Steering Committees that contain an equal number of representatives from both the Calgro M3 Group as well as the other shareholders"** [D005.7, p. 40]:
- Implication: Supports the joint-control judgement. The Steering Committee approves "budgets, project feasibilities, cash flow forecasts, distributions, potential variation orders, cost over runs, determination of sales prices and the appointment of all contractors and professional teams" — meaning **variation orders and cost overruns require unanimous consent**, which is a potential source of deadlock and delay risk on JV projects. Must verify in D007 whether any JV has experienced Steering Committee deadlock.

**Missing footnote text**: No footnote markers in this section have missing definitions — all `$`, `^`, `#`, `*` markers have corresponding definitions on p. 40 or p. 41.

12. Inventories                                       
    Accounting policy                                 
    Land owned by the Group which is being developed to get into a condition to start construction
    of the various projects is classified as inventory. The land may also be sold without any
    construction depending on the intention of management. Inventories are stated at the lower of
    cost or net realisable value. The cost of land under development held for sale includes design
    costs, building materials, direct labour, borrowing costs and other indirect costs.
    The amount of any write-down of inventories to net realisable value is recognised as an
    expense in the year which the write-down occurs. The amount of any reversal of any write-
    down of inventories is recognised as a reduction in the amount of inventories recognised as an
    expense in the year in which the reversal occurs. 
                                                      
    Individual units which do not form part of construction contracts are classified as inventory and
    are sold as a completed unit.                     
    Memorial park land costs are the remaining value of unsold grave sites, which consists of the
    unsold portion of the original cost price of the land and any other direct and indirect costs
    incurred to get the land to its intended use of being sold as a grave site.

--- Section D005.8 | [AFS] physical page 45 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 12,13 ---

     Significant estimates and judgements              
     In assessing the net realisable value of land under development held for sale, valuators
     consider title deed information, town planning conditions, locality and improvements made to
     the property.                                     
     Property vacancy rates in surrounding areas realised yields on comparative sales as well as
     micro- and macroeconomic conditions require judgement. In assessing the net realisable value
     of memorial park land costs, management considers the estimated number of graves available
     and the average current sales value of individual burial rights.

 13. Investments                                       
                                                       
     Accounting policy                                 
     The investments held are carried at fair value through profit or loss (“FVPL”) and relates to the
     invested funds for the Memorial parks maintenance fund.
     The classification of the financial asset is based on the characteristics and how the contractual
     cash flows are managed. The financial assets have been classified based on the contractual
     cash flow characteristics of the financial assets, which are assessed based on whether the
     cash flows consist solely of payments of principal and interest, and management’s business
     model for managing the financial asset.

- **Q17 [Medium] (remainder): Note 12 — inventories split land/stock/raw materials/WIP, write-downs, inventory turn vs residential revenue; check whether R852,124,160 future contract-asset costs are double-counted or separate.**
  - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D007 / Note 21)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: Note 12 [D005.8, physical PDF p. 45] discloses only a two-line inventory split: Memorial park land costs R170,506,162 (2025: R175,076,821) and Other land costs for future development R285,861,840 (2025: R344,491,202), total R456,368,002 (2025: R519,568,023). No separate raw-materials, finished-goods, or WIP line is presented, and no inventory write-down or reversal is disclosed in this section. The R852,124,160 "development cost for future contract assets" is **not** part of this R456.4m inventory balance — it sits inside construction contracts (Note 9 continued, p. 38) and is described there as "a form of inventory." The two are therefore separate balance-sheet captions, not double-counted, but the accounting boundary between them (when land/development cost moves from Note 12 inventory into contract assets) is not explained here. Inventory turn vs residential revenue and the transfer mechanism remain open.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) or table notes appear in the supplied D005.8 evidence. The qualifications present are **policy-level and estimate-level statements**, which carry forecast consequences:

- **Inventory NRV judgement (Note 12, "Significant estimates and judgements") [D005.8, physical PDF p. 45]**: NRV of land under development is assessed by valuators using "title deed information, town planning conditions, locality and improvements," and explicitly depends on "property vacancy rates in surrounding areas, realised yields on comparative sales as well as micro- and macroeconomic conditions." This is a **macro-sensitive valuation input**: a softening residential market or adverse town-planning outcome could trigger write-downs against the R285,861,840 "Other land costs for future development." No write-down was taken in FY2026 despite the balance falling R58,629,362 — but that fall is explained as a **transfer to construction contracts**, not a sale or write-down (see next point), so it is not evidence of NRV resilience.
- **Memorial park NRV judgement [D005.8, p. 45]**: NRV of memorial park land depends on "the estimated number of graves available and the average current sales value of individual burial rights" — a volume × price judgement on the R170,506,162 balance. No write-down disclosed.
- **Disposals and transfers qualification [D005.8, p. 45]**: "The disposals for the current year for completed units and other land costs for future development amounted to Rnil (2025: R27,391,838)." **This is a material forecast signal**: zero inventory disposals in FY2026 means the R63.2m inventory decline is **not** a sale — it is the R58,629,362 transfer to construction contracts plus small residual movements. It implies the residential land pipeline is being **fed into contract assets rather than sold as completed units**, consistent with a shift toward over-time construction recognition. It also means inventory is not currently generating point-in-time revenue.
- **"Inventories transferred to construction contracts ... R58,629,362 (2025: Rnil)" [D005.8, p. 45]**: First-year transfer mechanism. This is the accounting bridge between Note 12 inventory and the construction-contract caption (which includes the R852,124,160 future contract-asset cost). It confirms the two captions are linked by transfer, not duplication — but the **transfer pricing basis** (cost, NRV, or otherwise) is not stated and must be verified.
- **Investment purpose restriction (Note 13) [D005.8, p. 45]**: The R20,669,356 is ring-fenced — "funds to be utilised for the sole purpose of the future maintenance of the memorial parks business, once the parks have been fully developed and sold." This means the balance is **not available liquidity** for debt service or working capital, and it economically offsets (at least in part) the R66,328,209 maintenance provision flagged in Q87. It should be excluded from free cash flow and from any liquidity headroom calculation.
- **FVPL classification rationale (Note 13) [D005.8, p. 45]**: The policy text recites the SPPI/business-model test but the instrument is a "diversified investment fund" — the policy wording is generic and does not evidence the actual contractual cash-flow characteristics. The fair-value hierarchy level is absent; the cross-reference to Notes 5 and 25 must be followed in D007.

14. Property, plant and equipment                    
    Accounting policy                                
    The Group’s long life assets mainly provide the infrastructure to enable the Group to operate.
    The assets are initially measured at cost. The cost of the assets are then recognised in the
    statement of comprehensive income over the useful lives of the assets as a depreciation
    charge. Property, plant and equipment is subsequently stated at cost less accumulated
    depreciation and impairment losses.              
                                                     
    The cost of the asset includes the purchase price and any costs directly attributable to bringing
    the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the
    manner intended by management.                   
    The useful lives of the assets have been assessed as follows:
    Owned Item               Average useful life     
    – Land and buildings     Land: Unlimited, Buildings: Up to 50 years*
    – Plant and machinery    5 years                 
    – Furniture and fixtures and office equipment 6 years
    – Motor vehicles         4 years                 
    – IT equipment           3 years                 
    – Leasehold improvements 10 years                
    * Where the residual value of buildings exceeds the carrying amount, no depreciation is provided.
    Right-of-use asset                               
    – Office buildings Based on the shorter of lease period or useful life of the asset
