### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Useful-life footnote `*` — "Where the residual value of buildings exceeds the carrying amount, no depreciation is provided"** [D005.9, p.45]. This is the justification for **zero depreciation on Land and buildings** (carrying R6,897,434, cost R6,897,434, accumulated depreciation nil, unchanged 2025→2026) [D005.9, p.46]. Implication: the entire R6.9m buildings balance is assumed to have residual value ≥ carrying amount, so no depreciation charge will ever hit the P&L unless the residual-value assumption is revised. For forecasting, treat buildings depreciation as Rnil but flag residual-value reassessment risk. Verify the residual-value basis and whether land is separately identified (land: unlimited life).

- **"Significant estimates and judgements — Management uses judgement for useful life and residual values used"** [D005.9, p.46]. No sensitivity, no range, no independent review disclosed. This is a soft qualification: depreciation (R3,957,119) is small relative to the group (revenue scale ~R1bn+), so forecast impact is immaterial, but it confirms management discretion over the R6.9m buildings and R13.5m ROU carrying values.

- **ROU reconciliation arithmetic tension** [D005.9, pp.46–47]: Table on p.46 shows ROU closing carrying amount **R13,495,250**; reconciliation on p.47 shows closing **R13,495,248** (R2 difference). Gross totals: p.46 total carrying **R22,798,885**; p.47 gross totals closing **R22,798,883** (R2 difference). Immaterial rounding, but flag as a reconciliation check.

- **Depreciation allocation qualification** [D005.9, p.48]: "Depreciation expense of R3,957,119 ... has been charged to 'administrative expenses'". This means **no depreciation is embedded in cost of sales** for PPE/ROU. Implication for forecasting: gross margin is not burdened by PPE depreciation; all depreciation sits in opex/admin. Cross-check against Note 24 cost-of-sales build (Q22/Q54) — if cost of sales contains a depreciation line, it must be a different depreciation (e.g., amortisation of contract costs or inventory-related), not Note 14 PPE.

- **"No assets ... encumbered or held as security"** [D005.9, p.48]. Positive for bondholders/security analysis: PPE is unencumbered, so no asset-backed security over plant. But it also means the R1,380.3m borrowings are secured on **other** assets (likely inventory, contract assets, or unsecured) — verify security package in Note 20 (Q51/Q72/Q99).

- **Prior-year scrapping note** [D005.9, p.48]: "book value of R231 (Cost: R6,753,329, Accumulated depreciation: R6,753,098) was scrapped in the prior year". Fully depreciated assets scrapped — no P&L loss. Confirms asset base is largely written down; low ongoing capex intensity.

- **Regulation 25(3) register** [D005.9, p.48]: standard statutory boilerplate; no financial implication.

- **Missing footnote text**: No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*` other than the useful-life `*`) appear without definitions in this capture. The useful-life `*` is defined on p.45. No missing-footnote verification required for this section.

15. Investment property

fair value for the commercial properties was determined using valuation methods as described
in  note 4. Fair value adjustments are recognised in profit or loss. These properties are
included in the Memorial Parks business.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) are present in the supplied D005.10 evidence.** There are no table footnotes to unpack or missing footnote definitions to flag in this capture. The qualifications below are embedded in narrative text rather than footnotes.

- **Investment property valuation qualification** [D005.10, p. 48]: "The value of investment properties as at 28 February 2026 was determined by **management** using the Discounted Cash Flow ("DCF") method." This is a Level 3, management-driven valuation with no independent valuer named. The stated sensitivity — "A 5% increase/decrease in the growth rate or discount rate used in the valuations will not lead to a significant change in the fair value" — is a **management assertion, not a quantified sensitivity table**. It must be tested against Note 5 (estimates and assumptions) and Note 25 (fair-value inputs) to confirm the actual discount/growth rates and whether the R10.0m gain (44.5% of opening value) is plausible on a DCF with only a 5% rate sensitivity. The magnitude of the gain (R10.0m on R22.5m opening, +44.5%) versus the prior year's R0.35m (+1.6%) is a material swing that warrants scrutiny.

- **Goodwill impairment-test qualification** [D005.10, p. 49]: The value-in-use model uses **un-escalated** real cash flows, **zero terminal growth**, a **gross margin of 23.23%** (down from 27.45% in 2025), and a **pre-tax real discount rate of 15.88%** (up from 15.10%). The gross-margin assumption has been cut by 422 bps year-on-year — consistent with the Residential gross-margin compression flagged in D004/D005.1 — yet no impairment is recognised. The headroom statement ("a 5% decrease in gross margin to 18.23% ... would still not recognise an impairment") is the critical qualification: it implies substantial headroom, but the **discount-rate sensitivity is printed inconsistently** ("increased by 5% (increased to 10.88%)" — 15.88% × 1.05 = 16.67%, not 10.88%; 10.88% is actually a *decrease*). This must be verified in Note 5 / Note 25 to confirm the true sensitivity and whether the headroom claim is reliable.

- **Goodwill allocation qualification** [D005.10, p. 49]: R158,955,713 (99.6%) of goodwill sits in Residential Property Development — the segment with the compressed margin and the POC/feasibility-study revenue recognition risk flagged in Note 23. The impairment test is therefore highly sensitive to Residential cash-flow assumptions (selling prices, costs, availability of end-user cash). This links directly to Q114 (feasibility-study approval) and Q118/Q119 (future contract-asset costs).

- **Investment property segment qualification** [D005.10, p. 48]: "These properties are included in the **Memorial Parks** business." The R10.0m fair-value gain therefore sits in the Memorial Parks segment, not Residential — relevant to segmental margin analysis and to Q23/Q55 (other income decomposition, 85.6% Memorial Parks).

 17. Deferred tax assets/(liabilities)             
     Accounting policy                             
     Deferred tax assets and liabilities represent amounts of tax that will become recoverable
     or payable in future accounting years. They generally arise as a result of temporary
     differences, where the time at which profits and losses are recognised for tax purposes
     differs from the time at which the relevant transaction is recorded in the accounts.
                                                   
     A deferred tax asset represents a tax reduction that is expected to arise in a future year.
     A deferred tax liability represents taxes which will become payable in a future year as a
     result of a current or an earlier transaction. In respect of deferred tax assets, the Group
     only recognises a deferred tax asset when the availability of future taxable profits
     necessary to support the deferred tax asset is probable, when there is a history of recent
     tax losses, other convincing evidence is considered.
     Where a temporary difference arises in relation to the Group’s investment in subsidiaries
     or joint ventures a deferred tax liability can only be recognised by the Group if the Group
     cannot control the timing of the reversal of the temporary difference or it is probable that
     the temporary difference will reverse in future.

--- Section D005.11 | [AFS] physical page 50 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 17 ---
17. Deferred tax assets/(liabilities) (continued)
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset if the Group has a legally enforceable right to offset
current tax assets against current tax liabilities and the deferred tax assets and liabilities relate
to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority on either the same taxable entity or on
different taxable entities, but which the Group intends to settle on a net basis or realise
simultaneously.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply to
the year when the asset is realised or the liability is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws)
that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting year.
Estimates and key judgements
Management uses cash flow forecasts to determine whether deferred tax assets can be
recognised in terms of IAS 12 and when the recognised deferred tax assets will be recovered.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`$` footnote (tax losses recoverability)** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 50]`: *"The Group has concluded that the deferred tax assets relating to tax losses will be recoverable using the estimated future taxable income based on the approved business plans and budgets for the underlying subsidiaries."* This is a **key judgement** — R24,259,071 of tax-loss DTAs (2025: R9,479,593) are recognised on the strength of management's own budgets. The R14.8m YoY increase in recognised loss assets is a direct P&L credit that flatters the deferred tax charge; if forecast taxable profits disappoint, this DTA is at risk of write-down. Must be tested against the goodwill value-in-use budgets (Q156) and the forward ETR.
- **`*` footnote (gross DTL includes subsidiary DTAs)** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 50]`: *"Included in deferred tax liabilities are the deferred tax assets of subsidiaries where their net deferred tax position is a deferred tax liability."* This means the R409,486,025 gross DTL and R10,128,435 gross DTA are **not clean entity-level balances** — they are netted per-entity. The headline R399.4m net liability is the only meaningful consolidated figure; any analyst using the gross lines for segment/entity analysis would double-count. Confirms offsetting is applied per legal entity, not group-wide.
- **`#` footnote (gross DTA includes subsidiary DTLs)** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 50]`: mirror of the above — the R10,128,435 DTA line contains subsidiary DTLs. Reinforces that only the R399,357,590 net is reliable.
- **Accounting policy — DTA recognition threshold** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 49]`: *"only recognises a deferred tax asset when the availability of future taxable profits ... is probable, when there is a history of recent tax losses, other convincing evidence is considered."* The group has a history of tax losses (hence the "other convincing evidence" reliance) — this is a soft recognition test and a forecast risk if budgets are revised.
- **Accounting policy — JV/subsidiary temporary differences** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 49]`: DTL on investments in subsidiaries/JVs recognised only if the group cannot control reversal timing or reversal is probable. Relevant to the JV loan/investment balances (Q43, Q49) — no deferred tax appears to be recognised on undistributed JV earnings, implying management asserts control over reversal.
- **Measurement basis** `[D005.11, physical PDF p. 50]`: measured at **enacted/substantively enacted rates** at year-end; no rate-change sensitivity disclosed. Forward ETR should therefore track the statutory rate plus permanent differences, not rate changes.
- **Missing footnote text**: No footnote markers in this section are left undefined — all three (`$`, `*`, `#`) are printed. No missing-footnote verification question required here.

     Ordinary shares are classified as equity. Incremental costs directly attributable to the issue of
     new shares are shown in equity as a deduction, net of tax, from the proceeds.
     Where the Group purchases the Company’s equity share capital, the consideration paid,
     including any attributable transaction costs net of income taxes, is deducted from total
     shareholders’ equity as treasury shares until they are cancelled or re-issued.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `%` (Executive Share Scheme, 2026)** [D005.12, p.52]: Gross 440,000 shares vested; tax liability settled by Group = 198,000 shares; net 242,000 shares transferred to participants out of treasury held by Calgro M3 Developments at R4.72/share. **Implication**: The R1,142,240 "issue" is a treasury-share transfer, not new share issuance — no cash inflow; it is a non-cash equity reclassification. The 198,000 shares withheld for tax represent a cash tax settlement by the Group (PAYE on vesting) — verify whether this cash outflow is captured in the cash flow statement tax-paid line (Q41/Q107).

- **Footnote `%` (Executive Share Scheme, 2025)** [D005.12, p.52]: Gross 740,000 vested; 333,000 withheld for tax; 407,000 net at R5.65/share. Prior-year comparative.

- **Footnote `$` (Trusts)** [D005.12, p.52]: EBT and Empowerment Trust consolidated under IFRS 10; their shares carried as treasury on consolidation. **Implication**: 10,425,818 shares (R208,479,254) are permanently treasury — they will never be cancelled or reissued to the market unless trust rules change. Effective free float = 95,380,601 shares. For EPS/DPS forecasting, use 95.38m as the base, adjusted for any further buybacks.

- **Footnote `#` (Buyback)** [D005.12, p.52]: 1,327,525 shares repurchased and cancelled at average R5.01 = R6,662,637. **Implication**: Buyback at R5.01 vs stated capital per share of R0.298 (R28,389,249 ÷ 95,380,601) — the premium over par is debited against distributable reserves, not stated capital. Confirm in Statement of Changes in Equity (D004) that the R6,662,637 debit is split between stated capital and retained earnings. **Verification question raised** (see Q168 below).

- **"All issued shares are fully paid"** [D005.12, p.52]: Standard qualification; no call risk.

- **"Unissued ordinary shares are under the control of the Directors... authority remains in force until the next AGM"** [D005.12, p.52]: Directors have blanket authority to issue up to 500,000,000 − 95,380,601 = 404,619,399 unissued shares without further shareholder approval until next AGM. **Implication for forecast**: dilution risk is open-ended; any capital raise could be executed without a general meeting. Flag as a governance/dilution risk.

- **Arithmetic check on treasury reconciliation** [D005.12, p.51 vs p.52]: Opening treasury 17,915,449 (R366,824,503); less 242,000 issued to scheme (R1,142,240); closing 17,673,449 (R365,682,263). R366,824,503 − R1,142,240 = R365,682,263 ✓. Developments treasury: 7,489,631 → 7,247,631 (−242,000); R158,345,249 → R157,203,009 (−R1,142,240) ✓.

- **Arithmetic check on stated capital** [D005.12, p.51]: Opening R33,909,646 + R1,142,240 − R6,662,637 = R28,389,249 ✓.

- **Missing footnote text**: No footnote markers in this section lack a corresponding definition — all three (`%`, `$`, `#`) are defined on p.52.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `**` — Lease liability office building R20,560,844** [D005.13, p. 52]
- States: "This amount relates to the capitalisation of long-term leases. Refer to note 22."
- **Implication**: Confirms the IFRS 16 lease liability is presented **within trade and other payables**, not within borrowings. This resolves the Q85/Q149 question on whether leases sit inside the R1,380.3m debt stack — they do not. The lease liability is a separate R20.6m obligation. For forecasting, debt service and covenant calculations must treat this separately from the R1.38bn borrowings.

**Footnote `$` — Accrual for long service awards R3,064,908** [D005.13, p. 52]
- States: "The Group has a long-term service award for its employees based on years of service (10 years – two months salary, 15 years – three months salary, every subsequent five years thereafter – three months salary). To determine the value of the accrual, the following was taken into account: The average annual salary increases, the employee attrition rate, retirement age, discount rate and mortality rate."
- **Implication**: This is an actuarial-type long-service liability, up R73.4% (R1,767,372 → R3,064,908). The measurement depends on salary-increase and discount-rate assumptions not disclosed here. For forecasting, this is a small but growing non-financial liability; the discount rate used should be checked against the 12.72% incremental borrowing rate. The sharp increase may reflect either a change in assumptions or a growing tenured workforce — needs verification.

**Footnote `*` — Transaction cost amortisation (R7,405,595)** [D005.13, p. 53]
- States: "The transaction costs are amortised over the life of the facilities. It is expected that these costs will be fully amortised when the facilities are settled."
- **Implication**: This is the reconciling item between Note 5 gross borrowings (R1,387,696,888) and Note 20 amortised cost (R1,380,291,293). The R7,405,595 unamortised balance will unwind through finance costs over the remaining facility lives. For forecasting, this is a non-cash finance cost that must be added back in cash-flow modelling. The increase from R5,848,911 to R7,405,595 (+R1,556,684) reflects new facilities raised (CGR 61, CGR 62, Stanlib) net of amortisation.

**Footnote `%` — Repayment terms and covenants** [D005.13, p. 53]
- States: "All borrowings are unsecured." Then lists repayment terms: NHFC nine instalments from May 2026; Prescient bullet Oct 2027; ABSA 1 four equal instalments from Sep 2027; ABSA 2 eight instalments from Mar 2028; Standard Bank bullet May 2026; Stanlib eight equal instalments from Sep 2028. Covenants: DSCR >1.2x Group level; Net debt/equity <1.5:1; minimum liquidity ratio 1.2. "At the end of the financial year, the Group was not in breach of the above covenants or at risk of breaching the regulated covenants listed above."
- **Implication**: **All borrowings unsecured** is a critical finding — there is no asset security, only covenant protection. The covenant package is relatively light (three ratios). The "not at risk of breaching" statement is management assertion; the DSCR calculation (Note 3.2) includes new financial indebtedness of R566,425,000 per Q93, which flatters the ratio. The repayment profile shows **material amortisation commencing**: NHFC nine instalments from May 2026 (R215m over ~9 periods ≈ R24m per instalment), ABSA 1 four instalments from Sep 2027 (R155m ÷ 4 ≈ R39m), ABSA 2 eight instalments from Mar 2028 (R200m ÷ 8 = R25m), Stanlib eight instalments from Sep 2028 (R250m ÷ 8 ≈ R31m). This creates a rising debt-service burden from FY2027 onward that must be modelled.

**JIBAR transition qualification** [D005.13, p. 53]
- States: "The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease after its final publication on 31 December 2026, and the Group is therefore transitioning its JIBAR-linked financial instruments to the new transaction-based benchmark rate, ZARONIA … the Group does not expect the transition to result in a substantial modification of its financial instruments or to have a material financial impact, however, this will be continuously assessed."
- **Implication**: All DMTN notes, Prescient, ABSA 1/2 and Stanlib are JIBAR-linked (R1,093m of the R1,358m capital outstanding). The transition to ZARONIA by 31 Dec 2026 introduces basis risk and potential credit adjustment spread changes. Management asserts no material impact, but this is forward-looking and unquantified. For forecasting, the interest cost base is floating and will reprice; the ZARONIA transition could alter the effective margin. This is a key sensitivity.

**Maturity split inconsistency** [D005.13, p. 54]
- Note 20 states R133,000,000 within 12 months and R1,247,291,293 after 12 months. This **contradicts** the earlier maturity table (R224,317,034 <1yr) [D005.3, p. 32] and the liquidity table (all current) [D005.3, p. 34]. The R133m appears to capture only bullet maturities (Standard Bank R50m May 2026 + CGR 55 R50m + CGR 56 R33m Oct 2026) and **omits the NHFC instalments starting May 2026**. This is a material classification error or definitional inconsistency that must be resolved before modelling debt service.

**Incremental borrowing rate 12.72%** [D005.13, p. 54]
- States: "The Group's incremental borrowing rate as at 28 February 2026 was 12.72% (2025: 11.76%)."
- **Implication**: A 96 bps increase year-on-year. This is the rate likely used for lease measurement and capitalised borrowing cost determination. It also signals rising funding costs — consistent with the JIBAR+ margins of 3.9%–5.0% on the debt stack. For forecasting, the weighted average cost of debt is likely in the 12–13% range, and the capitalised interest of R102,143,192 (Q115) should be tested against this rate.

**"Directors have not breached … borrowing powers"** [D005.13, p. 54]
- Standard boilerplate; no incremental information.

21. Maintenance provision
Accounting policy
The Group recognises additions to the maintenance liability for sales of additional grave sites
in the year with the maintenance liability representing the present value of the expected future
costs to maintain the memorial park associated with the sold grave. The obligation is
recognised within cost of sales at the point at which revenue is recognised as the commitment
to maintain the memorial park is a key promise to the customer when selling a grave.
The measurement of the maintenance liability includes estimates of future direct costs such as
landscaping, security, and infrastructure upkeep, as well as a discount rate reflective of long-
term, low-risk returns. The Group holds dedicated investment funds for the sole purpose of
maintaining the park once the park is fully developed and sold out (refer to  note 13).

22. Lease liability                                    
    Accounting policy                                  
    The Group, as a lessee, recognises right-of-use assets representing its rights to use the
    underlying assets and lease liabilities representing its obligation to make lease payments.
                                                       
    Definition of a lease                              
    Under IFRS 16, a contract is, or contains a lease if the contract conveys a right to control the
    use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration.
    At inception or on reassessment of a contract that contains a lease component, the Group
    allocates the consideration in the contract to each lease and non-lease component based on
    their relative stand-alone prices. However, for leases of properties in which it is a lessee, the
    Group has elected not to separate non-lease components and will instead account for the
    lease and non-lease components as a single lease component.
    As a lessee                                        
    Under IFRS 16, the Group recognises right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for most leases
    (i.e. these leases are on-balance sheet).          
    The Group presents lease liabilities in the statement of financial position under trade and other
    payables. The Group recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the lease
    commencement date.                                 
                                                       
    The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not
    paid at commencement date, discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if that
    rate cannot be readily determined, the Group’s incremental borrowing rate is applied.
    The lease liability is subsequently increased by the interest cost on the lease liability and
    decreased by lease payments made. It is remeasured when there is a change in future lease
    payments arising from a change in an index or rate, a change in estimate of the amount
    expected to be payable under a residual value guarantee, or as appropriate, changes in the
    assessment of whether a purchase or extension option is reasonably certain to be exercised.
    The right-of-use asset is initially measured at an amount equal to the sum of the lease liability,
    initial direct costs, costs of removing and restoring the lease asset and payments made prior
    to the lease commencement. The right-of-use asset is subsequently measured at cost less
    accumulated depreciation and impairment loss and adjusted for certain remeasurements of
    the lease liability.                               
    The Group will apply judgement to determine whether it is reasonably certain to exercise
    renewal options, as such options impacts the lease term, which significantly affects the
    amount of lease liabilities and right-of-use assets recognised.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 21 — "present value of the expected future costs" + "discount rate reflective of long-term, low-risk returns"** [D005.14, p. 54]: The provision is a **discounted non-current liability**, so the R3,994,112 "interest" line is pure accretion (unwinding of discount), not cash. For forecasting, the provision grows mechanically each year even with zero new grave sales. The **discount rate is not printed** — cannot verify whether the R3,994,112 accretion is consistent with the stated rate; must be checked against Note 13/accounting policies. Also note the provision is recognised **within cost of sales at point of revenue recognition** — so Memorial Parks gross margin is structurally depressed by R4.6m of non-cash provision charge each year; this must be added back when assessing cash gross margin.
- **Note 21 — "The Group holds dedicated investment funds for the sole purpose of maintaining the park"** [p. 54]: Cross-reference to Note 13. The provision (R66.3m) materially exceeds the ring-fenced fund (R20.7m per earlier capture, D005.8 p. 45) — a **funding gap of ~R45.6m** that is a real future cash obligation not backed by dedicated assets. This is a forecast risk item and a potential covenant/liquidity consideration.
- **Note 22 — "presents lease liabilities ... under trade and other payables"** [p. 55]: This is a **classification qualification**. It means (a) the R1,380.3m "borrowings" excludes R20.6m of lease debt; (b) any Net Debt calculation must decide whether to include leases; (c) the Note 20 liquidity table [D005.3, p. 34] that showed all R1,380.3m as current must be checked for whether leases were separately shown or omitted. Also flags that "trade and other payables" contains a non-trade interest-bearing item — relevant to Q71/Q88 payables analysis.
- **Note 22 — "Group will apply judgement to determine whether it is reasonably certain to exercise renewal options"** [p. 55]: Lease term (54 months from 28 Feb 2026 for head office) is judgemental; renewal optionality could extend the R17.5m non-current lease liability. Low materiality but a forward commitment.
- **Note 22 — "No gains or losses arose from any sale and leaseback agreements"** [p. 56]: Confirms no off-balance-sheet financing via sale-and-leaseback; supports the "all borrowings unsecured" assertion (Q176) — no assets sold/leased back to raise funds.
- **Note 22 — "does not sub-lease right-of-use assets and therefore generates no income"** [p. 56]: Confirms no lessor income from ROU; the "as a lessor" policy (investment property operating leases) relates to Note 13 investment property, not ROU — no double-count risk.

  23. Revenue                                            
      Accounting policy                                  
      The Group derives revenue from contracts with customers for the supply of goods
      (infrastructure, fully and partially subsidised units, non-subsidised units, serviced land) and
      memorial park burial rights and memorial park maintenance services.
      Performance obligations are identified based on the type of contract entered into with
      customers on an individual basis. Consideration is given to whether the goods or services are
      distinct from one another. Once these performance obligations are identified the below
      consideration is given to the satisfaction of the performance obligation:
                                                         
      The Group recognises revenue over time if one of the following criteria is met:
      ` The Group creates or enhances an asset which the customer controls as the asset is
       created, which is generally applicable for those contracts entered into where construction
       services are provided on land owned by the customer; or
      ` The customer simultaneously receives and consumes all of the benefits provided by the
       Group, which is generally the case for services, including when another entity would not
       need to substantially re-perform work already completed to date; or
                                                         

--- Section D005.15 | [AFS] physical page 56 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 23 ---
                                                    
                                                    
  ` The Group does not create an asset with an alternative use to the Group and has an
    enforceable right to payment for the work completed to date. In assessing this consideration
    the Group considered the following:             
    – When units/dwellings/projects are built according to customer orders/specifications the
     asset that is created does not have an alternative use to the Group as it is contractually
     restricted from directing the asset to another use. This assessment is made at contract
     inception.                                     
    – Even though the Group only has an unconditional right to payment at agreed-upon
     milestones, the Group considers there to be an enforceable right to payment when it has
     a legal, contractual right or it is customary business practice to demand or retain
     payment for performance completed to date if the contract were to be terminated before
     completion for reasons other that the entity’s failure to perform work as promised.
  The Group recognises revenue at a point in time if the over time criteria is not met. Revenue is
  recognised when control is transferred, this is generally triggered by the transfer of legal
  ownership to the customer through title deeds and/or grave certificates being issued. This will
  generally coincide with the business becoming entitled to the right to payment.
  The Group measures revenue based on the specifications of each individual contract with a
  customer, excluding any amounts received on behalf of third parties.
                                                    
  The Group recognises retention debtors, if any, based on certified work completed for specific
  contracts. It should be noted that the retention payments are not considered to be variable
  consideration as the full amount is payable upon satisfying performance obligations. The
  retention payments have no impact on the contract price and are short term in nature (usually
  released within three to six months).             
  Revenue recognised on contracts that have retention debtors are done in terms of the Group’s
  revenue recognition policy (over time or point in time), depending on how control of the goods
  are transferred to the customer. Payment of any retention debtors are measured for
  recoverability in line with IFRS 9. Retention debtors are not considered to have a significant
  financing component due to the short-term nature thereof – in making this assessment the
  Group has applied the practical expedient as per IFRS 15.129.
  The cost incurred to obtain a contract, prior to finalisation of the revenue agreement, are
  expensed to profit or loss as and when the cost are incurred as the Group considers these
  costs not to be recoverable until an agreement has been reached to recover these costs.
  The transaction price for either a single performance obligation or multiple performance
  obligations is the contractually stipulated price and represents the stand-alone selling price at
  the time when the contract is entered into with the customer.

--- Section D005.15 | [AFS] physical page 57 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 23 ---
                                                       
 23. Revenue (continued)                               
                                                       
     Significant judgement and source of estimation uncertainty
     Property Development Segment                      
     With regards to revenue recognised over time, the Group makes use of the input method to
     measure progress towards completion of the performance obligation.
     In applying the input method a “percentage of completion” calculation is used whereby the
     Group calculates the cost of the construction services and activities performed to date
     (including land) as a proportion of the total cost of the construction services and activities to
     be performed. The Group considers this an appropriate method for recognising revenue as it
     accurately depicts the progress of the underlying contract.
     The Group performs this by comparing actual cost incurred on a unit/dwelling/project
     compared to the forecasted cost per the approved project feasibility of the unit/dwelling/
     project which equals the percentage of work completed (“percentage of completion”). Inputs
     can be reliably measured and results in the performance obligation being satisfied to the
     customer. The Group, therefore, has determined that this method depicts the Group’s
     performance in transferring control of the goods and services to the customer.
     The Group uses approved feasibilities to determine the overall expected cost and attributable
     margin to determine the transaction price on over time construction contracts and for services
     to be rendered on infrastructure projects where the Group is remunerated on a cost plus basis.
     Feasibilities are reviewed on a regular basis and approved by the Executive Committee
     (“Exco”).                                         
                                                       
     The relevant costs to complete a contract is calculated by qualified industry experts, where
     applicable, and is based on:                      
     ` Remaining scope of work to be performed on the contract;
     ` Pricing agreements in place with contractors, engineers and other suppliers;
     ` General cost allowances for unforeseen events. This will vary dependent on the complexity
      in the project conditions, design uncertainty, risks in projects and project maturity.
     The Group allocates non-unit specific cost which includes land, infrastructure, town planning
     and other project-related cost based on approved feasibilities. Estimates are made by
     management to calculate the forecasted cost of a project which includes non-unit specific cost
     to be allocated to units as and when they are constructed. The estimates used are in terms of
     the approved project feasibility.                 

--- Section D005.15 | [AFS] physical page 57 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 23 ---
                                                     
                                                     
   The Group applies judgement in determining whether contracts for the sale of land and the
   construction of residential housing include separately identifiable performance obligations or
   whether they should be grouped together as a single performance obligation. The Group
   applies this judgement based on transfer requirements for the property, if the land can be
   transferred without construction of the relevant unit then the transfer of land and construction
   of unit is determined to be two separately identifiable performance obligations.
   Variations on original contract prices are agreed with a customer and are accounted for as a
   contract modification where the original prices are modified to include the approved variation
   to the original contract. A cumulative catch up of revenue is performed when the variation is
   included for a contract where the revenue is accounted for over time. The revenue on variations
   for a point in time contract is only accounted for upon transfer of control of the relevant
   services and goods to the customer.

       The Company generates revenues from the sale of burial rights, which includes the allocation of a specific grave site and initial interment services (i.e., excavation of the grave). The Company also
       has an obligation to maintain the memorial parks into perpetuity, which is recognised as a liability in accordance with IAS 37 (refer to note 21).
       The selling price for burial rights is determined based on a cost-plus-margin approach. The cost base includes the original land price and all direct development and operational costs associated with
       establishing and managing the memorial parks, as well as a provision for future maintenance costs.    
       The Group revised the contractual terms for new customers for the interment service to be separately recognised once the service is required.
       These revisions only affected the interment services for customers. For interment services entered into in the previous financial year these services were part of the total cost of the burial.
       The Group assessed these changes in accordance with IFRS 15 as contract modifications or changes in estimates.
       These do not represent a change in the Group’s revenue recognition accounting policy as the revenue continues to be recognised consistent with the principles described above.
       This change did not impact any retrospective adjustment as it relates to new customers.               

--- Section D005.15 | [AFS] physical page 61 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Note 23 ---
                                                        
 23. Revenue (continued)                                
     A reasonable margin is applied to ensure viability and sustainability of the parks.
                                                        
     Prices are reviewed periodically by management, taking into account:
     ` Feasibility models for each park;                
     ` Projected development and operating costs; and   
     ` Industry benchmarks.                             
     The Company considers the sale of a burial plot and the associated interment service to
     represent two separate performance obligations under IFRS 15, based on the following:
     ` The burial right provides a distinct benefit to the customer, who obtains legal and
       transferable ownership upon full payment;        
     ` The interment service is performed at a future date and is not required for the customer to
       benefit from the burial right;                   
     ` Burial site excavation services excavation can only be executed by the Company, but the
       timing of execution is conditional on receipt of a valid death certificate and burial order;
     ` The sale price only includes the burial right;   
     ` The interment service is only charged as needed from the second year after ownership is
       taken of the burial right.                       
     Control is deemed to transfer at the point of full payment, as the customer:
     ` Gains legal ownership of the grave site;         
     ` Has the ability to transfer or on-sell the right;
     ` Receives a non-refundable burial right;          
     ` Prevents the Company from substituting or redirecting the site.
     Revenue for the burial right is recognised at a point in time, when full payment is received.
     Revenue for the burial (interment) service is recognised separately, at the point in time when
     the service is performed, based on receipt of the required regulatory documents and the
     execution of the burial.                           
     The Company offers customers the option to purchase burial rights on a lay-by (instalment)
     basis. In these cases, the customer pays over a defined period and only receives full rights to
     the grave site once payment has been completed in full. Revenue is not recognised on lay-by
     sales until the full purchase price has been received and the burial certificate is issued,
     transferring control of a specific grave site to the customer. Until that point, the transaction
     does not meet the criteria for revenue recognition under IFRS 15, as the Company retains
     control of the burial right and has not yet satisfied its performance obligation.
     Additional interments (e.g., second or third burials in the same grave site) are treated as
     separate revenue contracts/transactions and revenue is recognised at the point in time when
     the related services are rendered.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) or table notes are present in this section capture.** The disaggregated revenue table [D005.15, p.61] carries no footnotes. No missing-footnote verification question is required on that basis.
- **Qualification — enforceable right to payment (over-time criterion)**: The policy states the Group "only has an unconditional right to payment at agreed-upon milestones" but "considers there to be an enforceable right to payment when it has a legal, contractual right or it is customary business practice to demand or retain payment for performance completed to date if the contract were to be terminated" [D005.15, p.56]. This is a **judgemental qualification** — over-time revenue recognition on subsidised/infrastructure contracts depends on this enforceable-right assessment. Must be verified against contract terms and any auditor emphasis in D001.
- **Qualification — retention debtors**: "retention payments are not considered to be variable consideration... short term in nature (usually released within three to six months)" and "not considered to have a significant financing component" applying IFRS 15.129 practical expedient [D005.15, p.56]. This **contradicts the earlier assumption of 5–10% long-dated retentions**; the Group asserts 3–6 month release. Must be verified against Note 7 retention receivable aging.
- **Qualification — contract cost expensing**: "The cost incurred to obtain a contract, prior to finalisation of the revenue agreement, are expensed to profit or loss as and when the cost are incurred as the Group considers these costs not to be recoverable until an agreement has been reached" [D005.15, p.56]. This means **pre-contract bid/tender costs are expensed, not capitalised** — a margin drag that must be quantified in Note 24.
- **Qualification — feasibility-based POC**: "The Group uses approved feasibilities to determine the overall expected cost and attributable margin... Feasibilities are reviewed on a regular basis and approved by Exco" [D005.15, p.57]. POC and margin are **feasibility-model dependent** — prior-year feasibility revisions (Q4) remain a key risk; the "general cost allowances for unforeseen events" [D005.15, p.57] is an unquantified contingency embedded in cost-to-complete.
- **Qualification — Memorial Parks interment service contract modification**: "The Group revised the contractual terms for new customers for the interment service to be separately recognised once the service is required... assessed these changes in accordance with IFRS 15 as contract modifications or changes in estimates... did not impact any retrospective adjustment as it relates to new customers" [D005.15, p.60]. This **splits the burial right (point-in-time) from interment service (point-in-time on performance)** — forward Memorial Parks revenue will have a lower burial-right component and a deferred interment-service component; must be modelled.
- **Qualification — lay-by sales**: "Revenue is not recognised on lay-by sales until the full purchase price has been received and the burial certificate is issued" [D005.15, p.61]. Lay-by cash received but unrecognised sits as a **contract liability** — must be verified in Note 21/contract liabilities.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 26 footnote `*` — "Refer to notes 34, 35, 36 and 37 for further explanation of the relevant expenses"** `[D005.16, physical PDF p. 62]`. This footnote attaches to three lines: **Directors' fees – non-executive R3,943,908** (2025: R3,582,000), **Share scheme expense R7,703,555** (2025: R7,189,145), and **Employee costs R44,099,199** (2025: R43,000,195). Implication: the headline administrative-expense total of **R98,610,226** (2025: R95,477,969) contains a **R55,746,662 "Total employee and related fee costs"** block (2025: R53,771,340) that is only fully explained in Notes 34–37, which are **not in this capture**. Verification required: the split of the R7.7m share scheme expense between equity-settled (reserve) and cash-settled (liability), the vesting/forfeiture assumptions, and whether any portion is capitalised into contract costs (which would affect the gross margin read). Also note the arithmetic: R3,943,908 + R7,703,555 + R44,099,199 = **R55,746,662**, which ties exactly to the "Total employee and related fee costs" line — so the block is internally consistent, but the underlying Notes 34–37 definitions are unverified.

- **Note 28 closing qualification — "Refer to note 3.10 for the reconciliation of the expected credit losses/(gains) on financial and contract assets balances"** `[D005.16, physical PDF p. 62]`. This is the critical cross-reference. The Note 28 table shows a **net credit of R7,692,016**, but the composition is highly asymmetric: a **R6,413,164 credit on trade and other receivables** and a **R5,482,571 credit on JV loans** are offset by a **R4,203,719 charge on contract assets**. Implication for forecasting: the net credit flatters FY2026 earnings by ~R7.7m; if the trade-receivable and JV-loan credits are one-off reversals (e.g., collection of previously provided municipal debt, or JV loan recovery), the FY2027 ECL run-rate reverts to a charge. The Note 3.10 reconciliation (D005.2) must be checked to confirm whether the credits are releases due to cash collection (sustainable, lower forward charge) or model/assumption changes (non-recurring). The contract-asset charge of R4,203,719 is the only "normal" ECL charge and should be the baseline for forward contract-asset provisioning.

- **Note 25 fair-value line references — "Note 13" and "Note 15"** `[D005.16, physical PDF p. 62]`. The **R10,004,897 investment-property fair-value gain (Note 15)** and **R1,472,886 FVTPL fair-value gain (Note 13)** are non-cash and non-recurring. Implication: FY2026 "Other income" of R19,054,484 is **~60% non-cash fair-value gains** (R11,477,783). For forecasting, the recurring other-income base is closer to **R7.6m** (rentals R6,361,809 + bond commissions R758,668 + SETA/other R313,626 + profit on disposal R142,598), not R19.1m. The investment-property gain must be traced to Note 15 (D005.10) to confirm the revaluation basis and whether it is a one-off revaluation or a recurring annual fair-value adjustment.

- **Note 24 — no footnote markers present** `[D005.16, physical PDF p. 61]`. The cost-of-sales table is presented without footnotes, so there is no buried qualification in this note. However, the **absence** of a nature-of-expense breakdown (materials/subcontractors/labour/plant/depreciation) is itself a disclosure gap for a construction/materials group and is the reason Q22/Q54 remain partially open.

- **Note 27 — "Other expenses" of R257 (2025: R127,746)** `[D005.16, physical PDF p. 62]`. Trivial in amount but the 99.8% decline is unexplained; likely a reclassification of residential rental costs into Note 24 "Residential property development other costs" (which rose R19.7m). Low priority but worth a one-line confirmation in D005.1/D005.15.

**Q46 [Low] (remainder): Note 32 — reconcile finance income received R55.2m and finance cost paid R135.6m to D004 accruals (Notes 29/30); explain R92.1m gap; reconcile capitalised borrowing costs R102,143,192.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D006 cash flow statement)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 29 finance income totals R56,062,035 (2025: R64,252,797), of which R46,878,079 is JV interest (non-cash accrual) and only R5,599,123 is bank interest [D005.17, p.63]. Note 30 gross finance cost is R145,636,241, less R102,143,192 capitalised to construction contracts (2025: R63,728,343) and nil capitalised to inventory (2025: R12,164,129), giving R43,493,049 recognised in P&L [D005.17, p.63]. The R92.1m gap between cash interest paid (R135.6m) and P&L finance cost (R43.5m) is largely explained by the R102.1m capitalised borrowing cost — but the cash-flow statement reconciliation (interest paid vs accrual movement) still needs checking in D006.

**Q50 [High] (remainder): Notes 29/30 — decompose finance costs (bond/term/overdraft/lease, capitalised interest R102,143,192, IFRS 16); reconcile cash paid R135.6m to accrual R43.5m (R92.1m gap); explain finance costs −27.9% vs borrowings +24.8%.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D006)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Gross finance cost R145,636,241 comprises bank R5,440,883, unwinding of maintenance provision R2,446,625, lease liability R2,784,794, and interest-bearing borrowings R134,963,939 [D005.17, p.63]. The −27.9% P&L finance-cost fall is explained by the step-up in capitalised interest to R102,143,192 (from R63,728,343) — i.e. more borrowing cost capitalised into construction contracts, not lower gross cost (gross cost actually rose from R136,195,746 to R145,636,241). Cash-paid reconciliation still open for D006.

**Q26 [High] (remainder): Notes 29/30 — decompose finance income (JV loan interest vs cash) and finance costs; reconcile to D003 debt; explain finance costs −27.9% vs borrowings +24.8%; reconcile capitalised borrowing costs R102,143,192.**

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` on Note 32 working-capital lines (Maintenance provision / Trade and other payables)** [D005.17, p.64]:
> "The Maintenance provision has been reclassified from trade and other payables (previously 'Deferred maintenance revenue – Memorial Parks') to a separate line item in the current period. This presentation better reflects its nature as a provision for future maintenance obligations, rather than a payable."

- **Implication**: The FY2025 comparative for trade and other payables (R70,561,738) and maintenance provision (R10,027,683) are restated. This means the previously reported trade-payables movement (Q71/Q88) must be re-based — the R72.2m fall in trade payables may be partly a reclassification artefact, not pure supplier-credit substitution. **Must verify** in Note 19/Note 21 that the reclassified maintenance provision is excluded from trade payables and that the FY2025 comparative is consistently restated.

**Note 30 accounting policy — capitalisation of borrowing costs** [D005.17, p.63]:
> "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of 'land under development' (classified as inventories) are capitalised... Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the construction of the developments are treated as part of the construction contract costs... The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation is determined as follows: actual borrowing costs on funds specifically borrowed... less any temporary investment... weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the entity on funds generally borrowed... The borrowing costs capitalised do not exceed the total borrowing cost incurred."

- **Implication**: The R102,143,192 capitalised to construction contracts (2025: R63,728,343) is on **general borrowings** (explicitly stated). This is a critical earnings-quality issue: P&L finance cost of R43,493,049 is only ~30% of gross finance cost R145,636,241. If capitalisation rates normalise (e.g. as construction work completes), P&L finance cost could rise sharply. **Must verify** in Note 20 the weighted-average capitalisation rate and in Note 24 whether capitalised interest is embedded in contract cost-to-complete (affecting POC margin).

**Note 31 accounting policy — deferred tax asset recognition** [D005.17, p.63]:
> "Management uses cash flow forecasts due to the complexity of taxation legislation to determine whether deferred tax assets can be recognised in terms of IAS 12 and when the recognised deferred tax assets will be recovered."

- **Implication**: The sharp rise in estimated tax losses to R91,971,218 (2025: R34,222,876) [D005.17, p.64] implies a large DTA recognition judgement. If cash-flow forecasts supporting DTA recognition weaken, a DTA write-down could hit the P&L. **Must verify** in Note 17 the DTA recognised against these losses and the forecast period assumed.

**Note 31 reconciliation — duplicated line labels** [D005.17, p.64]:
> "Items non-taxable for tax purposes (4.30)% ... Accounting adjustments not deductible (4.30)% ... Other items 0.13% ... Other 0.13%"

- **Implication**: The reconciliation table appears to have duplicated/mislabelled rows (the (4.30)% and 0.13% lines appear twice). The arithmetic still sums to 23.87% ETR, but the labels are unreliable. **Must verify** the underlying tax computation in the tax note workings.

**Note 34 footnote `*` — Belhar Calgro M3 Development** [D005.17, p.65]:
> "No non-controlling interest is accounted for relating to Belhar Calgro M3 Development Company Proprietary Limited. In terms of the shareholders agreement the Group has a preferential right to a share of the profits before any distributions may be made to the other shareholder."

- **Implication**: Belhar is 51%-owned but no NCI is recognised — a departure from standard NCI accounting justified by a preferential profit right. This affects the NCI line and EPS. **Must verify** the shareholders' agreement terms and whether this treatment is consistent with IFRS 10.

**Note 34 footnote `#` — Procurement companies** [D005.17, p.65]:
> "The procurement companies relate to Calgro M3 Procurement Management Proprietary Limited (holding entity), Calgro M3 Procurement Services Proprietary Limited, Calgro M3 Contractors Proprietary Limited and Calgro M3 Property Sales Proprietary Limited."

- **Implication**: Four procurement entities consolidated with 51% NCI and negative equity (R(24,374)). These are loss-making (NCI −R12,408). **Must verify** whether these entities carry any guarantee/contingent liability exposure to the Group.

**Note 34 — CTE Consulting "Correction" R3,184,750 (2025)** [D005.17, p.65]:
> "Correction of CTE Consulting Proprietary Limited – 3,184,750"

- **Implication**: A prior-year correction of R3,184,750 in CTE Consulting equity — this is a prior-period error correction that needs explanation. **Must verify** in the statement of changes in equity (D004) and any prior-period restatement note.

**Note 33 — JV→joint operation non-cash tax impact R99,268** [D005.17, p.64]:
- **Implication**: Confirms the Bankenveld reclassification had a tax effect. Small, but confirms the reclassification is real and flows through tax. **Must verify** in Note 39 the full tax and equity impact.

--- Section D005.18 | [AFS] physical page 66 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 35 ---
                                          
 35. Share-based payments                 
                                          
     Accounting policy                    
     Share-based compensation benefits are provided to employees via
     Share Appreciation Rights Schemes or Calgro M3 Share Schemes.
     Share Appreciation Rights Schemes are settled in equity, i.e. the
     employees receive shares or options at settlement. The year in
     which the employee renders services to the Group to obtain the
     award is the year in which the expense is recognised in the
     statement of comprehensive income with a corresponding increase
     recognised in equity. The expense is determined by measuring the
     fair value of the scheme on inception of the scheme and amortised
     over the life of the scheme.         
     The fair value of shares granted to Directors and employees under
     Calgro M3 Share Schemes are recognised as an expense over the
     relevant service period. The fair value is measured at the grant date
     of the shares and is recognised in equity in the share-based
     payment reserve.                     
     If the share-based payments granted do not vest until the
     counterparty completes a specified period of service, the Group
     accounts for those services as they are rendered by the counterparty
     during the vesting period on a straight-line basis over the vesting
     period. If the share-based payments vest immediately, the services
     received are recognised in full.     
     If an equity-settled award is cancelled, it is treated as if it had vested
     on the date of cancellation, and any expense not yet recognised for
     the award is recognised immediately. 
     However, if a new award is substituted for the cancelled award, and
     designated as a replacement award on the date that it is granted,
     the cancelled and new award are treated as if they were a
     modification of the original award, as described in the previous
     paragraph.                           
     Significant judgement and source of estimation uncertainty
     Management uses generally accepted valuation methods to
     determine the value of the share-based payment schemes.

 Valuation of schemes                          
 Valuation of the instruments for both schemes is achieved by performing a Monte Carlo
 simulation involving the CGR share, volatility, risk free rates, and certain dividend
 assumptions.                                  
 The process assumed is risk-neutral geometric Brownian motion. If vesting is achieved
 according to the vesting schedules, the number of shares issued to settle the vested
 share appreciation rights is calculated as:   
 N = TSR x (S – K)/S                           
                                               
 where:                                        
                                               
 S  The 30-day VWAP of CGR on each vesting date
 K  The base price; being the 30-day VWAP of CGR on commencement date
 N  The number of share appreciation rights granted
                                               
 TSR The percentage vesting according to the vesting schedule

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `[^#]` (Management – FY22 scheme)** [D005.18, p.68]: "This share scheme was implemented in the FY22 financial year." — Definitional only; confirms vintage. No financial impact beyond confirming the FY22 tranche is in its final vesting year (final vesting September 2026 per p.67), so remaining 322,595 SARs will vest/cancel within FY2027 — relevant to FY2027 SBP expense run-rate.
- **Footnote `&` (Management – FY24)** [p.68]: "implemented in the prior financial year" — confirms FY24 tranche first vesting September 2026 (p.67), i.e., **no FY2026 vesting yet**; the 423,080 cancelled/vested in the table must therefore be cancellations/forfeitures, not vesting. This is a tension worth flagging: the table labels the column "vested/cancelled/not vested" but FY24 Management first vesting is Sept 2026, so the (423,080) movement in FY2026 is forfeiture — verify.
- **Footnote `%` (Executive – FY24)** [p.68]: "implemented in the FY24 financial year" — first vesting January 2024, annual five tranches to January 2028. The (4,320,000) movement includes 720,000 (Naicker) + 600,000 (Langson) retained and 1,500,000 + 1,500,000 (Williams, Joubert) fully cancelled — i.e., **two executives forfeited entire awards** (Williams, Joubert show nil remaining). This is a governance/retention signal and confirms SBP expense reversal.
- **Footnote `@` (FY26 schemes)** [p.68]: "implemented in the current financial year" — Executive FY26 (4.5m SARs, base R5.26) and Management FY26 (995,000 SARs, base R4.90) are new; first vesting Jan 2026 (Exec) and Sept 2027 (Mgmt). The (900,000) and (200,000×2 + 500,000) movements in FY2026 are **cancellations/forfeitures in year one**, not vesting — flag as unusual (high early forfeiture).
- **Arithmetic tension — total remaining SARs**: p.67 table totals "Remaining number of SAR 6,351,412"; p.68 reconciliation totals "Remaining not vested 7,251,412". **Difference of 900,000** — the p.67 total appears to omit the Executive FY26 900,000 tranche or a footing error. Flag as verification question.
- **Arithmetic tension — intrinsic value columns**: p.68 "Intrinsic value of share scheme on commencement date" total R45,522,209 vs "Intrinsic value not vested" R(7,648,559) vs "Intrinsic value on reporting date" R48,220,768. The "not vested" column is labelled as a negative but the "to be released per vesting period" total R7,648,559 equals the absolute of it — internally consistent but the sign convention is ambiguous. Also, "intrinsic value on reporting date" (R48.2m) exceeds "commencement" (R45.5m) despite share price falling from R5.26/R4.90 base to reporting date — verify the share price used and whether "intrinsic value" is actually fair value (Monte Carlo) not intrinsic.
- **Valuation methodology** [p.67]: Monte Carlo, risk-neutral GBM, TSR formula N = TSR × (S−K)/S. **No volatility, risk-free rate, dividend yield, or expected life inputs are disclosed** — a significant omission for a scheme with R48.2m fair value. Flag for D007/Note 1 or auditor (D001) key audit matter.
- **Performance condition** [p.67]: Management schemes require "Total shareholder return of 20% per vesting period, measured against the base price." This is a **steep hurdle** (20% per vesting period, not cumulative) — high probability of non-vesting, which supports the large forfeiture/cancellation movements and the negative reserve. Relevant to forecasting future SBP expense (likely lower than gross grant-date fair value suggests).
- **Accounting policy** [p.66]: "If an equity-settled award is cancelled, it is treated as if it had vested on the date of cancellation, and any expense not yet recognised is recognised immediately." — This means the FY2026 cancellations (Williams/Joubert full forfeiture, FY26 early cancellations) triggered **accelerated expense recognition** in FY2026, inflating the R7,703,556 SBP expense. Flag: FY2027 SBP expense should normalise lower absent new grants.
- **No footnote text missing** in this capture — all four footnote markers (`#`, `&`, `%`, `@`) have definitions present on p.68.

 36. Employee costs                                     
                                                        
     Accounting policy                                  
     (a) Defined contribution plans                     
         A defined contribution plan is a pension plan under which the Group pays fixed
         contributions into a separate entity. The Group has no legal or constructive obligations
         to pay further contributions if the fund does not hold sufficient assets to pay all
         employees the benefits relating to employee service in the current and prior years.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

**Q236 [Medium]: SBP expense R7,703,556 (note 25) vs Note 26 R7,703,555 — R1 rounding; confirm Note 25 vs Note 26 cross-reference correct.**
- **Status**: `Resolved`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 36 (Employee costs) confirms "Share scheme expenses" of **R7,703,556** for 2026 [D005.19, physical PDF p. 69], matching the Note 25 figure of R7,703,556 [D005.18, p. 69] and differing from Note 26's R7,703,555 [D005.16, p.62] by R1 (rounding). The Note 36 table is the employee-cost build; the R1 difference is a rounding artefact, not a reconciliation failure. No further action required.

**Q234 [Medium]: Williams and Joubert (Executive FY24) fully forfeited 1,500,000 SARs each; FY26 schemes show 900,000 + 900,000 early cancellations in year one; confirm reasons and accelerated expense per policy.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D005.18/D001)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 38 footnote  confirms the acceleration mechanism: "The share-based payment expense includes the acceleration of the remaining expense of the long-term share incentive scheme for WA Joubert and W Williams. Due to his resignation in the financial year the total amount remaining under this scheme has been expensed in the respective financial year. This was a non-cash movement in the period." [D005.19, physical PDF p. 71]. This confirms the *reason* (resignation → full acceleration) and *non-cash* nature. It does **not** reconcile the 900,000 + 900,000 early-cancellation tranches flagged in Q234 — that reconciliation remains open for D005.18/D001.

**Q233 [High]: Vesting of shares −R6,031,799 to reserve; 198,000 shares withheld for tax; confirm cash tax paid on vesting (PAYE) in "tax paid" R3,890,706; quantify PAYE; confirm no cash outflow for R6,031,799.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D006)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 37(iii) footnote * confirms "This amount relates to the share-based payment expense recognised in the statement of comprehensive income and is **not a cash consideration paid to Directors**" [D005.19, physical PDF p. 70]. Note 38 footnote  reiterates "This was a **non-cash movement** in the period" [D005.19, p. 71]. This confirms no cash outflow for the SBP expense itself. The PAYE quantification and its inclusion in "tax paid" R3,890,706 remains open for D006.

**Q35 [Medium]: Note 35 — share-based payment reserve movement to −R1,540,004: composition, reversal/forfeiture, recurring SBP expense.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D005.18)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 37(iii) provides the director-level SBP expense build for 2026: WA Joubert –; W Williams R3,039,474; BP Malherbe R1,223,236; SU Naicker R1,322,979; AJ Langson R1,184,031; total directors R6,769,720; prescribed officers R–; **total R6,769,720** [D005.19, p. 70]. Note 38 confirms total Executive Directors SBP expense R6,769,719 [D005.19, p. 71] (R1 rounding). This is the director-attributable portion of the R7,703,556 total; the residual ~R933,836 relates to non-director employees. Composition of the reserve movement itself (reclassification −R3,697,458) remains open for D005.18.

**Q232 [High]: Monte Carlo valuation discloses no volatility, risk-free rate, dividend yield, or expected life inputs; fair value R48,220,768; locate inputs.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D001/D005.18)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 37(iii) confirms the number of shares granted in 2026: BP Malherbe 2,500,000; SU Naicker 1,000,000; AJ Langson 1,000,000; total directors 4,500,000 [D005.19, p. 70]. This is the grant-volume input to the Monte Carlo valuation but does **not** supply the missing volatility/risk-free/dividend/expected-life inputs. Those remain open for D001/D005.18.

**Q231 [High]: Total remaining SARs: p.67 = 6,351,412 vs p.68 = 7,251,412 — 900,000 difference; reconcile.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D005.18)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 37(iii) shows 2026 grants of 4,500,000 director SARs (Malherbe 2,500,000; Naicker 1,000,000; Langson 1,000,000) [D005.19, p. 70]. This confirms the FY26 grant tranche volume but does not resolve which 900,000 tranche is omitted/double-counted between the two Note 25 tables. Remains open for D005.18.

**Q238 [Low]: Check D001 for SBP as key audit matter or scope limitation given R48.2m fair value with undisclosed inputs.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D001)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 38 footnote  confirms the acceleration of Joubert/Williams remaining expense was a **non-cash** movement [D005.19, p. 71], and Note 37(iii) footnote * confirms SBP is non-cash [D005.19, p. 70]. This supports the non-cash character but does not address the auditor's KAM treatment. Remains open for D001.
