### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote 1 — Note 38, p. 71: `#` performance incentive definition.**
- **Quote**: "The performance incentive relates to the expense raised in the current financial year, the amount payable in relation to the long-term performance incentive is included below." [D005.19, physical PDF p. 71]
- **Implication**: The R2,252,437 "Long term" column in the 2026 Executive Directors table is an **expense**, not a cash payment; the cash settlement is shown separately in the "Incentive settled in FY26" column (R3,662,678 total) [D005.19, p. 72]. This creates a timing difference between P&L expense and cash outflow that must be modelled separately. Verify in D006 whether the R3,662,678 settled in FY26 is captured in "cash paid to employees" or a separate line.

**Footnote 2 — Note 38, p. 71: `$` Williams resignation.**
- **Quote**: "$ Resigned 30 June 2025." [D005.19, p. 71]
- **Implication**: Williams' R1,921,914 guaranteed remuneration and R3,039,474 SBP expense are for a **half-year** only. Annualising would overstate run-rate director cost by ~R1.9m guaranteed + ~R3.0m SBP. The FY2027 director cost base should exclude Williams entirely. Verify in D007/D001 whether a replacement was appointed.

**Footnote 3 — Note 38, p. 71: `^` signing bonus.**
- **Quote**: "^ Signing bonus as agreed with Remuneration and Nomination Committee on joining the Group as part of negotiation of annual salary package." [D005.19, p. 71]
- **Implication**: AJ Langson's R225,000 signing bonus is **non-recurring**; FY2027 director cost should be reduced by this amount. Verify no further signing bonuses in FY2027.

**Footnote 4 — Note 38, p. 71: `·` Langson appointment date.**
- **Quote**: "· Appointed 6 September 2024, the amount disclosed includes the remuneration portion applicable for services as an Executive Director of the Calgro M3 Group." [D005.19, p. 71]
- **Implication**: Langson's FY2025 figures are **part-year** (from 6 Sep 2024); FY2026 is the first full year. FY2026 guaranteed R3,150,000 is the run-rate baseline. Verify in D007 whether any further appointment-date adjustments apply.

**Footnote 5 — Note 38, p. 71: `` Joubert/Lategan resignation marker.**
- **Quote**: " Resigned 31 December 2024." [D005.19, p. 71]
- **Implication**: Joubert and Lategan FY2025 figures are **part-year**; FY2026 excludes them entirely. The FY2025 comparative total of R22,996,661 is inflated by their part-year cost; FY2026 R17,685,459 is the clean run-rate. Verify in D007 that no residual obligations remain.

**Footnote 6 — Note 38, p. 71: `` SBP acceleration.**
- **Quote**: " The share-based payment expense includes the acceleration of the remaining expense of the long-term share incentive scheme for WA Joubert and W Williams. Due to his resignation in the financial year the total amount remaining under this scheme has been expensed in the respective financial year. This was a non-cash movement in the period." [D005.19, p. 71]
- **Implication**: This is the **critical** footnote. It confirms (a) the SBP expense is **non-cash**, (b) the acceleration is triggered by **resignation**, and (c) the full remaining expense was recognised in the year of resignation. This means FY2026 SBP expense of R7,703,556 is **inflated by acceleration** and is **not a run-rate**. FY2027 SBP expense should be materially lower (only ongoing schemes, no acceleration). Verify in D005.18 the split between normal and accelerated SBP expense; verify in D006 that no cash outflow corresponds to the accelerated portion.

**Footnote 7 — Note 37(iii), p. 70: `*` SBP non-cash.**
- **Quote**: "* This amount relates to the share-based payment expense recognised in the statement of comprehensive income and is not a cash consideration paid to Directors." [D005.19, p. 70]
- **Implication**: Confirms SBP is a **non-cash** charge; the R6,769,720 director SBP expense has no cash counterpart. This is a key add-back in the CFO reconciliation. Verify in D006 that the R7,703,556 total SBP expense is added back in the cash-flow statement.

**Footnote 8 — Note 37(iii), p. 70: `#` resignation dates.**
- **Quote**: "# WA Joubert resigned on 31 December 2024 and W Williams resigned on 30 June 2025." [D005.19, p. 70]
- **Implication**: Confirms the resignation dates driving the SBP acceleration (Footnote 6) and the part-year director costs. Williams' FY2026 SBP expense of R3,039,474 is entirely **accelerated** (he resigned 30 June 2025, so no FY2026 service). This is a non-recurring charge. Verify in D005.18 the normal vs accelerated split.

**Footnote 9 — Note 37(iii), p. 70: `%` appointment/resignation reference.**
- **Quote**: "% For Directors and prescribed officers' appointments and resignations, refer to note 38." [D005.19, p. 70]
- **Implication**: Cross-reference to Note 38 for appointment/resignation dates; no new information, but confirms Note 38 is the authoritative source for director tenure.

**Footnote 10 — Note 38, p. 72: `$` LTI unwinding.**
- **Quote**: "$ This balance includes the unwinding of the discounted value of the long-term performance incentives." [D005.19, p. 72]
- **Implication**: The LTI balances (2024 R1,057,164; 2026 R1,195,273; total R2,252,437) include **unwinding of discount** — i.e., a finance-cost-like accretion embedded in the LTI expense. This is a non-cash charge that grows as the discount unwinds. Verify in D007 whether the unwinding is classified in employee costs (Note 36) or finance costs (Note 30); the classification affects the operating margin.

**Footnote 11 — Note 38, p. 73: `#` performance incentive split.**
- **Quote**: "# The performance incentive included above is split between a short-term incentive payable in the 2026 financial year and a long-term incentive vesting in two tranches starting in the 2026 financial year." [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: Confirms the LTI vests in **two tranches** starting FY2026; the FY2026 expense is only the first tranche. FY2027 will carry the second tranche, so LTI expense is **not** a one-off — it recurs. Verify in D005.18 the tranche schedule and FY2027 expected LTI expense.

**Footnote 12 — Note 38, p. 73: `*` LTI definition.**
- **Quote**: "* Long-term performance incentive" [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: Definitional only; no new information.

**Footnote 13 — Note 38, p. 73: `$` LTI unwinding (prescribed officers).**
- **Quote**: "$ This balance includes the unwinding of the discounted value of the long-term performance incentive as disclosed in the prior year." [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: Same as Footnote 10 but for prescribed officers; confirms the unwinding is a recurring non-cash charge.

**Footnote 14 — Note 36, p. 69: `*` Executive Directors emoluments definition.**
- **Quote**: "* The Executive Directors emoluments' includes only the guaranteed remuneration, cash-settled long-term incentive and the short-term incentive." [D005.19, p. 69]
- **Implication**: The R17,685,459 Executive Directors emoluments in Note 36 **exclude** share-based payment (R6,769,719) and the LTI unwinding. The total director cost is therefore R17,685,459 + R6,769,719 = R24,455,178, plus the LTI unwinding embedded in the R2,252,437. This is a **material** reconciliation: Note 36's R21,629,367 total directors' emoluments is **not** the full economic cost. Verify in D007 the full director cost including SBP and LTI unwinding.

**Footnote 15 — Note 36, p. 69: "Amounts allocated to qualifying assets (construction contracts)".**
- **Quote**: "Less: Amounts allocated to qualifying assets (construction contracts) (44 944 299) (48 902 740)" [D005.19, p. 69]
- **Implication**: R44,944,299 of employee costs (2025: R48,902,740) is **capitalised** into construction contracts, reducing the P&L employee expense from R100,690,961 to R55,746,662. This is a **non-cash** capitalisation that sits inside contract cost-to-complete and therefore affects the POC margin. The 8.1% decline in capitalised employee costs (R48.9m → R44.9m) may signal either lower construction activity or a shift in labour mix. Verify in D007 whether this capitalisation is embedded in the contract-asset movement and whether the decline is consistent with revenue growth.

**Footnote 16 — Note 37(a)(iii), p. 70: Calgro M3 Educational Trust independence.**
- **Quote**: "Calgro does not control Calgro M3 trust as the trustees are independent and the Trust is not reliant on specified funding from Calgro." [D005.19, p. 70]
- **Implication**: Confirms the Trust is **not consolidated** and no NCI/contingency arises. The R395,170 trade payable is an arm's-length related-party balance. Verify in D001 that the auditor concurs with the non-control assessment.

**Footnote 17 — Note 37(b)(ii), p. 70: JV finance income and net contract revenue.**
- **Quote**: Table showing finance income received: Table View R2,884,438 (2025: R18,310); Witpoortjie R42,423,488 (2025: R44,023,725); South Hills R1,570,153 (2025: R4,732,265); total R46,878,079 (2025: R48,774,300); net contract revenue received from South Hills R81,890,185 (2025: R37,547,649) [D005.19, p. 70].
- **Implication**: This is the **cash** JV interest received, which is ~85% of total finance income R55.2m. The **+118% increase** in South Hills net contract revenue received (R37.5m → R81.9m) is a material positive signal for JV activity and contradicts the earlier "South Hills revenue −63.9%" note (Q56). The **−3.9% decline** in total JV finance income received is modest, not the −44.1% JV profit decline noted earlier (Q25) — confirming the profit decline is margin-driven, not volume-driven. Verify in D007 the JV profit share and margin.

**Footnote 18 — Note 38, p. 72: 2025 LTI no additional allocation.**
- **Quote**: "In the 2025 financial year, no additional allocation was made to the long-term performance incentive for Executive Management. The vesting of the previous financial years allocations will be paid upon reaching the predetermined vesting conditions. The first tranche of the 2024 long-term performance incentive along with the second tranche of the 2023 long-term performance incentive will vest in May 2025." [D005.19, p. 72]
- **Implication**: Confirms FY2025 had **no new LTI grants** — the FY2025 LTI expense of R5,024,886 is entirely **vesting of prior-year allocations**. FY2026 introduced new grants (R1,195,273), so FY2027 will carry both the FY2026 vesting and any new FY2027 grants. Verify in D005.18 the FY2027 LTI vesting schedule.

**Footnote 19 — Note 38, p. 73: 2025 LTI vesting May 2026.**
- **Quote**: "The first tranche of the 2024 long-term performance incentive along with the second tranche of the 2023 long-term performance incentive will vest in May 2026." [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: Confirms a **May 2026 cash vesting** of prior-year LTIs — this will be a cash outflow in FY2027 (or late FY2026). The "Incentive settled in FY26" column shows R3,662,678 settled in FY2026 [D005.19, p. 72]; the May 2026 tranche will add to FY2027 cash costs. Verify in D006 the cash settlement timing and in D007 the FY2027 LTI cash obligation.

**Footnote 20 — Note 38, p. 73: 2023 first tranche vested May 2024.**
- **Quote**: "The first tranche of the 2023 long-term performance incentive vested in May 2024." [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: Confirms the two-tranche vesting pattern (May 2024, May 2026 for 2023 LTI). This is a **recurring biennial** cash cost pattern. Verify in D005.18 the full tranche schedule.

**Footnote 21 — Note 38, p. 73: "In the 2026 financial year, there were no Prescribed Officers."**
- **Quote**: "In the 2026 financial year, there were no Prescribed Officers." [D005.19, p. 73]
- **Implication**: AJ Langson was a prescribed officer in FY2025 (R1,622,368 total) but was appointed Executive Director on 6 Sep 2024, so his FY2026 cost is in the Executive Directors table (R5,984,560). The FY2026 prescribed-officer cost is **nil** — a R1.6m reduction vs FY2025. Verify in D007 that no new prescribed officers were appointed.

**Footnote 22 — Note 38, p. 73: 2025 prescribed officer LTI table anomaly.**
- **Quote**: The 2025 prescribed officer LTI table shows columns "2023 long-term performance incentive", "2024 long-term performance incentive", "2026 long-term performance incentive", "2026 long-term performance incentive", "Total long-term performance incentive", "Incentive settled in FY25" — with AJ Langson all nil [D005.19, p. 73].
- **Implication**: The column headers appear **mislabelled** (two "2026" columns, no "2025" column). This is a presentation error that should be flagged. The nil values for Langson are consistent with his FY2025 prescribed-officer status being superseded by his Executive Director appointment. Verify in D007 whether the table is corrected in the final AFS.

**Footnote 23 — Note 36, p. 69: Bonus plans policy.**
- **Quote**: "The Group recognises an expense for bonuses, based on a formula that takes into consideration the profit attributable to the Group's shareholders after certain adjustments. The Group recognises an accrual where contractually obliged or where there is a past practice that has created a constructive obligation. The Group expects these liabilities to be settled within 12 months." [D005.19, p. 69]
- **Implication**: Bonus accruals are **profit-linked** and settled within 12 months. This means the bonus expense is **variable** with HEPS and should be modelled as a % of profit, not a fixed cost. The "certain adjustments" language is vague — verify in D007 whether the bonus formula is disclosed and whether it excludes SBP/one-offs.

**Footnote 24 — Note 36, p. 69: Short-term benefits policy.**
- **Quote**: "The costs of short-term employee benefits include those expected to be settled wholly within 12 months after the service is rendered, such as paid vacation leave, sick leave, and bonuses. The expected cost of compensated absences is recognised as an expense as the employees render services that increase their entitlement or, in the case of non-accumulating absences, when the absence occurs." [D005.19, p. 69]
- **Implication**: Leave accruals are recognised as service is rendered; this is a **recurring** non-cash accrual that reverses on payment. Verify in D007 the leave accrual balance and whether it is material.

**Footnote 25 — Note 36, p. 69: Defined contribution policy.**
- **Quote**: "A defined contribution plan is a pension plan under which the Group pays fixed contributions into a separate entity. The Group has no legal or constructive obligations to pay further contributions if the fund does not hold sufficient assets to pay all employees the benefits relating to employee service in the current and prior years. Payments to defined contribution retirement benefit plans are charged as an expense as they fall due." [D005.19, p. 69]
- **Implication**: No defined-benefit pension risk — a **positive** for balance-sheet solvency. Retirement costs are cash-as-they-fall-due, so no actuarial deficit risk. Verify in D007 the retirement cost amount (not separately disclosed in Note 36) and whether it is material.

  39. Investments in joint operations                    
     Joint arrangements are arrangements in which the Group shares joint control with one or more
     parties. Joint control is the contractually agreed sharing of control of an arrangement and
     exists only when decisions about the activities that significantly affect the arrangement’s
     returns require the unanimous consent of the parties sharing control. Joint arrangements are
     classified as either joint operations or joint ventures based on the rights and obligations of the
     parties to the arrangement. In joint operations, the parties have rights to the assets and
     obligations for the liabilities relating to the arrangement, whereas in joint ventures, the parties
     have rights to the net assets of the arrangement.   
     Joint arrangements that are structured through a separate vehicle may be either joint
     operations or joint ventures depending on the specific facts and circumstances of the
     arrangement.                                        
     In these cases, consideration is given to the legal form of the separate vehicle, the terms of the
     contractual arrangement and, when relevant, other facts and circumstances. When the
     activities of an arrangement are primarily designed for the provision of output to the parties,
     and the parties are substantially the only source of cash flows contributing to the continuity of
     the operations of the arrangement, this indicates that the parties to the arrangements have
     rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities.
     These arrangements are primarily designed for the provision of output to the parties sharing
     joint control, indicating that the parties have rights to substantially all the economic benefits of
     the assets. The liabilities of the arrangements are in substance satisfied by cash flows received
     from the parties; this dependence indicates that the parties effectively have obligations for the
     liabilities. It is primarily these facts and circumstances that give rise to the classification as joint
     operations.                                         
                                                         
     The Group holds a 50% interest in Bankenveld District City Proprietary Limited (“BDC”) which
     operates in Johannesburg, South Africa. The nature of the activities of BDC is the installation of
     bulk services for the development of the mixed use residential and commercial precinct. This has
     historically been accounted for as a joint venture and therefore recognised using the equity
     method in accordance with IFRS 11: Joint Arrangements and IAS 28: Investments in Associates
     and Joint Ventures.                                 
     Following changes, effective 1 September 2025, the Group has obtained rights to the assets and
     obligations for the liabilities on the basis that the arrangement is designed to provide outputs to
     the parties involved in the arrangement. As a result, the joint arrangement has been classified as
     a joint operation under IFRS 11.                    
                                                         
     Management has exercised significant judgement in assessing the joint arrangement structure
     and the rights and obligations arising from the revised contractual terms (IFRS 11.15).

--- Section D005.20 | [AFS] physical page 74 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 39,40 ---
                                                     
  Based on this evaluation, the arrangement meets the definition of a joint operation because the
  parties now have in substance rights to assets and obligations for liabilities on the basis that the
  arrangement is designed to provide outputs to the parties involved in the arrangement.
                                                     
  From the effective date, the Group derecognised the equity-accounted investment and recognised
  its proportionate share of the joint operation’s assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses in
  accordance with IFRS 11.20–21. This change reflects a change in facts and circumstances which
  is accounted for prospectively.                    
  At the date of transition, the following financial impacts are recognised (based on the latest
  available financial information of the arrangement):
  ` Cash and cash equivalents                        
  ` Trade and other receivables                      
  ` Inventories/construction contracts               
  ` Deferred income tax asset                        
  ` Trade and other payables                         
  ` Current income tax liabilities                   
  ` Loans to joint ventures                          
  As the arrangement is accounted for as a joint operation, the Group no longer recognise a single
  “share of profit of equity-accounted investees”. Instead, the Group will present its proportionate
  share of:                                          
  1. Revenue                                         
  2. Cost of sales                                   
  3. Administration expenses                         
  4. Finance income/expenses                         
  5. Tax expenses                                    
  6. Rental income                                   
  7. Operating expenses                              
  The classification change occurred from 1 September 2025, when the revised terms became
  binding. The change has been applied prospectively in accordance with IFRS 11.

  40. Earnings per share (and other performance indicators)
      Accounting policy                                 
      Basic earnings per share                          
      Earnings per share is calculated using the weighted average number of ordinary shares in issue
      during the year and is based on the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders.
                                                        
      Diluted earnings per share                        
      Diluted earnings per share is calculated by adjusting the weighted average number of ordinary
      shares outstanding to assume conversion of all dilutive potential ordinary shares and is based
      on the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders, adjusted for the after-tax dilutive effect.
      For the share schemes, a calculation is done to determine the number of the Group’s shares
      that would be required at fair value to settle the monetary value of the rights, after deducting
      the unamortised share-based payment value. For the purposes of this calculation, the average
      annual market share price of the Group is used.   
      Headline earnings per share                       
      Headline earnings per share is calculated using the weighted average number of ordinary
      shares in issue during the year and is based on the earnings attributable to ordinary
      shareholders, after excluding those items as required by Circular 1/2023 issued by the South
      African Institute of Chartered Accountants (“SAICA”).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 39 — BDC joint-operation transition table is blank** [D005.20, p.74]: The table listing "Cash and cash equivalents / Trade and other receivables / Inventories/construction contracts / Deferred income tax asset / Trade and other payables / Current income tax liabilities / Loans to joint ventures" shows **only line labels with no amounts**. This is a material omission: the transition-date carrying amounts of assets and liabilities brought on (and derecognised equity-accounted investment) are **not visible in this capture**. The R19,252,380 direct debit to retained income (per earlier sections) cannot be verified here. **Verification question raised**: obtain the transition-date amounts and reconcile to the R19.25m equity adjustment and to Note 32/Note 39.

- **Note 39 — "prospectively" applied** [D005.20, p.74]: The change is accounted for **prospectively** as a change in facts and circumstances (not a prior-period error). This means **no restatement of comparatives**; FY2026 revenue/expenses will include BDC's proportionate share only from 1 September 2025 (4 months). Forecast implication: **partial-year consolidation** — FY2027 will carry a full year of BDC proportionate revenue/costs, creating a **year-on-year step-up** that must be modelled separately from organic growth.

- **Note 39 — "Management has exercised significant judgement"** [D005.20, p.74]: Explicit IFRS 11.15 judgement qualification. This is a **key audit matter candidate** — check D001 for auditor's assessment of the joint-operation classification (rights to assets / obligations for liabilities).

- **Note 40 — EPS presentation "Gross pre-tax and non-controlling interest" vs "Net"** [D005.20, p.75]: Two columns presented. Gross profit attributable to shareholders R207,593,763 (2026) vs Net R160,235,004 (2026). The **R47,358,759 difference = tax + NCI**. Basic EPS 216.83c (gross) vs 167.36c (net). **Forecast must use the Net column** (167.36c) for EPS/HEPS modelling. Note the **gross figure is pre-tax and pre-NCI** — do not confuse with headline.

- **Note 40 — Headline adjustments** [D005.20, p.75]: Only two adjustments in 2026: profit on disposal of PP&E/software −R142,598 and fair-value adjustment on investment properties −R10,004,897. **No scrapping, no impairment, no onerous-contract add-back** in 2026. This is a **clean headline** — but the R10.0m investment-property fair-value gain is **non-cash and non-recurring**; strip it from underlying earnings. 2025 had only −R345,798 fair-value adjustment plus trivial scrapping.

- **Note 40 — Dilutive share-scheme adjustment fell from 2,113,191 to 1,404,290 shares** [D005.20, p.75]: Consistent with **forfeitures/cancellations** of SARs (Q234/Q235). Diluted EPS 213.69c (gross) / 164.94c (net); diluted HEPS 203.25c (gross) / 154.50c (net) [D005.20, pp.75–76]. The **dilution gap is narrowing** — forecast dilution should use the lower 1.4m share adjustment unless new schemes are granted.

- **Note 40 — NAV per share** [D005.20, p.76]: Net assets R1,571,178,648 ÷ 95,380,601 shares = 1,647.27c. **Total assets R3,690,857,834; total liabilities R2,119,679,186.** This confirms the **balance-sheet totals** for the forecast model and the **equity base** (R1,571.2m). Note NAV rose 10.8% despite profit falling — driven by **retained earnings + reserve movements**, not new equity.

- **Note 40 — "number of shares in issue" 95,380,601 vs weighted average 95,742,067** [D005.20, pp.75–76]: The **161,466-share gap** reflects the **buyback timing** (shares repurchased during the year, so weighted average > year-end). Consistent with Q168 buyback. Forecast should use **year-end 95,380,601** for forward NAV/EPS unless further buybacks.

41. Going concern                                      
   The Group and Company financial statements have been prepared on the going concern basis.
   The basis presumes that funds will be available to finance future operations and that the
   realisation of assets and settlement of liabilities, contingent obligations and commitments will
   occur in the ordinary course of business.           
                                                       
   The Board has considered the Group’s cash flow forecasts for the foreseeable future, with the
   consideration given to the uncertainty in operational performance, Company specific risks and
   other wider macroeconomic environment risks.        
   The Group maintains sufficient liquidity throughout the period to furnish its liabilities as they fall
   due.                                                
                                                       
   In considering the going concern assumption the following factors have a potential market impact
   on the Group:                                       
   ` The current reduction in the interest rates has not impacted the granting of the 100% home
     loans in the lower to middle tier of the market.  
   ` Government committed to the need for dignified housing in the recent budget speech held on
     25 February 2026.                                 
   Our belief is that this will bring about new opportunities in the sector.
   The geopolitical events currently have no impact on the Group’s cash flow forecasts, this will be
   assessed on an ongoing basis.                       
                                                       
42. Events after the reporting year                    
   No events have occurred subsequent to the reporting date that require adjustment to, or
   disclosure in, the consolidated and separate financial statements to be taken into account.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in this section** `[D005.21, p. 76]`. The section consists of two narrative notes (41 Going concern; 42 Events after the reporting year) with no tables and no footnote definitions. No missing-footnote-text flag is required.

- **Note 41 — Going concern (qualification unpacking)** `[D005.21, p. 76]`:
  - The basis "presumes that funds will be available to finance future operations and that the realisation of assets and settlement of liabilities, contingent obligations and commitments will occur in the ordinary course of business." This is a **standard-form going-concern boilerplate**, not a quantified liquidity demonstration. It does **not** disclose: committed undrawn facility headroom, covenant compliance status, maturity profile, or lender-support arrangements — all of which are material given the earlier finding that all R1,380.3m borrowings are unsecured and CFO was negative R14.8m. Must be verified against D001 (auditor's going-concern conclusion / material uncertainty) and Note 20 (facility headroom, covenants).
  - "The Board has considered the Group's cash flow forecasts for the foreseeable future, with the consideration given to the uncertainty in operational performance, Company specific risks and other wider macroeconomic environment risks." — **No forecast period, no sensitivity, no headroom quantification** is given. The phrase "uncertainty in operational performance" is a soft qualification that should be tested against the negative CFO and working-capital absorption already identified.
  - "The Group maintains sufficient liquidity throughout the period to furnish its liabilities as they fall due." — **Assertion only**; no liquidity ratio, current ratio, or undrawn-facility figure. Must be reconciled to Note 20 maturity table and Note 6 cash composition.
  - Market-impact factors cited: (i) "current reduction in the interest rates has not impacted the granting of the 100% home loans in the lower to middle tier of the market" — implies the Group's subsidised/GAP housing demand is rate-insensitive; (ii) "Government committed to the need for dignified housing in the recent budget speech held on 25 February 2026" — **forward-looking policy expectation, not a contracted order**; must not be capitalised into the order book without evidence of awarded tenders; (iii) "geopolitical events currently have no impact on the Group's cash flow forecasts, this will be assessed on an ongoing basis" — **unquantified macro-risk disclaimer**; flag for sensitivity.
  - **Forecast implication**: The going-concern note provides **no hard numbers** to anchor a liquidity forecast. It raises, rather than resolves, the tension between the negative CFO (R−14.8m) and the "sufficient liquidity" assertion. The 25 February 2026 budget-speech reference is a **post-year-end policy signal** that could support FY2027 order intake but is not yet contracted revenue.

- **Note 42 — Events after the reporting year** `[D005.21, p. 76]`:
  - "No events have occurred subsequent to the reporting date that require adjustment to, or disclosure in, the consolidated and separate financial statements." — A **clean subsequent-events representation**. Note the tension: Note 41 cites the **25 February 2026 budget speech** as a going-concern factor, which is a post-year-end event; Note 42 nonetheless asserts no disclosable subsequent events. This is not necessarily contradictory (the budget speech is a market factor, not a transaction affecting the financial statements), but the **asymmetry should be noted**: management treats the budget speech as relevant to going concern yet not as a disclosable subsequent event. No litigation, no dividend declared after year-end, no new borrowings, no impairments, no BDC-related post-year-end adjustments are disclosed. Must be cross-checked against D001 (auditor's subsequent-events review) and D004 (any post-year-end equity movements).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note reference "50"** at the foot of the stated-capital column `[D009, p. 78]`: the stated-capital movements (opening R192,254,895; buyback −R6,662,638; closing R185,592,257) are cross-referenced to **Note 50** (Company notes, D011). The footnote text itself is **not present in this section capture** — only the note number. Verification question raised: confirm in D011 Note 50 the buyback share count, price per share, and confirmation that the entire R6,662,638 was debited to stated capital with no share premium account (see Q168/Q259 carried forward).

- **Dividend qualification** `[D009, p. 78]`: "The Board has approved a dividend on 15 May 2026 of 8.63703 cents per share. In the 2025 financial year the Board approved a dividend of 8.63703 cents per share which was paid in June 2025."
  - This is a **post-year-end dividend declaration** (15 May 2026, after 28 Feb 2026 year-end) — correctly **not accrued** in the FY2026 SOCE. The FY2026 dividend line of R9,879,171 therefore relates to the **FY2025 declared dividend paid in June 2025**, not a FY2026 dividend.
  - **Arithmetic tension**: R9,879,171 ÷ R0.0863703 = **~114.38m shares**, which is materially higher than the year-end 95,380,601 shares and the weighted average 95,742,067 shares. This is a **reconciliation discrepancy** — either the DPS, the total, or the share count is misstated, or the dividend was struck on a different (pre-buyback / pre-scheme) share base. Flagged as a verification question for D011 Note 50 / dividend note.
  - The FY2027 forecast must use the **15 May 2026 declared dividend** (8.63703 cps × current share count) as the FY2027 cash outflow, not the FY2026 SOCE line.

- **"Other comprehensive income – nil"** both years `[D009, p. 78]`: confirms no OCI at Company level; Group OCI still to be confirmed in D003.

- **Footer qualification** `[D009, p. 78]`: "The notes on pages 77 to 88 are an integral part of these consolidated financial statements." — Note the wording says **"consolidated"** even though this is the **Company** SOCE. This is a labelling inconsistency (Company vs consolidated) and reinforces the page-label reconciliation issue (Q10/Q267/Q269 carried forward). Also confirms Company notes run to printed p. 88, not p. 92 as the map suggests.

- **D010 (Statement of cash flows, p. 78)**: The selected evidence contains **no cash-flow statement content** — only the SOCE table and dividend note. The D010 section is effectively **not captured** in this upload. No cash-flow figures can be verified here; all D006/D010 cash-flow questions remain fully open.

# Refer to  note 50 for further details on the related external borrowings which is linked to the Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited Treasury loans. The interest rate charged on the loans to or from Group companies is linked to the rate charged by
the external debt providers. This balance includes the interest accrual as at 28 February 2026.
The treasury loan is subject to JIBAR rates.
The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease after its final publication on 31 December 2026, and the Group is therefore transitioning its JIBAR-linked financial instruments to the
new transaction-based benchmark rate, ZARONIA, which is now published daily by the SARB and required for all new contracts from March 2026; existing contracts will transition using an industry-endorsed
credit adjustment spread to ensure economic neutrality, and the Group does not expect the transition to result in a substantial modification of its financial instruments or to have a material financial impact;
however, this will be continuously assessed as the transition arrangements are agreed with the Group’s lenders.
All loans to/(from) Group companies will be settled within the next 12 months for the current and prior year.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `#` — Note 47, `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 80]`**
- **Text**: "Refer to note 50 for further details on the related external borrowings which is linked to the Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited Treasury loans. The interest rate charged on the loans to or from Group companies is linked to the rate charged by the external debt providers. This balance includes the interest accrual as at 28 February 2026. The treasury loan is subject to JIBAR rates."
- **What it changes**: The parent's R1,308,000,000 Treasury loan to Calgro M3 Developments is **not standalone intercompany funding** — it is the on-lending of external borrowings raised at Company level (Note 50). This means:
  1. The parent's finance cost (R131,638,014) is driven by external debt, and finance income (R124,424,869) is the on-charge to the subsidiary at JIBAR + margin. The **net cost R7,213,145** is effectively the margin spread retained at parent — a structural, recurring item, not a one-off.
  2. The R29,696,888 interest accrual sits inside the R1,337,720,213 receivable; it is non-cash and must be stripped out when forecasting cash interest received.
  3. **Impairment risk**: the receivable is unsecured and repayable on demand, funded by external debt. If the subsidiary's construction cash flows deteriorate (consolidated CFO was R−14.8m per D005), the parent has no security and no disclosed ECL provision. This is a material forecast risk — the parent's solvency is effectively levered to subsidiary performance.
  4. **Covenant linkage**: because the intercompany rate is linked to external debt provider rates, any repricing or covenant breach at external level flows straight through to the parent's net finance cost.

**JIBAR → ZARONIA transition qualification — `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 80]`**
- **Text**: JIBAR ceases after final publication 31 December 2026; Group transitioning JIBAR-linked instruments to ZARONIA (published daily by SARB, required for all new contracts from March 2026); existing contracts transition using industry-endorsed credit adjustment spread to ensure economic neutrality; no substantial modification or material financial impact expected; continuously assessed with lenders.
- **What it changes**: The R1,308,000,000 Treasury loan (and the linked external borrowings in Note 50) will reprice off ZARONIA from 2027. Management asserts economic neutrality, but the **credit adjustment spread is not quantified** — this is a forecast assumption to test. Any spread above JIBAR-equivalent would raise the parent's finance cost and compress the R7.2m net spread. Also flags that Note 50 external borrowings are JIBAR-linked (floating), consistent with Q84's floating-rate exposure concern.

**Note 43 — Significant judgements qualification — `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 79]`**
- **Text**: "management applied estimates and assumptions in determining which investments to classify as subsidiaries. Refer to the investments in subsidiaries note (note 48)."
- **What it changes**: The only Company-level significant judgement is **subsidiary classification** — i.e., control assessment over investments. This is a red flag given the BDC JV→joint-operation reclassification (Q32/Q69/Q241) and procurement companies' negative equity (Q225). The judgement is not quantified here; Note 48 must be checked for carrying values and impairment indicators.

**Note 47 — "All loans to/(from) Group companies will be settled within the next 12 months for the current and prior year." — `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 80]`**
- **What it changes**: This statement **contradicts** the table's own split showing R1,204,720,213 of loans to Group as "to be settled after more than 12 months." This is a direct internal inconsistency — either the maturity classification is wrong or the sentence is boilerplate. It matters for the current/non-current split of the parent's balance sheet and for liquidity forecasting. Flag as a verification question.

**Note 47 — "Repaid" repayment term on the R(59,563,136) prime loan from Calgro M3 Developments — `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 80]`**
- **What it changes**: The loan is labelled "Repaid" yet carries a R59.6m balance (up from R45.3m). The label appears to be a template error; the balance is live and prime-linked. Confirm actual repayment terms.

**Note 44 — no restricted cash / cash-pooling disclosure — `[D011.1, physical PDF p. 79]`**
- **What it changes**: Company cash of R596,645 is presented gross with no overdraft netting or restriction note. Given the parent funds a R1.3bn Treasury loan, the absence of any cash-pooling disclosure is notable — confirm in Note 6 cross-reference and Note 52 whether Company cash is part of a Group cash pool.

48. Investment in subsidiaries
Accounting policy
Investments in subsidiaries are carried at cost less any accumulated impairment.
Significant judgement and sources of estimation uncertainty
Although the Group has a minority shareholding in Belhar Calgro M3 Development Company Proprietary Limited, it does have control, as the Board comprises only of representatives from the Group.
The Group appoints the chairman which has the casting vote. The investment is therefore accounted for as a subsidiary as the Group has control over the relevant activities of the entity.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `#` (p. 81–82)**: *"These companies have been incorporated under the new Companies Act 71 of 2008. The value of the shares are stated at no par value."* `[D011.2, physical PDF p. 82]`
  - **Implication**: Confirms nil-par-value shares for the flagged entities (Calgro M3 Real Estate, Memorial Parks Holding, Rectification Company, Jabulani, Procurement Services, Contractors, Property Sales, CTE Consulting, Memorial Park Bloemfontein, Municipal Memorial Parks). This is a **disclosure-only** note; it does **not** change carrying amounts. However, it flags that several nil-carrying-amount subsidiaries are nonetheless incorporated and potentially trading — relevant to Q225 (procurement negative equity) and Q249 (guarantees). Must verify in D007 Note 21 whether any of these nil-carrying entities carry Group guarantees or performance bonds.

- **Footnote `%` (p. 81–82)**: *"Although Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited only has 49% shareholding in Calgro M3 Procurement Management Proprietary Limited, it has all the voting rights in the Company. 51% of Calgro M3 Procurement Management Proprietary Limited is owned by Calgro M3 Educational Trust, which the Group does not control."* `[D011.2, physical PDF p. 82]`
  - **Implication**: This is a **control-without-majority-ownership** judgement (IFRS 10). The Group consolidates Procurement Management on 100% voting rights despite 49% economic holding. **Critical forecast implication**: the 51% economic interest sits with the Educational Trust (not NCI in the traditional sense — the note says the Group "does not control" the Trust's 51%, yet consolidates the company). This creates a **consolidation vs attribution tension**: if the Trust's 51% is not NCI, where does its economic share go? Must verify in D007 Note 39 (NCI reconciliation) and D004 (NCI attribution) whether any NCI is recognised for Procurement Management. Also relevant to Q225 (negative equity) — if losses are 100% consolidated but only 49% economically owned, the Group may be absorbing losses attributable to the Trust.

- **Footnote `$` (p. 82)**: *"Although Calgro M3 Land Proprietary Limited only has 49% shareholding in Belhar Calgro M3 Development Company Proprietary, Calgro M3 Land Proprietary Limited maintains 100% control of the Board and decision making."* `[D011.2, physical PDF p. 82]`
  - **Implication**: Confirms **BDC is consolidated as a subsidiary** on board-control grounds despite 49% economic holding. This directly **contradicts** the joint-operation treatment referenced in Q32/Q69/Q241. **Critical forecast implication**: if BDC is a subsidiary (per Note 48), the R19,252,380 "direct debit to retained income" and joint-operation transition (Q32/Q69) are inconsistent with this note — either the classification changed during the year (JV→joint operation→subsidiary?) or the notes are internally inconsistent. Must verify in D007 Note 39 and D004. Also: 51% economic interest in BDC sits outside the Group — confirm NCI recognition (Q224: Belhar 51%-owned but no NCI due to preferential profit right).

- **Significant judgement paragraph (p. 81)**: *"Although the Group has a minority shareholding in Belhar Calgro M3 Development Company Proprietary Limited, it does have control, as the Board comprises only of representatives from the Group. The Group appoints the chairman which has the casting vote."* `[D011.2, physical PDF p. 81]`
  - **Implication**: This is the **IFRS 10 control judgement** for BDC. It is a **key judgement** (consistent with Note 43 p. 79 flag per Q261). The casting-vote mechanism is the sole basis for control — if the shareholders' agreement changes (e.g., deadlock resolution, reserved matters), control could be lost. **Forecast implication**: BDC consolidation is judgement-dependent; a change in the shareholders' agreement could trigger deconsolidation. Must verify in D001 (auditor KAM) and D007 Note 39.

- **Trust paragraph (p. 82)**: *"On 12 February 2016, the Company founded the Calgro M3 Educational Benefit Trust and the Calgro M3 Employee Benefit Trust. In accordance with the principles of IFRS Accounting Standards, both the trusts are controlled by the Company and are considered to be agents of the Company. There is no financial impact on transactions between the Company and the trusts."* `[D011.2, physical PDF p. 82]`
  - **Implication**: The **Educational Benefit Trust** (which owns 51% of Procurement Management) is itself **controlled by the Company as an agent**. This resolves the footnote `%` tension: the Trust's 51% is effectively **not** a third-party NCI — it is an agent of the Group. **Forecast implication**: Procurement Management is 100% consolidated with **no NCI** (the Trust is an agent). This is consistent with Q225 (NCI −R12,408 is small). Must verify in D007 Note 39 that no NCI is attributed to Procurement Management. Also: "no financial impact" — confirm no SBP or trust expense flows through the Company.

- **Missing footnote text**: The table on p. 81 contains a marker `Calgro M3 Procurement Management Proprietary Limited#%` — the `#` and `%` definitions are present on p. 82. **No missing footnote text identified** in this capture. However, the `*` marker on `CTE Consulting Proprietary Limited*[^#]` (p. 82) has **no corresponding `*` definition** in the supplied evidence — **footnote text is missing from this section capture**. Must verify the `*` definition in D011.2 continuation (p. 83+) or D011.3.

- **Arithmetic check**: Direct investment R291,008,869 (p. 81) + indirect R493,403,884 (p. 82) = **R784,412,753** total portfolio carrying amount. Note 48 does **not** present a total row reconciling to the parent's R291,008,869 — the R493,403,884 is the *indirect* portfolio (subsidiaries of subsidiaries), which is **not** carried at the parent level. **Flag**: the R493,403,884 indirect total includes Fleurhof Ext 2 R243,000,000 and Calgro M3 Land R188,146,234 — these are carried at the *subsidiary* level, not the parent. Confirm no double-counting in the parent's R291,008,869. Also: R493,403,884 total — check arithmetic: 188,146,234 + 100 + 100 + 243,000,000 + 100 + 49 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 1,002 + 3,000,000 + 4,500,100 + 54,755,699 = **R493,403,884** ✓ (arithmetic reconciles).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `^` (p.85) — Interest accrual reclassification:**
> "Accrued interest has been reclassified to borrowings in the current financial year, as a better representation of the outstanding debt balance. The prior year interest accrual remains unchanged within trade and other payables (refer to note 49)."

- **What it changes**: The 2026 borrowings balance of R1,330,291,294 **includes R29,696,888 of accrued interest** that in 2025 sat in trade and other payables. This means:
  - The 2026 vs 2025 borrowings comparison is **not like-for-like**: 2025 closing R836,285,282 excludes the R17,221,670 accrual (which sat in payables), while 2026 closing includes R29,696,888. On a consistent basis, 2025 borrowings would be ~R853,506,952.
  - The cash flow reconciliation (p.86) treats the R12,475,218 increase in accrual as a **non-cash item**, correctly.
  - **Verification needed**: Note 49 (Company trade and other payables) must confirm the prior-year accrual of R17,221,670 is still embedded there, and that the 2026 payables no longer contain it. This affects the working-capital forecast and the Net Debt definition (does Net Debt include the R29.7m accrual?).

**Footnote `*` (p.85) — Transaction cost amortisation:**
> "The transaction costs are amortised over the life of the facilities. It is expected that these costs will be fully amortised when the facilities are settled."

- **What it changes**: Transaction cost amortisation of R7,405,594 (2025: R3,936,388) is a **non-cash finance cost** embedded in the R1,330,291,294 carrying amount. The p.86 reconciliation shows net transaction costs amortised R3,469,206 and amortised expense through SoCI R438,960, with transaction costs paid R3,030,246. The R7,405,594 amortisation vs R3,469,206 net amortised in the cash flow reconciliation is a **reconciliation discrepancy** — the difference (~R3.9m) needs explanation (possibly capitalised vs expensed split, or opening vs closing balance treatment). This matters for forecasting finance costs: the non-cash amortisation component will decline as facilities are settled.

**Footnote `%` (p.85) — Repayment terms:**
> "The NHFC loan is repayable in nine instalments, starting from May 2026. Prescient is repayable in one instalment in October 2027. ABSA 1 is repayable in four equal instalments, starting from September 2027. ABSA 2 is repayable in eight instalments, starting from March 2028. Stanlib is repayable in eight equal instalments, starting from September 2028."

- **What it changes**: This is the **maturity profile for forecasting debt repayment cash flows**:
  - NHFC R215,000,000 ÷ 9 ≈ **R23.9m per instalment from May 2026** (i.e., FY2027 has ~8 instalments = ~R191m, FY2028 has 1 = ~R24m).
  - Prescient R100,000,000 bullet **Oct 2027** (FY2028).
  - ABSA 1 R155,000,000 ÷ 4 = **R38.75m per instalment from Sept 2027** (FY2028–FY2031).
  - ABSA 2 R200,000,000 ÷ 8 = **R25m per instalment from March 2028** (FY2029–FY2036).
  - Stanlib R250,000,000 ÷ 8 = **R31.25m per instalment from Sept 2028** (FY2029–FY2036).
  - **Critical**: The DMTN floating rate notes (CGR 52–62) have **no stated repayment terms** in the footnote — they are presumably bullet repayments at expiry. CGR 52 (R50m) and CGR 53 (R40m) expire **30 June 2026 and 28 February 2026** respectively — both within FY2027. CGR 55 and CGR 56 (R50m + R33m) expire **2 October 2026** — also FY2027. This means **~R173m of DMTN notes mature in FY2027** and must be refinanced or repaid. This is a major refinancing risk not flagged in the narrative.

**Qualification — "All borrowings are unsecured" (p.85):**
- **What it changes**: No security is pledged, so there is **no asset encumbrance** but also **no secured lending headroom**. The R1,308,000,000 gross facilities are all unsecured, relying on covenant compliance and lender relationships. This is consistent with the consolidated Note 20 disclosure (Q176) but raises the stakes on covenant headroom — if covenants are breached, lenders could demand repayment without security to fall back on.

**Qualification — "All floating rate notes listed on the DMTN listed debt programme were in compliance with the programme memorandum" (p.85):**
- **What it changes**: This is a **compliance assertion, not a covenant headroom disclosure**. The DMTN programme memorandum typically contains financial covenants (e.g., Net Debt/EBITDA, interest cover, minimum NAV). The report does **not** disclose the covenant ratios, the actual ratios achieved, or the headroom. This is a material gap for forecasting — a covenant breach could trigger cross-default across all facilities.

**Qualification — JIBAR→ZARONIA transition (p.85):**
- **What it changes**: All borrowings (except NHFC) are JIBAR-linked. JIBAR ceases **31 December 2026**. The Group expects no material impact, but the **credit adjustment spread is not quantified**. For forecasting, the repricing impact on finance costs is unknown — a 25bp spread widening on R1,093m of JIBAR debt (R1,308m less NHFC R215m) would cost ~R2.7m p.a.

**Qualification — "The Directors have not breached the requirements of the Company's Memorandum of Incorporation in terms of their borrowing powers" (p.86):**
- **What it changes**: This confirms the **borrowing powers limit** in the MOI has not been exceeded. It does **not** confirm covenant compliance — that is a separate matter. The MOI borrowing power limit is not quantified.

**NHFC loan transfer (p.86):**
> "NHFC loan transferred from Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited (non-cash item) (107 500 000)"

- **What it changes**: The R107,500,000 NHFC loan was **moved from subsidiary to parent** during the year as a non-cash transaction. This explains part of the R50,000,001 gap between Company and consolidated borrowings (Q258) — the parent now carries the NHFC facility. It also means the **consolidated borrowings are unchanged** by this transfer (it's an intra-group reallocation), but the **parent's balance sheet grosses up** by R107.5m. For forecasting, the parent's finance cost will now include NHFC interest that previously sat at subsidiary level.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 58 footnote `*`** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: *"This relates to the dividend received (note 52) from Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company."* — This is the critical qualification: the entire (39.40%) non-taxable adjustment and the resulting negative ETR of (10.18%) is driven by the R12.0m intercompany dividend. **Implication**: the parent's tax credit is not a sustainable operating tax benefit — it is a function of subsidiary dividend policy. If the subsidiary stops paying dividends, the parent's ETR reverts toward 27% + non-deductibles. Also note the footnote cross-references **note 52** for the dividend — but Note 52 in this capture is Borrowings (p.85–86), not a dividend note. **This is a note-numbering contradiction** (see new Q330). The footnote also confirms Calgro M3 Developments is a **wholly owned** subsidiary — relevant to Q296/Q308 (no NCI at that subsidiary).

- **Note 58 reconciliation structure** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: The reconciliation shows "Items non-deductible for tax purposes 2.22%" and "Non-deductible items considered partial in nature 2.22%" as duplicate rows, and "Items non-taxable for tax purposes (39.40%)" and "Exempt income* (39.40%)" as duplicate rows. **Implication**: the reconciliation is presented with duplicated/mislabelled rows (same issue flagged in Q226 at Group level). The arithmetic 27.00% + 2.22% − 39.40% = −10.18% ✓ ties, but the presentation is confusing and the "partial in nature" descriptor is unexplained — verify in D007 Note 31 whether the Group reconciliation has the same duplication.

- **Note 59 arithmetic check** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: PBT 8,223,686 − finance income 124,424,869 + finance cost 131,638,014 − receivables 1,499 − payables 1,927,395 = **13,507,937** ✓ ties to printed CFO. **However**, the reconciliation contains **no line for the R12,000,000 dividend received** (Note 54) — a dividend received is a cash inflow and is already in PBT via Other income, so no adjustment is needed for cash purposes; but it is **not** an operating cash flow under IAS 7 (dividends received are investing or operating depending on policy). **Implication**: the R13.5m "cash generated from operations" is inflated by the R12.0m dividend — underlying operating cash generation at parent is only ~R1.5m. This is a material qualification for forecasting parent standalone cash.

- **Note 60 arithmetic discrepancy** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: Opening R77,915; current tax for the year nil; closing R(116,159); printed tax paid R(38,244). Arithmetic: 77,915 − 0 − (−116,159) = **194,074**, not 38,244. **The three-line reconciliation does not tie to the printed R(38,244).** This is a **mathematical tension flagged** — either a missing line (e.g., a payment/receipt not shown) or a sign/presentation error. Must be verified against the full Note 60 in D011.5 continuation (see new Q329).

- **Note 53 revenue recognition qualification** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 86]`: *"Revenue only consists of management fees... recognised over time as the services are performed on a monthly basis, which coincides with the billing which also occurs on a monthly basis in arrears."* — **Implication**: no contract asset/liability arises at parent level (billing = recognition timing), so parent revenue is a clean cash-like recharge. The R15,880,000 is a **cost-recharge/management fee** from subsidiary — it is an intercompany item that eliminates on consolidation; it should **not** be forecast as external revenue.

- **Note 54 dividend qualification** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 86]`: Other income is **entirely** a dividend from Calgro M3 Developments (R12.0m vs R5.0m). **Implication**: parent "Other income" is non-operating, non-recurring in nature (depends on subsidiary distributable reserves and board declaration), and eliminates on consolidation. Do not capitalise into parent earnings forecast.

- **Note 55 audit fee step-up** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 86]`: Auditor's remuneration – audit R4,640,422 (2025: nil); non-audit R61,500 (2025: nil). **Implication**: the parent did not bear audit fees in 2025 (presumably borne by subsidiary or Group); the 2026 step-up of R4.7m is a structural reallocation, likely recurring. Advertising R1,007,001 (2025: nil) is new — verify recurrence.

- **Note 56/57 finance income/cost composition** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: Finance income includes Bank R3,311,554 + SARS R3,241 + Other R8,389 — small non-Group items. Finance cost includes Bank nil (2025: R25,774) — no bank overdraft cost in 2026. **Implication**: parent is a pure intercompany treasury conduit; external borrowings interest R122,575,248 sits at parent, funded by on-lending to subsidiary (interest income R121,101,685) — the parent runs a **negative carry of ~R1.5m** on the intercompany on-lending (R122.6m cost vs R121.1m income), plus R9.1m cost on Group loans-from. This negative carry is structural and must be forecast.

- **Note 58 cross-reference to "note 52" for dividend** `[D011.5, physical PDF p. 87]`: As noted, Note 52 in this capture is Borrowings — **note-numbering contradiction** (new Q330).

  63. Risk management                                    
     Financial risk management                           
     Due to the fact that the Company is a holding company, the most significant risks the Company
     is exposed to are market risk (via cash flow interest rate), credit risk and liquidity risk.
     (i) Market risk (cash flow interest rate risk)      
         The Company has interest-bearing loans to and from Group companies and external
         borrowings. The loans issued at variable rates expose the Company to cash flow interest
         rate risk.                                      
                                                         
         The Group Executive Committee monitors the interest of the Company on a cash basis.
         Refer to the finance income ( note 56) and finance cost ( note 57) notes for the interest
         received/paid.                                  
         The impact on post-tax profit of a 2% shift in the interest rate would be a maximum
         increase/decrease of:                           
                                                         
                                          2026     2025  
         2% increase/(decrease) on finance charges on    
         interest-bearing borrowings   21 010 062 13 638 639
         2% increase/(decrease) on finance income on     
         interest-bearing assets       19 530 715 12 267 577
                                                         
         A 2% shift is considered appropriate by management taking into account the current
         economic environment in which the Group operates.
                                                         
     (ii) Credit risk                                    
         Credit risk consists mainly of loans to Group companies, cash deposits and cash
         equivalents.                                    
         The Company only deposits cash with major banks with a minimum rating of “BB” and
         limits the exposure to any one counter party. No credit risk is associated to other
         receivables as this consists of prepayments.    
         The Company considers its credit risk relating to the loans owing by Group companies on
         a case by case basis. Any credit risk related to loans to Group companies is mitigated by
         the fact that management has insight into the financial position of the Group companies
         as a result of the relationship.                

--- Section D011.6 | [AFS] physical page 89 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 61,62,63,64,65,66 ---
                                                       
                                                       
      The treasury loans, including inter-company interest accruals with Calgro M3
      Developments Proprietary Limited (refer to note 45) are directly linked to the
      repayment of the borrowings and its maturity profile (refer to note 50). In line with the
      DMTN listed programme, Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited guarantees the
      repayment of the listed debt programme. Based on cash flow forecasts and maturity
      analysis performed, sufficient cash flow will be available to settle the treasury loan, and
      in turn the borrowings. As Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited is solvent and
      liquid, no expected credit loss provision was recognised on the treasury loan as there
      was no probability of default.                   
      For loans to Group companies and cash and cash equivalents, the maximum exposure to
      credit risk is limited to what is disclosed in the statement of financial position.
  (iii) Liquidity risk                                 
      Prudent liquidity risk management implies maintaining sufficient cash, as well as the
      availability of funding through an adequate amount of committed credit facilities.
                                                       
      Due to the dynamic nature of the underlying businesses, the Executive Committee
      maintains flexibility in funding by maintaining availability under committed credit lines.
      The Company manages liquidity risk by monitoring forecasted cash flows.
                                                       
      The Company strives to match the maturity profile of borrowings with expected cash flows
      from the development projects.                   
      A specific liquidity risk associated with the Company is the raising of loans at specified
      dates of repayment, against delivery of construction projects that have the same maturity
      profile.                                         
                                                       
      The related cash inflows from these construction projects are, however, uncertain and
      dependent on factors not under the control of the Company.
      The financial liabilities to be settled within one year will be funded by cash and cash
      equivalents as well as the realisation of the treasury loans.
                                                       
      The table below analyses the Company’s financial liabilities into relevant maturity based
      on the remaining year at the reporting year date to the contractual maturity date.
      The amounts disclosed in the table are the contractual undiscounted cash flows which
      include future interest payable. Balances due within 12 months equal their carrying
      balances as the impact of discounting is not significant.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` — Note 62 p.88 (Borrowings fair value):**
> "* Included in this balance are the borrowings relating to the DMTN listed debt programme where the fair value is based on quoted prices on the Bond Exchange. Term loans included in this balance are carried at amortised cost which approximates the fair value, when excluding transaction cost amortised."

- **What it changes**: The R1,113,961,370 "fair value" column for borrowings is a **mixed measurement** — DMTN at quoted market price (Level 1), term loans at amortised cost approximating fair value *excluding* transaction cost amortisation. This means the R1,113,961,370 is **not** directly comparable to the Note 52 carrying amount of R1,330,291,294. The difference of R216,329,924 likely comprises (a) transaction costs not yet amortised and (b) the fair-value discount on DMTN (quoted price below par). **Must verify**: reconcile Note 52 carrying R1,330,291,294 → Note 62 fair value R1,113,961,370; confirm DMTN quoted price vs par; confirm transaction cost balance.

**Note 63 p.89 — Credit risk qualification (treasury loan to Calgro M3 Developments):**
> "The treasury loans, including inter-company interest accruals with Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited (refer to note 45) are directly linked to the repayment of the borrowings and its maturity profile (refer to note 50). In line with the DMTN listed programme, Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited guarantees the repayment of the listed debt programme. Based on cash flow forecasts and maturity analysis performed, sufficient cash flow will be available to settle the treasury loan, and in turn the borrowings. As Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited is solvent and liquid, no expected credit loss provision was recognised on the treasury loan as there was no probability of default."

- **What it changes**: This is a **critical structural disclosure**. The parent's R1,337,720,213 loans to Group companies (Note 62 p.88) are almost entirely to Calgro M3 Developments, and the parent's ability to repay its R1,330,291,294 borrowings depends on Calgro M3 Developments repaying the treasury loan. The DMTN is **guaranteed by Calgro M3 Developments** — so the "unsecured" label in Note 52 is misleading: the DMTN has a subsidiary guarantee. **No ECL provision** is recognised on the treasury loan because Calgro M3 Developments is "solvent and liquid" — this is a management assertion, not an audited fact. **Must verify**: Calgro M3 Developments' standalone solvency/liquidity (NAV, current ratio, cash flow); the legal enforceability of the guarantee; whether the guarantee is disclosed as a contingent liability in the consolidated financials (Note 21).

**Note 63 p.89 — Liquidity risk qualification:**
> "The related cash inflows from these construction projects are, however, uncertain and dependent on factors not under the control of the Company."

- **What it changes**: Management explicitly acknowledges that the parent's liquidity depends on **uncertain construction project cash inflows** — a candid admission of cash-flow risk. Combined with the going-concern reliance on subsidiary support (Note 65), this is a material qualification. **Must verify**: D001 auditor's going-concern conclusion; whether an Emphasis of Matter or Material Uncertainty paragraph is included.

**Note 63 p.90 — Liquidity table qualification:**
> "The above amounts will be repaid by utilising cash generated from operations, available cash, working capital facilities and the refinancing of borrowings."

- **What it changes**: The R1,747,933,935 undiscounted borrowings (including future interest) will be repaid via **refinancing** — i.e., the parent is reliant on rolling over debt. With CFO negative at Group level (R−14.8m per Q38), "cash generated from operations" is not a credible repayment source. **Must verify**: committed refinancing facilities; DMTN rollover confirmation; covenant compliance certificates.

**Note 65 p.90 — Going concern qualification:**
> "The Company has received commitment from Calgro M3 Developments Proprietary Limited, its main trading subsidiary who will provide additional liquidity to the entity, which will enable Calgro M3 Holdings Limited to pay its liabilities as they fall due."

- **What it changes**: The parent's going-concern basis is **explicitly dependent on a subsidiary commitment**. This is a material uncertainty that should be tested by the auditor. The word "commitment" is not defined — it could be a board resolution, a letter of support, or an informal undertaking. **Must verify**: D001 auditor's treatment; whether the commitment is a formal, enforceable letter of support; quantum and duration.

**Note 66 p.90 — Subsequent events:**
> "No events have occurred subsequent to the reporting date that require adjustment to, or disclosure in, the Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements to be taken into account."

- **What it changes**: Clean representation. But note the DMTN maturities (CGR 52 R50m exp 30 Jun 2026, CGR 53 R40m exp 28 Feb 2026) fall **after** year-end — if these were not refinanced before the audit report date, they would be a subsequent event. The clean statement implies they were either repaid or refinanced before the report date. **Must verify**: D001 report date; DMTN refinancing confirmation.

**Note 61 p.88 — Related party table (no footnote, but structural anomaly):**
- The table shows only **Calgro M3 Developments** as a related party — management fees R15,880,000 (2025: R8,860,000), finance income R121,101,685 (2025: R98,959,324), finance costs R9,062,766 (2025: R4,933,996). No other subsidiaries appear. This is surprising given Note 48 lists numerous subsidiaries. **Must verify**: whether other subsidiaries had nil transactions or were omitted; whether the R121.1m finance income reconciles to Note 56 (Q325).
